title: electron-builder macOS target is `dir` on arm64 only — no installable artifact and no Intel build
summary: The mac target produces an unpacked directory for arm64 only, while a dmg config block and a GitHub publish provider are configured and the release workflow searches for .dmg/.zip artifacts.
evidence: apps/core-app/electron-builder.yml:120-122 `target:\n    - target: dir\n      arch: arm64` with :128 an empty `dmg:` block and :163-166 `publish: provider: github`. .github/workflows/build-and-release.yml:563 `DMG_COUNT=$(find apps/core-app/dist -name "*.dmg" -type f ...)` and :565 `ZIP_COUNT=$(find apps/core-app/dist -name "*.zip" ...)`. apps/core-app/scripts/build-target.js:501 `const defaultArch = normalizedTarget === 'mac' ? 'arm64' : 'x64'` — no target override is injected.
failure_scenario: `pnpm core:build:release:mac` (and the macOS release job) emit only `dist/mac-arm64/tuff.app`. DMG_COUNT and ZIP_COUNT are both 0, so the release publishes no macOS installer, and Intel (x64) Macs get no build at all. The `dmg:` config block and the `publish: github` provider are inert.
recommendation: Set the mac target to `dmg`/`zip` and add an x64 (or universal) arch entry, or delete the dmg block and document that macOS is arm64-unpacked-only.

title: tuffex build uses `node --loader ts-node/esm`, an experimental flag Node warns may be removed
summary: The component library build depends on the deprecated ESM loader hook flag instead of the supported module.register() entry point.
evidence: packages/tuffex/package.json:45 `"build": "node --loader ts-node/esm ./node_modules/gulp/bin/gulp.js -f packages/script/build/index.ts"`. Running the same flag on the repo's pinned Node (24.18.0, .node-version) prints: `ExperimentalWarning: '--experimental-loader' may be removed in the future; instead use register(): --import 'data:text/javascript,import { register } from "node:module"; ...'` plus `[DEP0180] DeprecationWarning: fs.Stats constructor is deprecated.` from ts-node itself.
failure_scenario: Once Node drops the loader-hook flag, `pnpm tuffex:build` fails with an unknown-option error. Every downstream build depends on it: apps/core-app's `typecheck:web` script (apps/core-app/package.json:17) and apps/nexus's `build` script both invoke `pnpm -F @talex-touch/tuffex run build` first, so the whole repo's typecheck and site build go down together.
recommendation: Switch to `node --import ./register-ts-node.mjs` using module.register(), or run the gulpfile through tsx/esno (esno is already a devDependency).

title: @talex-touch/utils publishes raw TypeScript with no types field, exports map, or build step
summary: `main`/`module` both point at `index.ts` and there is no `types`, no `exports` map, and no build script. The published tarball in-tree contains 295 `.ts` files and 2 `.js` files, so Node cannot load the package at all.
evidence:
"main": "index.ts",
  "module": "./index.ts",
failure_scenario: An external plugin developer runs `npm i @talex-touch/utils` and writes `require('@talex-touch/utils')` in a plain Node prelude, or `import { TuffInputType } from '@talex-touch/utils/transport'` in a bundler that does not transpile `node_modules`. Node resolves `index.ts` and fails with `SyntaxError: Unexpected token 'export'`; the subpath has no `index.js` to resolve at all.
recommendation: Add a build (tsup/tsc) emitting `dist/*.js` + `.d.ts`, and declare `types`, `exports` subpaths, and a `prepublishOnly` script.

title: Unauthenticated telemetry endpoint accepts an attacker-chosen userId
summary: /api/telemetry/record (and /api/telemetry/batch line 43) has no auth guard -- only IP rate limiting -- yet writes the client-supplied userId verbatim into telemetry_events.user_id and uses it as the platform-governance actorId.
evidence:
await recordTelemetryEvent(event, {
    eventType,
    userId: userId || undefined,
    clientId: clientId || undefined,
failure_scenario: An unauthenticated attacker POSTs {"eventType":"visit","userId":"<victim-user-id>","metadata":{...}} to /api/telemetry/record. recordTelemetryEvent binds it to user_id (telemetryStore.ts:245) and derives actorId (line 229) for recordPlatformGovernanceEvent. The victim then sees forged activity in GET /api/dashboard/telemetry/me, admin COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) dashboards are inflated, and governance/abuse attribution points at the victim.
recommendation: Ignore any client-supplied userId -- resolve it from getOptionalAuth(event) and store client-supplied identifiers only in the anonymous client_id/device_fingerprint columns.

title: English locale missing 4 capability-test keys; en-US defines them under the wrong namespace
summary: CapabilityTestInput.vue reads settings.intelligence.userMessageLabel / userMessagePlaceholder / promptVariablesLabel / promptVariablesPlaceholder. zh-CN.json defines all four under settings.intelligence, but en-US.json defines them under settings.settingAISDK instead, so the English lookup misses.
evidence: <label class="input-label">{{ t('settings.intelligence.userMessageLabel') }}</label>  — en-US.json has settings.settingAISDK.userMessageLabel = "User message" and settings.intelligence.userMessageLabel = undefined; zh-CN.json has settings.intelligence.userMessageLabel = "用户消息"
failure_scenario: A user running the app in English opens Settings > Intelligence > capability test panel. The two field labels and both textarea placeholders render as the literal dot-paths 'settings.intelligence.userMessageLabel' and 'settings.intelligence.promptVariablesPlaceholder' instead of readable text, so they cannot tell which box takes the user message and which takes prompt variables. Chinese users see correct text, hiding the bug from zh-first testing.
recommendation: Move the four keys in en-US.json from settings.settingAISDK to settings.intelligence (or repoint the component at settingAISDK) so both locales resolve.

title: ErrorLogViewer references 20 download.* i18n keys that exist in neither locale file
summary: Nearly every visible string in the download error-log viewer resolves to a key absent from both en-US.json and zh-CN.json. en-US.json has a download namespace with 141 keys, but none of these 20 are among them.
evidence: {{ t('download.clear_logs') }} ... <TuffSelectItem :label="t('download.last_50_lines')" :value="50" /> — missing from BOTH locales: download.no_logs, download.load_logs_failed, download.logs_cleared, download.clear_logs_failed, download.no_logs_to_download, download.logs_downloaded, download.error_logs, download.clear_logs, download.last_50_lines, download.last_100_lines, download.last_500_lines, download.all_logs, download.total_errors, download.network_errors, download.timeout_errors, download.disk_errors, download.download_logs, download.clear_logs_confirm_title, download.clear_logs_confirm_message, download.view_logs
failure_scenario: Any user in any locale who opens the download error log sees the panel title, the four log-length dropdown options, the four error-count stat labels and both action buttons rendered as raw dot-paths ('download.last_50_lines'). The dropdown becomes unusable because all four options look like near-identical key strings.
recommendation: Add the 20 download.* keys to both en-US.json and zh-CN.json.

title: MigrationProgress renders raw keys: download.migration.* and common.yes/no/retry are undefined
summary: The download migration progress panel references 11 keys missing from both locales. common.yes, common.no and common.retry do not exist — the common namespace only contains cancel, save, confirm, delete, edit, add, remove, close, open, content, capsLock, refresh, loading, error, success, warning, info, seconds, minutes, hours, import, comingSoon.
evidence: {{ result?.migratedConfig ? t('common.yes') : t('common.no') }} — missing from BOTH locales: common.yes, common.no, common.retry, download.migration.title, download.migration.subtitle, download.migration.tasks, download.migration.history, download.migration.config, download.migration.duration, download.migration.errors, download.migration.pleaseWait
failure_scenario: A user upgrading the app sees the data-migration dialog. The boolean result rows read 'common.yes' / 'common.no' rather than Yes/No, so they cannot tell whether their config and history actually migrated, and the retry button is labelled 'common.retry'.
recommendation: Add the 11 keys to both locale files; common.yes/no/retry are generic and likely needed elsewhere.

title: IntelligencePromptSelector references 8 intelligence.* keys missing from both locales
summary: The prompt-selection dropdown labels every group header, empty state and action with keys that resolve in neither en-US.json nor zh-CN.json. An intelligence root namespace does exist, so these are genuinely absent rather than a namespace-root problem.
evidence: :aria-label="t('intelligence.managePrompts')" (line 109) — missing from BOTH locales: intelligence.managePrompts (109), intelligence.selectPrompt (121), intelligence.builtinPrompts (133), intelligence.builtin (149), intelligence.customPrompts (158), intelligence.custom (174), intelligence.createNewPrompt (180), intelligence.promptSelectedHint (204)
failure_scenario: Any user picking a prompt for an AI capability sees the selector's placeholder, both option-group headings ('intelligence.builtinPrompts' / 'intelligence.customPrompts') and the create action rendered as dot-paths, making it impossible to distinguish built-in from custom prompts. Line 109 feeds aria-label directly, so a screen-reader user hears the manage-prompts control announced as the literal string 'intelligence.managePrompts'.
recommendation: Add the 8 intelligence.* keys to both locale files.

title: Every plugin card's action button renders the raw key 'base.details'
summary: PluginCard's primary button uses $t('base.details'), but the base namespace in en-US.json contains only last_step, step and touchCaptcha. The key is absent from both locales.
evidence: {{ $t('base.details') }}
failure_scenario: Every user browsing the plugin list sees the call-to-action on each plugin card labelled 'base.details' instead of 'Details'. This repeats once per installed plugin, so the whole grid looks broken.
recommendation: Add base.details to both locale files, or reuse an existing details/view key.

title: Window settings 'start silent' row shows raw keys; settings.window.startSilent undefined in both locales
summary: settings.window exists in en-US.json with groupTitle, groupDesc, closeToTray, closeToTrayDesc, startMinimized, startMinimizedDesc, autoStart, autoStartDesc — but not startSilent or startSilentDesc, which SettingWindow.vue references.
evidence: t('settings.window.startSilent') (line 163) and t('settings.window.startSilentDesc') (line 164) — neither key exists in en-US.json or zh-CN.json
failure_scenario: A user opening Settings > Window sees one toggle row whose title reads 'settings.window.startSilent' and whose description reads 'settings.window.startSilentDesc'. They have no way to know what the switch controls before flipping it.
recommendation: Add settings.window.startSilent and startSilentDesc to both locale files.

title: Download history durations render raw keys although common.seconds/minutes/hours already exist
summary: HistoryCard formats elapsed time with download.seconds / download.minutes / download.hours. Those three keys are missing from both locales, while the equivalents common.seconds, common.minutes and common.hours are present in both.
evidence: t('download.seconds') (line 116), t('download.minutes') (120), t('download.hours') (124) — absent from both locale files; en-US.json common namespace does contain 'seconds', 'minutes', 'hours'
failure_scenario: A user reviewing download history sees each entry's duration rendered as e.g. '42 download.seconds' instead of '42 seconds', in every locale.
recommendation: Point the component at the existing common.seconds/minutes/hours keys.

title: User profile dialog falls back to hardcoded Chinese for 5 keys missing from both locales
summary: Five t(key, default) calls in the account dialog supply Chinese literals as the default message, and none of the five keys exist in en-US.json or zh-CN.json, so the Chinese default is what actually renders in every locale.
evidence: <template #name>{{ t('userProfile.overview', '概览') }}</template> — missing from BOTH locales: userProfile.overview ('概览'), userProfile.security ('安全与登录'), userProfile.securityActions ('登录与安全选项'), settingUser.syncSecurity ('同步安全'), settingUser.stepUp ('二次验证')
failure_scenario: An English-locale user opens their account/profile dialog and sees Chinese section names ('概览', '安全与登录') mixed into an otherwise English UI. Because the fallback masks the missing key, no missing-translation warning surfaces.
recommendation: Add the 5 keys to both locale files with proper English and Chinese values.

title: File index failure dialog is entirely hardcoded Chinese, bypassing i18n
summary: Every user-facing string in this dialog — title, error message, disclosure summary, both action buttons and the checkbox label — is a Chinese literal in the template with no t() call anywhere in the file.
evidence:
title="文件索引初始化失败" ...

文件索引初始化失败，可能导致搜索功能无法正常使用。

... 查看错误详情 ... {{ rebuilding ? '重建中...' : '重新建立索引' }} ... 稍后处理 ... 不再提醒
failure_scenario: An English-locale user whose file index fails to build gets a fully Chinese modal explaining that search is broken and offering a rebuild. They cannot read the explanation or tell the 'rebuild' button from the 'later' button, so they are likely to dismiss a recoverable failure.
recommendation: Extract all six strings into both locale files and render via t().

title: WidgetFrame error and status text is hardcoded Chinese
summary: The widget host's failure and loading states return Chinese string literals from computed properties, and the error title in the template is a Chinese literal, with no i18n indirection.
evidence:
if (widgetFailure.value) return 'Widget 编译失败' if (rendererState.value === 'loading') return 'Widget 加载中' if (!props.rendererId) return 'Widget renderer 缺失' return 'Widget renderer 未注册' (lines 112-115); if (!props.rendererId) return '缺少 rendererId' (119);
Widget 渲染失败
(413)
failure_scenario: An English-locale user whose plugin widget fails to compile sees 'Widget 渲染失败' / 'Widget 编译失败' in the result panel and cannot tell a compile error from a missing-renderer error, which blocks self-diagnosis of a broken plugin.
recommendation: Move the five status strings and the error title into both locale files.

title: CoreBox preview history panel hardcodes Chinese labels and states
summary: The history panel's heading, count summary, loading state and empty state are all Chinese literals in the template with no t() usage.
evidence:
最近处理 (55); 共 {{ items.length }} 条 (56);
加载中...
(60);
暂无记录
(61)
failure_scenario: An English-locale user opening the CoreBox preview history sees a Chinese heading and, when the list is empty, a Chinese empty-state ('暂无记录') that they cannot distinguish from an error.
recommendation: Extract the four strings into both locale files; the count line needs a pluralizable interpolated key.

title: CoreBox preview result card hardcodes Chinese action and fallback labels
summary: The result card's copy action, history action and default result label are Chinese literals, including a JS fallback used when the payload supplies no label.
evidence: 复制结果 (line 80); 最近处理 (84); {{ resolvedPayload?.primaryLabel || '结果' }} (91)
failure_scenario: An English-locale user running a CoreBox action sees the copy button labelled '复制结果' and, for any plugin that omits primaryLabel, the result section headed '结果'.
recommendation: Route the three strings through t() with entries in both locale files.

title: Division box header window controls use hardcoded Chinese tooltips and alt text
summary: The three window-control buttons in the detached CoreBox header carry Chinese title attributes and Chinese TuffIcon alt text, hardcoded in the template.
evidence: <button type="button" class="control-btn" title="透明度" @click="handleOpacity"> ... <TuffIcon :icon="{ type: 'class', value: opacityIcon }" alt="透明度" :size="18" /> (111-112); title="调试" / alt="调试" (114-115); title="置顶" / alt="置顶" (121,126)
failure_scenario: An English-locale user hovering the detached CoreBox window controls gets Chinese tooltips, and an English screen-reader user hears the icons announced as '透明度' / '调试' / '置顶', so the only accessible names for these three controls are in the wrong language.
recommendation: Route title and alt through t() for all three controls.

title: CoreBox pin button's accessible name is hardcoded Chinese in two headers
summary: The pin toggle's alt text is the Chinese literal '固定 CoreBox' in both MainBoxHeader.vue and CoreBox.vue, even though the adjacent send button on CoreBox.vue:869 correctly uses t('corebox.send', '发送').
evidence: <TuffIcon :icon="pinIcon" alt="固定 CoreBox" @click="handleTogglePin" /> (MainBoxHeader.vue:93); <TuffIcon v-else :icon="pinIcon" alt="固定 CoreBox" @click="handleTogglePin" /> (views/box/CoreBox.vue:874)
failure_scenario: An English screen-reader user tabbing the CoreBox header hears the pin control announced as '固定 CoreBox' while the neighbouring send button is announced in English, so the pin control is unidentifiable to them.
recommendation: Add a corebox.pin key to both locales and use it for the alt on both call sites.

title: Clipboard and file tag labels hardcode Chinese, including a Chinese-only counting phrase
summary: The CoreBox input tags that describe pasted clipboard content build their labels from Chinese literals and Chinese measure words, with no i18n indirection.
evidence: {{ imageCount > 1 ? `${imageCount} 张图像` : '图像' }} (ClipboardImageTag.vue:47); if (filePaths.value.length === 0) return '文件准备中...' (views/box/tag/UnifiedFileTag.vue:85); return `${preview.substring(0, maxLength)}... 共${totalLength}字` (views/box/tag/TagSection.vue:51)
failure_scenario: An English-locale user pasting an image or files into CoreBox sees the attachment chip labelled '3 张图像' or '文件准备中...'. The Chinese measure word 张 and character-count phrase 共N字 are not translatable by string swap alone — they need plural-aware keys.
recommendation: Introduce pluralizable keys in both locales for image count, file-pending and character-count.

title: Capability test result metrics hardcode Chinese labels
summary: The AI capability test result panel labels its latency metric and stability section with Chinese literals in the template, while sibling components in the same directory use t().
evidence:
耗时 (65);
稳定性分析
(88)
failure_scenario: An English-locale user running an AI capability test sees the elapsed-time metric labelled '耗时' next to an English 'Token 速度' label, and the analysis section headed '稳定性分析', so they cannot interpret the test output.
recommendation: Extract both labels into t() keys present in both locales.

title: Plugin performance panels hardcode Chinese headings
summary: The plugin runtime performance chart and status bar use Chinese literals for their section titles rather than i18n keys.
evidence: 性能趋势 (PluginPerfCharts.vue:71); 性能 (components/plugin/runtime/PluginPerfStatusBar.vue:136)
failure_scenario: An English-locale developer inspecting a plugin's runtime performance sees the chart section headed '性能趋势' and the status bar labelled '性能' inside an otherwise English plugin detail page.
recommendation: Move both headings into the locale files.

title: PluginFeatures builds user-facing toasts and labels from Chinese literals
summary: Toast notifications and a dynamically composed preview-size label are Chinese string literals, bypassing i18n even for interpolated content.
evidence: toast.warning('Widget 重新加载失败') (747); toast.success('已触发全部 Widget 重新加载') (760); return 'Dev Server 已断开连接' (73); const customLabel = `自定义 ${previewFrameSize.value.width}×${previewFrameSize.value.height}` (166); subtitle: 'Widget 预览' (322)
failure_scenario: An English-locale plugin developer reloading a widget gets a Chinese success or failure toast, and the custom preview-size option in the size dropdown reads '自定义 800×600', so they cannot tell success from failure at a glance.
recommendation: Route the toasts and the composed label through t() with interpolation params.

title: StorePluginMetaHeader hand-rolls locale branching with an isZh ternary instead of i18n
summary: Rather than using a translation key, this component inlines both language variants and picks between them with a boolean, so the string only ever supports Chinese and English and is invisible to the locale files.
evidence: items.push(`${isZh.value ? '更新于' : 'Updated'} ${updatedText.value}`)
failure_scenario: A user in any locale other than zh-CN gets the English branch regardless, and the string cannot be translated by adding a locale file — a future third locale silently falls back to English while the rest of the page translates.
recommendation: Replace the ternary with a single interpolated t('store.updatedAt', { time }) key defined in both locale files.

title: CoreBox action panel shows Chinese fallback for missing key corebox.actionUnsupported
summary: The unsupported-action message passes a Chinese default to t(), and the key resolves in neither locale file, so the Chinese literal is what every user sees.
evidence: t('corebox.actionUnsupported', '暂不支持该操作') — corebox.actionUnsupported is absent from both en-US.json and zh-CN.json
failure_scenario: An English-locale user who triggers an unsupported CoreBox action gets the Chinese message '暂不支持该操作' with no English equivalent, and cannot tell whether the action failed or is simply unavailable.
recommendation: Add corebox.actionUnsupported to both locale files.

title: Copy actions in FailedFilesListDialog render raw keys common.copy / common.copied
summary: The dialog's copy button and its post-copy confirmation use common.copy and common.copied, neither of which exists in the common namespace of either locale file.
evidence: :title="t('common.copy')" (line 107) and t('common.copied') (line 41) — the common namespace in en-US.json contains cancel, save, confirm, delete, edit, add, remove, close, open, content, capsLock, refresh, loading, error, success, warning, info, seconds, minutes, hours, import, comingSoon
failure_scenario: A user inspecting which files failed to index hovers the copy control and gets the tooltip 'common.copy'; after clicking, the confirmation reads 'common.copied', giving no readable feedback that the paths reached the clipboard. Because line 107 sets the title attribute, that raw key is also the control's accessible name for screen-reader users.
recommendation: Add common.copy and common.copied to both locale files.

title: Audit log pagination button renders raw key common.loadMore
summary: The intelligence audit log's pagination control uses common.loadMore, which is absent from the common namespace in both locale files.
evidence: t('common.loadMore') — not present in en-US.json or zh-CN.json common namespace
failure_scenario: A user paging through AI audit logs sees the pagination button labelled 'common.loadMore' and may not recognise it as a control at all.
recommendation: Add common.loadMore to both locale files.

title: Download destination error toast references a missing settings key
summary: The failure path for choosing a download folder emits a message keyed on settings.settingDownload.messages.destinationSelectFailed, which exists in neither locale file.
evidence: t('settings.settingDownload.messages.destinationSelectFailed') — absent from both en-US.json and zh-CN.json
failure_scenario: A user whose download-folder picker fails (permission denied, unmounted volume) sees the raw string 'settings.settingDownload.messages.destinationSelectFailed' as the error, with no indication of what went wrong or how to recover.
recommendation: Add the key to both locale files.

title: Eight settings.intelligence keys exist only in en-US.json, leaving zh-CN incomplete
summary: en-US.json defines 4463 leaf keys and zh-CN.json 4455. Beyond the four capability-test keys reported separately, eight settings.intelligence keys are present only in English, so any future consumer of them will fall back to English for Chinese users.
evidence: Present in en-US.json but missing from zh-CN.json: settings.intelligence.addBinding, settings.intelligence.removeBinding, settings.intelligence.modelOrder, settings.intelligence.noModelsConfigured, settings.intelligence.dragToReorder, settings.intelligence.addFirstModel, settings.intelligence.providerSelection, settings.intelligence.modelSelection
failure_scenario: None of the eight is currently referenced from renderer code, so no user-visible breakage today; the drift means a Chinese user hits untranslated English the moment the model-binding UI starts using them, and it masks real drift in automated key-parity checks.
recommendation: Either add Chinese translations for the eight keys or delete them if the model-binding UI was dropped; add a CI key-parity check between the two locale files.

title: Document lang is hardcoded 'en' and never updated on locale switch
summary: The renderer's root HTML declares lang="en" statically, and nothing in the renderer source ever writes document.documentElement.lang, so the declared document language stays English even when the UI is rendering Chinese.
evidence: <html lang="en"> — a repo-wide search for documentElement.lang across apps/core-app/src/renderer/src returns no matches, and the language-switching code in src/modules/lang/ does not set it
failure_scenario: A screen-reader user who switches the app to zh-CN has every Chinese string announced by an English speech synthesiser, which renders Chinese text as unintelligible sounds or skips it entirely. It also breaks browser-level font selection and hyphenation heuristics for CJK.
recommendation: Set document.documentElement.lang from the active locale wherever the language preference is applied.

title: Primary navigation menu items are plain divs with no role, tabindex or key handler
summary: TouchMenuItem is the app's main sidebar navigation item (used by TouchMenu.vue) and routes on click, but its root is a bare div with no role, no tabindex and no keydown handler.
evidence:
<div
    ref="dom"
    v-wave
    :data-route="props.route"
    class="TouchMenuItem-Container fake-background"
    flex
    items-center
    :class="{ active, disabled }"
    @click="handleClick"
  >
failure_scenario: A keyboard-only user cannot reach or activate any top-level navigation entry — the divs are not in the tab order and Enter/Space do nothing, so the entire app becomes unnavigable without a mouse. A screen-reader user gets no link/button role and no indication that the active item is current, since 'active' is conveyed only by a CSS class.
recommendation: Render as <button> or add role="link", tabindex="0", @keydown.enter/@keydown.space and :aria-current for the active item.

title: Add-plugin control is an empty div with no accessible name and no keyboard access
summary: The 'add plugin' affordance is a self-closing div whose only visual is a CSS pseudo-element plus sign. It has no text content, no aria-label, no role, no tabindex and no key handler.
evidence: <div id="newPluginBtn" class="new-plus" @click="() => emits('add-plugin')" /> — the plus glyph comes from .PluginList-Add:before in the scoped stylesheet, so there is no text node at all
failure_scenario: A screen-reader user reaches the end of the plugin list and finds an element with no name, no role and no announced purpose, so installing a plugin is undiscoverable. A keyboard-only user cannot focus or activate it at all, making plugin installation impossible without a mouse.
recommendation: Use a <button type="button"> with an aria-label naming the action.

title: TSelectItem options are divs with no option role, tabindex or key handling
summary: The shared select-option component renders a click-only div. Selection state is expressed purely through the 'selection' CSS class, with no aria-selected and no role.
failure_scenario: A keyboard-only user who opens any dropdown built on TSelectItem cannot move between options or choose one — the options are not focusable and no arrow/Enter handling exists, so the control is a dead end. A screen-reader user hears the options as unlabelled generic text with no indication of which is currently selected.
recommendation: Add role="option", :aria-selected="isActive", tabindex and Enter/Space handling, with a role="listbox" container.

title: TLabelSelectItem options are click-only divs with no role or keyboard support
summary: The labelled variant of the select option has the same problem as TSelectItem: a bare div with @click, no role, no tabindex and no key handler.
evidence:
<div
    data-type="label-select-item"
    :data-value="value"
    class="TLabelSelectItem"
    @click="refresh(value)"
  >
failure_scenario: A keyboard-only user cannot select any option in the label-style selects; a screen-reader user hears only the option's text with no role or selected state, so they cannot tell it is a choice rather than static content.
recommendation: Add role="option", aria-selected, tabindex="0" and Enter/Space activation.

title: FlatCodeInput digit keys are click-only spans, unusable by keyboard
summary: The pattern/code entry keypad renders each of its nine digits as a span with @click only — no role, no tabindex, no key handler — and conveys both active and disabled state through CSS classes alone.
evidence: <span v-for="i in 9" :class="{ active: codes.includes(i), disabled: codes.length > 0 && codes[codes.length - 1] !== i }" class="FlatCodeInput-Item" @click="inputCode(i)" v-text="i" />
failure_scenario: A keyboard-only user cannot enter a code at all, because none of the nine digit targets is focusable and there is no key handling. A screen-reader user hears nine bare numbers with no role and no announcement of which are already selected or currently disabled, since that is class-only styling.
recommendation: Use <button type="button"> per digit with :disabled and :aria-pressed, so state is exposed and keyboard activation works.

title: Provider deactivate control is an icon-only div with no name or keyboard access
summary: The close/deactivate affordance on each active CoreBox provider pill is a div whose only content is a UnoCSS icon class, with no text, no aria-label, no role, no tabindex and no key handler.
evidence:
<div
          v-if="props.closable"
          cursor-pointer
          i-carbon-close
          @click="emit('deactivate-provider', getUniqueKey(provider))"
        />
failure_scenario: A screen-reader user navigating the active-provider pills encounters an unnamed element and cannot tell it removes a provider, nor which provider it belongs to. A keyboard-only user cannot deactivate a provider at all and gets stuck in a filtered search scope.
recommendation: Use <button type="button"> with an aria-label naming the provider being removed.

title: TuffDrawer has no dialog semantics, no Escape handling and stays focusable when closed
summary: The shared drawer (used by IntelligenceCapabilityInfo, AISDKCapabilityDetails, PluginLogs and IntelligenceChannelsPage) has no role="dialog", no aria-modal, no Escape key handler, no focus trap and no focus restore. It is also never removed from the DOM — closing only translates it offscreen via CSS, with no v-if, no aria-hidden and no display:none on the panel.
evidence: <div class="TuffDrawer z-1998 absolute inset-0 transition-cubic" :class="{ display }"> ... <div class="TuffDrawer-Main ... "> — the closed state is only `--tuff-drawer-xoffset: 100%` with `transform: translateX(var(--tuff-drawer-xoffset))` on -Main and `pointer-events: none` on the root; the file contains no Escape, role, aria-modal, keydown or focus() reference anywhere
failure_scenario: A screen-reader user tabbing the page walks into the closed drawer's entire contents, which are still in the accessibility tree and the tab order despite being invisible offscreen (pointer-events:none blocks the mouse but not the keyboard), so they hear panel content that is not on screen. When the drawer is open, focus is never moved into it, Escape does not close it, and focus can leave it into the inert page behind — leaving keyboard users unable to dismiss the drawer without a mouse click on the mask.
recommendation: Gate the panel with v-if or aria-hidden plus inert when closed, and add role="dialog", aria-modal, an Escape handler, focus trap and focus restore.

title: CommandDetailDrawer modal lacks dialog role, aria-modal and Escape handling
summary: The plugin command detail overlay is dismissible only by clicking the backdrop or the close button. The file contains no Escape handler, no role="dialog", no aria-modal, and no focus management.
evidence: <div v-if="visible" class="command-drawer-overlay" @click.self="closeDrawer"> — a grep for Escape, role="dialog", aria-modal, focus() and keydown in this file returns no matches
failure_scenario: A keyboard-only user who opens a command's details cannot press Escape to close the overlay and, because focus is never moved into the drawer, must tab through the whole page behind it to reach the close button. A screen-reader user is never told a dialog opened and continues reading the obscured page underneath.
recommendation: Add role="dialog" aria-modal="true", an Escape listener, and move focus into the drawer on open with restore on close.

title: CommandDetailDrawer close button is icon-only with no accessible name
summary: The drawer's close button contains only an icon element and carries no aria-label, aria-labelledby or title, so it exposes an empty accessible name.
evidence:
<TxButton variant="bare" class="close-button" @click="closeDrawer">
            <i class="i-ri-close-line" />
          </TxButton>
failure_scenario: A screen-reader user tabbing the command detail drawer hears an unnamed button and, since Escape is also unhandled in this component, has no discoverable way to dismiss the overlay.
recommendation: Add an aria-label naming the action on the close button.

title: Image preview renders an with no alt attribute
summary: The preview addon's main image element has no alt attribute, so assistive technology falls back to announcing the src URL or filename.
evidence: — note the sibling error state on line 33 does provide text ('Failed to load image'), so only the success path is unlabelled
failure_scenario: A screen-reader user previewing an image in CoreBox hears the raw file path or a generic 'image' with no description, so they get no information about what was previewed — while the failure state is correctly announced, making success less accessible than failure.
recommendation: Add an alt describing the previewed image, or alt="" plus an adjacent text label if it is purely decorative.

title: CoreBox prefix app icon is an with no alt attribute
summary: The icon shown at the head of the CoreBox input has no alt attribute, so it is announced by src rather than being labelled or hidden.
failure_scenario: A screen-reader user focusing the CoreBox search field hears the icon's image path announced before the input, adding noise ahead of the control they actually want.
recommendation: Add alt="" to mark it decorative, since the adjacent indexing state is already conveyed separately.

title: Custom background preview image has no alt attribute
summary: The theme settings' custom-background preview omits alt, leaving the element unnamed in the accessibility tree.
failure_scenario: A screen-reader user adjusting theme settings hears the blob or file URL of their chosen wallpaper announced instead of a description, and gets no confirmation that a background image is actually loaded.
recommendation: Add an alt describing it as the custom background preview.

title: TxSwitch exposes role=switch with no accessible name
summary: The shared switch component sets role="switch" and aria-checked but renders only a decorative thumb span, providing no text content and no label prop or default aria-label, so its accessible name is empty unless every call site remembers to pass one.
evidence:
<button
    type="button"
    role="switch"
    :aria-checked="isActive"
    :aria-disabled="disabled"
    :disabled="disabled"
    class="tuff-switch" :class="[...]"
    @click="toggle"
  >
    <span class="tuff-switch__thumb" />
  </button>
failure_scenario: A screen-reader user tabbing a settings page hears 'switch, on' repeatedly with no indication of what each toggle controls, wherever a consumer did not manually attach aria-label or aria-labelledby. Declaring role="switch" without a name is worse than a plain unnamed button because the role promises a labelled state control.
recommendation: Add a label/ariaLabelledby prop and wire it to aria-labelledby, preferring the project's aria-labelledby-over-aria-label convention when a visible label exists.

title: Nexus outline-border demo images have no alt attribute
summary: Both avatar images in this documentation demo omit alt, so the rendered example itself models an inaccessible pattern for readers copying it.
evidence: — identical unlabelled img repeated at line 28
failure_scenario: A screen-reader user reading the TxOutlineBorder documentation hears the GitHub avatar URL announced twice with no context. Because docs demos are copy-paste sources, the missing alt propagates into consumer code.
recommendation: Add alt="" (decorative in this demo) to both images.

title: IntelligenceMessage forked between utils and tuff-intelligence, shapes have drifted
summary: The same conceptual IPC payload type is declared twice in two published packages, and the two declarations have already diverged: the tuff-intelligence copy carries a `metadata` field that the @talex-touch/utils copy does not. Main-process code imports the utils copy, renderer components import the tuff-intelligence copy, so nothing typechecks the two against each other.
failure_scenario: A renderer component builds an IntelligenceMessage with `metadata` (legal against the tuff-intelligence declaration it imports) and sends it over IPC. The main-process handler is typed against the utils declaration, which has no `metadata`, so the field is invisible to every main-side type check and any narrowing/serialization that rebuilds the object silently drops it. Neither `typecheck:node` nor `typecheck:web` reports anything, because each side only ever sees its own copy of the interface.
recommendation: Delete the local IntelligenceMessage in tuff-intelligence and re-export it from @talex-touch/utils/types/intelligence, as that file already does for the 58 context-family types.

title: tuff-intelligence hand-lists 58 re-exported utils types, hiding new shared types from renderer
summary: packages/utils/types/intelligence.ts declares 210 exported symbols. tuff-intelligence forwards exactly 58 of them via a hand-maintained `export type { ... }` list and redefines the rest locally. There is no wildcard forward, so every new shared type has to be added to this list manually or renderer code cannot see it.
failure_scenario: A developer adds a new shared type (say `ContextRedactionRule`) to packages/utils/types/intelligence.ts and wires it into a main-process transport handler. Renderer components import intelligence types from '@talex-touch/tuff-intelligence' (e.g. apps/core-app/src/renderer/src/components/intelligence/audit/context-package-log-summary.ts:1), so the new type resolves to nothing there and the renderer author either re-declares it locally or falls back to `any` — reintroducing exactly the fork that produced the IntelligenceMessage divergence.
recommendation: Replace the 58-name manual list with `export type * from "@talex-touch/utils/types/intelligence"` and keep only genuinely tuff-intelligence-specific types local.

title: Two exported `logLevelToString` / `LogLevelString` in @talex-touch/utils return opposite casing
summary: @talex-touch/utils exports two different functions named `logLevelToString` and two different types named `LogLevelString` from two subpaths. The `base` copy produces UPPERCASE strings, the `common/logger` copy produces lowercase. Which one a caller gets depends only on which import path they picked.
failure_scenario: logger-manager.ts:154 persists the level with `this.config.globalLevel = logLevelToString(level)` and gets 'debug'. A developer adding a new call site who imports `logLevelToString` from '@talex-touch/utils/base' (the name autocompletes from both paths, and packages/utils/index.ts line 4 re-exports './base') writes 'DEBUG' into the same config field. Any consumer comparing that field with `===` against a lowercase literal, or using it as an object key, silently stops matching.
recommendation: Rename one of the pair (e.g. keep `logLevelToString` uppercase in base, expose the lowercase one only as `logLevelToLowerString`) so the two casings cannot be reached under one name.

title: Nexus runtime-server resolution duplicated across main and renderer with drifted APIs
summary: The policy that decides which Nexus backend the app talks to (including the legacy `authServer` -> `runtimeServer` migration and the coercion of unknown values) is implemented twice, once for the main process and once for the renderer. The two copies already have different signatures and different function sets.
failure_scenario: Adding a third runtime target (e.g. 'staging') requires editing `normalizeRuntimeServer` in both files. Because both copies coerce anything that is not 'local' to 'production' (`return value === 'local' ? 'local' : 'production'`), missing one file does not fail a build or a test — the un-updated process silently keeps pointing at the production Nexus backend while the other process points at staging, so main and renderer disagree about which server the session is authenticated against.
recommendation: Move the normalization and legacy migration into a single shared module (packages/utils/env already owns resolveTuffNexusBaseUrl) and have each process supply only its settings accessor.

title: Circular import between search-core and plugin-features-adapter, both module-scope singletons
summary: search-core.ts and plugin/adapters/plugin-features-adapter.ts import each other's default export, and both construct their singleton at module evaluation time. Whichever module the bundler happens to evaluate second sees a partially-initialized binding for the other.
failure_scenario: Today this survives only because `SearchEngineCore`'s constructor (search-core.ts:268) does not touch `PluginFeaturesAdapter` — the reference is deferred to `registerDefaults()` (line 332, `this.registerProvider(PluginFeaturesAdapter)`). Moving that single `registerProvider` call into the constructor, or adding any other module-scope use of the adapter, registers `undefined` as a search provider: plugin features silently stop appearing in CoreBox results with no error at startup.
recommendation: Break the cycle by having plugin-features-adapter receive the search engine through registration (search-core calls `adapter.attach(this)`) instead of importing the singleton back.

title: coreBoxManager and ipcManager singletons form an import cycle across three CoreBox files
summary: core-box/manager.ts imports the `ipcManager` singleton and core-box/ipc.ts imports the `coreBoxManager` singleton; key-transport.ts extends the cycle to three files. Both singletons are created at module scope.
failure_scenario: `ipc.ts` reaches into `coreBoxManager` from ~20 handler bodies (e.g. line 150 `if (coreBoxManager.isUIMode)`, line 333 `return await coreBoxManager.search(...)`). All of them are currently deferred inside callbacks, so evaluation order is masked. Any refactor that reads a `coreBoxManager` property at ipc.ts module scope — for example hoisting a config value out of a handler — resolves against the still-uninitialized binding and throws `Cannot access 'coreBoxManager' before initialization` at app boot, before any window exists to show the error.
recommendation: Have manager.ts pass itself into `ipcManager.register(this)` and drop ipc.ts's import of the manager singleton.

title: permission/channel-guard.ts imports its own barrel, cycling the IPC permission gate
summary: channel-guard.ts imports `getPermissionModule` from './index', while index.ts re-exports channel-guard's own public API. The permission enforcement path therefore depends on the barrel that depends on it.
failure_scenario: This is the module that guards IPC channels against unauthorized plugin access. Because the guard resolves `getPermissionModule` through a barrel that is mid-evaluation whenever `./index` is the entry point, adding any module-scope initialization to index.ts (for example eagerly building a permission registry) makes `getPermissionModule` undefined inside channel-guard at the moment the first channel registers, and the failure surfaces as a permission check that never runs rather than as a crash.
recommendation: Import `getPermissionModule` from the module that actually defines it rather than from './index'.

title: analytics-module.ts imports from its own barrel instead of the defining file
summary: analytics-module.ts imports `getStartupAnalytics` from '.', but index.ts's first statement re-exports analytics-module itself, so importing the analytics barrel enters a cycle. The symbol is actually defined in ./startup-analytics.
failure_scenario: The call at analytics-module.ts:173 (`const startup = getStartupAnalytics().getCurrentMetrics()`) is inside a method, so the cycle is currently benign. But the self-import forces every consumer of analytics-module to pull in the whole barrel including ./types and ./startup-analytics, and any future module-scope use of `getStartupAnalytics` in analytics-module.ts resolves to undefined and throws on first metrics collection.
recommendation: Import directly: `import { getStartupAnalytics } from './startup-analytics'`.

title: storage-maintenance.ts: 357 lines of storage-cleanup code with zero production callers
summary: The service that implements per-domain storage cleanup (clipboard, file index, logs, temp, analytics, usage, OCR, downloads, intelligence, config, updates) exports 11 async cleanup functions. Nothing in the application imports this module. The only importer in the whole repo is its own test file, and that test exercises exactly one of the 11 functions.
failure_scenario: Grepping the repo for each of the 11 exported names returns zero non-test references (`cleanupClipboard` 0, `cleanupFileIndex` 0, `cleanupLogs` 0, `cleanupAnalytics` 0, `cleanupUsage` 0, `cleanupOcr` 0, `cleanupDownloads` 0, `cleanupIntelligence` 0, `cleanupConfig` 0, `cleanupUpdates` 0; `cleanupTemp` matches only the unrelated DownloadEvents.maintenance.cleanupTemp handler). The user-facing storage-cleanup feature therefore does nothing. Worse, the module still imports live Drizzle schema tables and `clipboardModule`, so a schema rename forces a developer to fix 357 lines of code that can never run, and anyone debugging 'cleanup did not free space' will read this file and find the logic correct.
recommendation: Either wire these into the storage-maintenance IPC surface or delete the module and its test; do not leave it as a plausible-looking implementation of a feature that is not connected.

title: common.test.ts mocks service/storage-maintenance, a module common.ts never imports
summary: The test suite for channel/common.ts declares an 11-function vi.mock for '../service/storage-maintenance'. The module under test contains no reference to storage-maintenance at all, so the mock is a leftover from a removed wiring and silently does nothing.
evidence:
vi.mock('../service/storage-maintenance', () => ({
  cleanupAnalytics: vi.fn(),
  cleanupClipboard: vi.fn(),
  cleanupConfig: vi.fn(),
  cleanupDownloads: vi.fn(),
  cleanupFileIndex: vi.fn(),
  cleanupIntelligence: vi.fn(),
  cleanupLogs: vi.fn(),
  cleanupOcr: vi.fn(),
  cleanupTemp: vi.fn(),
  cleanupUpdates: vi.fn(),
  cleanupUsage: vi.fn()
}))
failure_scenario: grep for 'storage-maintenance', 'cleanupClipboard', 'cleanupFileIndex', 'cleanupLogs' and 'cleanupTemp' in apps/core-app/src/main/channel/common.ts returns nothing. The mock therefore never intercepts anything, but its presence is the strongest available signal that common.ts is expected to register storage-cleanup channels. A maintainer auditing whether storage cleanup is covered by tests reads this block, concludes it is, and ships the regression described in the storage-maintenance.ts finding.
recommendation: Delete the stale vi.mock block, or restore the wiring it was written for and assert on it.

title: update-asset-utils.ts: 8 of 9 exported helpers unused, including the only update-asset scoring logic
summary: This 107-line module exports 9 functions. Only normalizeUpdateAssetKey is imported anywhere (update-system.ts:38). The other 8 — including calculateUpdateAssetScore, the app's sole implementation of update-installer ranking — have no callers and no tests.
failure_scenario: A grep for 'score' across the whole update module matches only inside update-asset-utils.ts itself, confirming no other ranking implementation exists — so the updater does not score candidate assets at all. When a user reports that the updater downloaded the wrong artifact on a platform that ships several installers, a developer finds calculateUpdateAssetScore, reads its priority table (core +200, tuff +20, latest-release +10), fixes the weights, and ships a change that provably cannot affect behaviour.
recommendation: Delete the 8 unreferenced helpers, or call calculateUpdateAssetScore from the real asset-selection path in update-system.ts.

title: TouchPlugin holds 11 capability factories as static mutable state across 3 hand-synced lists
summary: Every plugin capability (snipaste, system actions, browser open/data, translation, intelligence context, window manager, window preset, workspace scripts, plus transport and runtime service) is injected into TouchPlugin as a private static field with a matching static setter. Every TouchPlugin instance reads the same statics, and correctness depends on three separate lists in plugin-module.ts staying in sync by hand.
failure_scenario: Adding a 12th capability requires four coordinated edits: the static field, the static setter, the install block at plugin-module.ts:2504, and the teardown block at plugin-module.ts:2669. Nothing enforces the fourth. Omitting it leaves a factory closure over the destroyed PluginModule alive on the class object for the lifetime of the process, so after a dev hot-reload the new PluginModule's plugins call into the previous module's transport and capability instances — the exact cross-generation leak the existing 11 runCleanup lines were written to prevent.
recommendation: Replace the 11 static slots with a single injected capability registry object (one set call, one clear call) so adding a capability cannot desynchronize init and destroy.

title: packages/utils: 22 import cycles, all via an event-type file importing the analytics client
summary: transport/events/types/app.ts re-exports 12 analytics symbols as values from '../../../analytics'. That barrel pulls in analytics/client.ts, which imports the transport SDK, which imports back into transport/events/index.ts. Every one of the 22 cycles detected in packages/utils runs through this single edge.
failure_scenario: An event *type* module ends up depending on a runtime transport client. Because `useTuffTransport` is a value import, bundlers cannot tree-shake the analytics client out of any consumer that only wanted event type definitions, and the evaluation order of transport/events/index.ts (2671 lines of defineEvent calls executed at module scope) becomes dependent on which file the importer touched first. Adding any module-scope initialization to analytics/client.ts — for example eagerly resolving the transport — makes AppEvents undefined at the moment the event table is built, producing event descriptors with undefined channels that fail only at the first IPC send.
recommendation: Make the re-export type-only (`export type { ... } from '../../../analytics/types'`) and point it at analytics/types rather than the analytics barrel, which removes the value edge and all 22 cycles.

title: CommonChannelModule leaks two powerMonitor listeners that re-arm a global poll after destroy
summary: setupBatteryStatusBroadcast registers powerMonitor 'on-ac' and 'on-battery' handlers without keeping a disposer. onDestroy clears the interval and the transport disposers but never removes them, so the handlers outlive the module and can re-register a task on the global PollingService singleton after teardown.
failure_scenario: Destroy the module (hot-reload in dev, or module teardown on quit) and then unplug the laptop. The surviving 'on-battery' handler runs startPolling(), which calls pollingService.register(BATTERY_POLL_TASK_ID, ...) with a 120s interval and pollingService.start() on the process-wide PollingService.getInstance() (common.ts:141). The only unregister call in the file is inside the local stopPolling closure (line 904), which onDestroy never invokes, so the task runs forever, broadcasting through the `transport` captured in the closure even though onDestroy set this.transport = null. Each init/destroy cycle adds another pair of powerMonitor listeners.
recommendation: Push `() => powerMonitor.off('on-ac', h)` / `off('on-battery', h)` and `stopPolling()` into transportDisposers, exactly as network-module.ts:104 already does for its 'resume' handler.

title: PluginLogModule discards all 8 handler disposers; onDestroy releases only one of them
summary: The plugin log service registers one touchEventBus listener and seven transport handlers, throwing away every disposer that transport.on returns. onDestroy releases only the unrelated uninstall-invalidator disposer, so all eight registrations survive module teardown.
failure_scenario: pluginLogModule is a module-scope singleton (`const pluginLogModule = new PluginLogModule()`), so the same instance is reused across init/destroy cycles. After a dev hot-reload the previous generation's seven transport handlers are still registered for the same event names as the new generation's, so every plugin-log IPC request is served twice — once by a handler closed over the stale `this.transport` (which onDestroy left set) and once by the live one. The PLUGIN_LOG_APPEND listener also keeps the old `subscriptions` map reachable, holding WebContents references past window close.
recommendation: Collect the disposers returned by touchEventBus.on and each transport.on into a disposers array and drain it in onDestroy, matching the transportDisposers pattern used in addon-opener.ts and network-module.ts.

title: SentryServiceModule leaks app 'browser-window-created' listener and a latch that blocks re-attach
summary: ensureWindowPerformanceListeners registers an app-level 'browser-window-created' listener guarded by an instance latch. onDestroy stops the perf monitors but removes neither the listener nor the latch, and the module is a process-lifetime singleton, so the two get permanently out of sync.
failure_scenario: After a destroy/re-init cycle the latch is still true, so ensureWindowPerformanceListeners early-returns and the `for (const win of BrowserWindow.getAllWindows()) attach(win)` loop never runs — windows that already exist stop being monitored for 'unresponsive'. Meanwhile the leaked app-level listener still fires for newly created windows and attaches three more win.on handlers each time. Unresponsive-window telemetry silently becomes partial: new windows are measured, pre-existing ones are not, and nothing logs the gap.
recommendation: Capture `app.off('browser-window-created', handler)` plus the per-window listener removals in a disposer list drained by onDestroy, and reset windowPerfListenersReady there.

title: Plugin capability auth is hardcoded name matching across 16 main-process files
summary: Privileged plugin capabilities (intelligence context, browser open/data, system actions, window manager, window presets, workspace scripts, process control) are gated by comparing the plugin's name against a literal string. Sixteen separate files in the main process embed these names, and no shared constant exists. The manifest permission system that packages/utils/plugin exposes is not what authorizes these capabilities.
failure_scenario: Renaming any of the seven extracted plugins — the exact refactor the 2026-02 extraction invites — silently revokes its capabilities: every gate falls through to invalid() or returns null, so the plugin loads, registers, and then fails at the moment a user triggers the feature, with no build error and no startup warning. Grepping for the shared constant that should make this a one-line change returns nothing (no OFFICIAL_PLUGIN/PRIVILEGED_PLUGIN/TRUSTED_PLUGIN symbol exists anywhere in apps/core-app/src/main or packages/utils), so the rename must be applied correctly in all 16 files.
recommendation: Introduce one exported allowlist mapping capability -> plugin names (or move the decision into the existing manifest permission registry) and have all 16 gates consult it.

title: plugin-runtime-rollout.ts gates nothing: its 22-name allowlist has no production consumer
summary: This module is named as a rollout gate and exports a frozen 22-entry allowlist of preludes deemed 'runtime compatible'. No production code reads the list — the only references are in its own test file. The module's one live export returns a hardcoded true.
failure_scenario: Every reference to PLUGIN_RUNTIME_COMPATIBLE_OFFICIAL_PRELUDES outside this 30-line file is in plugin-runtime-rollout.test.ts. The runtime is therefore installed for every plugin regardless of the list. A developer adding a 23rd official plugin hits the test's `expect(official).toHaveLength(22)` assertion, adds their plugin's name to the allowlist to make it pass, and reasonably concludes they have opted the plugin into the new runtime — while in reality the runtime was already active for it, including for a prelude that still uses the Node/Electron APIs the test's `forbidden` patterns are meant to keep out.
recommendation: Either make shouldInstallPluginRuntimeServiceByDefault consult the allowlist, or delete the allowlist from the production module and move it into the test that actually scans prelude sources.

title: Nexus provider identity constant and predicate duplicated between main and renderer
summary: TUFF_NEXUS_PROVIDER_ID and isNexusManagedProvider are declared independently in the main process and the renderer with byte-identical bodies. The renderer copy decides which edit/delete affordances a provider gets; the main copy decides runtime behaviour. Nothing keeps them equal.
failure_scenario: The renderer gates the official badge and the edit/delete buttons on this predicate (IntelligenceProviderHeader.vue lines 223, 286, 300, 314; IntelligenceApiConfig.vue:68 uses `!isNexusManagedProvider(props.modelValue)`), while the main process gates runtime provider resolution on it (provider-runtime.ts:18, provider-models.ts:205). Changing the origin marker or the provider id on one side — e.g. adding a second managed origin — leaves the other side classifying the provider the old way, so the UI offers Delete on a provider the main process refuses to delete, and the user gets a silent no-op.
recommendation: Move both symbols into packages/utils (alongside the existing Nexus env helpers) and import from there on both sides.

title: Six vi.mock blocks target modules absent from the subject's transitive import graph
summary: Resolving every relative vi.mock target in apps/core-app/src/main against the subject's full transitive import graph leaves six mocks whose target the module under test can never load. They are inert today and silently reactivate if a future import re-introduces the dependency.
failure_scenario: apps/core-app/src/main/core/index.ts owns the real TouchApp singleton (`let touchApp: TouchApp | null = null`; genTouchApp constructs `new TouchApp(app, ...)` and touches Electron). The three '../../core' mocks were what kept tests from building a real TouchApp; the subjects have since migrated off that import, so the mocks do nothing. If any refactor pulls '../../core' back into the transitive graph of plugin.ts, ocr-service.ts or omni-panel/index.ts, these mocks silently activate and substitute a two-field stub `{ channel: {}, window: { window: { id: 1 } } }` for the real app object — the suite keeps passing while no longer exercising the wiring it claims to cover. preview-inventory.ts only mentions currency-ability as a string path in an inventory list (line 44), never as an import, so that mock is inert for the same reason.
recommendation: Delete the six stale vi.mock blocks; add a lint or test-time assertion that every relative vi.mock target is reachable from the module under test.

title: app-provider.ts is a 4540-line single-class module that also closes an import cycle with search-core
summary: One AppProvider class spans 4540 lines with 142 methods over 19 shared mutable instance fields, mixing platform app scanning, icon hydration scheduling, database transactions and dead-letter sweeping, search-index upserts, and startup/renderer-readiness sequencing. It is instantiated at module scope and imports search-core, which imports it back.
failure_scenario: 39 commits touched this file in the last 90 days, so it is under active change, and its 3592-line sibling test suite must be re-reasoned for each one. The size is what makes the cycle dangerous: AppProvider's constructor is currently a single log call (line 510-512), which is the only reason the mutual module-scope instantiation with search-core does not break. Any of the 142 methods being promoted into constructor-time initialization — a natural move when adding eager startup work — dereferences `searchEngineCore` while search-core is still evaluating, and the app fails at boot rather than at the call site.
recommendation: Split the scanning, icon-hydration and index-write responsibilities into separate modules, and break the cycle by having search-core register itself with the provider instead of the provider importing the engine.

title: TouchPlugin: 4013-line class mixing capability policy, feature lifecycle and storage paths
summary: A single TouchPlugin class holds 119 methods, 12 instance fields and 11 static fields, and combines concerns that change for unrelated reasons: capability injection, feature triggering and abort handling, storage/config/log path resolution, business-feature hosting, icon containment checks, permission gating, and hardcoded per-plugin authorization rules.
failure_scenario: 39 commits from 2 authors touched this file in the last 90 days against a 3572-line test suite, so unrelated workstreams (adding a plugin capability, changing storage paths, fixing icon containment) all collide in one file. Concretely, the authorization rules at lines 2083/2096/2135 sit inside the same class as triggerFeature and abortFeatureControllers, so a reviewer checking a feature-lifecycle change has to re-verify capability policy in the same diff, and the class's 11 static capability slots mean the policy is shared process-wide across every plugin instance rather than scoped per plugin.
recommendation: Extract the capability policy (the name-based gates plus the 11 static slots) into a separate authorization module, and move storage-path and icon handling into collaborators, leaving TouchPlugin as feature lifecycle only.

title: tuff-cli ships a dead forked island of 4 CLI modules that has already drifted from tuff-cli-core
summary: packages/tuff-cli/src/cli/ contains forked copies of args.ts, repositories.ts, runtime-config.ts and device.ts. The shipped binary imports all of those symbols from @talex-touch/tuff-cli-core instead. The four files import only each other, so nothing outside the island reaches them — and the copies have already fallen behind the real implementation.
failure_scenario: Repo-wide grep finds zero importers of cli/args.ts, cli/repositories.ts and cli/device.ts; cli/runtime-config.ts is imported only by the other two dead files. packages/tuff-cli/src/index.ts is `export {}` and cli/index.ts re-exports only ./commands, ./i18n and ./prompts, so the island is unreachable through every entry point. A maintainer fixing a CLI argument bug greps for parsePublishArgs, finds the tuff-cli copy first (it is the package named after the binary), edits it, tests by hand, and ships nothing — exactly the situation that let --non-interactive land in core and never reach the fork.
recommendation: Delete packages/tuff-cli/src/cli/{args,repositories,runtime-config,device}.ts and re-export from @talex-touch/tuff-cli-core if any of those names must stay available.

title: Two useWindowAnimation implementations in @talex-touch/utils; the GSAP one has no consumers
summary: packages/utils/animation exports useWindowAnimation twice with the same public API but different engines: window.ts drives it with GSAP, window-node.ts with PollingService plus a hand-rolled easeInOutCubic. Only the window-node variant is imported anywhere. Both are reachable through the package's published 'animation' export.
failure_scenario: Grepping the repo for imports of 'animation/window' that are not 'animation/window-node' returns nothing, so the GSAP copy is dead — yet 'animation' is listed in packages/utils/package.json exports (line 23), so an external plugin developer can import it. Because both files export the identical symbol name with matching signatures, picking the wrong subpath compiles cleanly and then fails at runtime in the main process, where GSAP has no requestAnimationFrame to drive it: the CoreBox window simply never resizes, with no error. Any easing or duration fix applied to the live variant also has to be duplicated or the two visibly disagree.
recommendation: Delete packages/utils/animation/window.ts, or rename it to make the renderer-only requirement explicit in the module name.

title: Four copies of the 'is Nexus provider' rule; the privacy copy uses AND, the others OR
summary: The predicate that decides whether an AI provider is Nexus-managed is implemented independently in four places. Three combine the id check and the origin-metadata check with OR; the fourth — the one that classifies a provider for the privacy disclosure — combines them with AND, so it recognizes strictly fewer providers than the rest of the app.
failure_scenario: provider-disclosure.ts:125 uses this predicate as the first branch of destinationFor: `if (isNexusProvider(provider)) return 'nexus-managed'`, falling through to `hasLoopbackEndpoint(...) -> 'local'` and finally `return 'remote'`. A provider carrying metadata.origin === 'tuff-nexus' under any id other than the literal 'tuff-nexus-default' — which the AI runtime, the model resolver and the renderer all already treat as Nexus-managed — is classified 'remote' by the disclosure instead of 'nexus-managed'. The user is then shown a privacy disclosure naming the wrong data destination for a provider the rest of the app knows is Nexus-managed.
recommendation: Export one predicate from packages/utils and have all four sites call it; if the disclosure genuinely needs the stricter AND, name it differently and document why.

title: 'tuff-nexus-default' provider id is a magic string repeated across 4 modules and 6 config entries
summary: The identity of the built-in Nexus provider is written as a bare string literal in the shared default-capability table (6 occurrences) and re-declared as a separate exported constant in both the main process and the renderer, with two further inline literals in the privacy and provider modules. No single definition exists.
evidence:
// packages/utils/types/intelligence.ts — 6 literal occurrences (2940, 2992, 3051, 3061, 3074, 3087)
    id: "tuff-nexus-default",
      { providerId: "tuff-nexus-default", priority: 1, enabled: false },

// two independent constant declarations of the same literal
apps/core-app/src/main/modules/ai/provider-runtime-shared.ts:1
export const TUFF_NEXUS_PROVIDER_ID = 'tuff-nexus-default'
apps/core-app/src/renderer/src/modules/intelligence/nexus-provider.ts:4
export const TUFF_NEXUS_PROVIDER_ID = 'tuff-nexus-default'

// two further inline literals
apps/core-app/src/main/modules/privacy/provider-disclosure.ts:96
apps/core-app/src/main/modules/ai/providers/nexus-provider.ts:238
failure_scenario: Renaming the built-in provider requires finding all ten sites across three packages, two of which are the constants that a developer would reasonably assume are the single source of truth. Missing the six literals inside DEFAULT_CAPABILITIES leaves every capability route pointing at a provider id that no longer resolves, so text.chat, embedding.generate and the four other capabilities silently fall through to their next-priority provider — a behaviour change with no error and no failing test, since DEFAULT_CAPABILITIES is data rather than code.
recommendation: Define the id once in packages/utils (next to DEFAULT_CAPABILITIES), export it, and replace all ten sites with references to it.

title: file-protocol dedupe Set grows without bound for every failing tfile path
summary: loggedErrorPaths is a module-level Set that records every blocked or unreadable path to deduplicate logs. It is never trimmed and never cleared, not even in onDestroy().
failure_scenario: A renderer view that renders thumbnails for a large, churning result set (clipboard history with deleted image temp files, or a plugin emitting unique tfile URLs) adds one retained string per distinct missing path for the whole session; on a long-lived launcher process this is an unbounded string retainer.
recommendation: Cap the set (LRU or clear past N entries) and clear it in onDestroy().

title: apps/core-app/.npmrc store-dir resolves two levels above the repo, splitting the pnpm store
summary: The core-app .npmrc sets a relative store-dir written as if it resolved against the .npmrc's own directory, but pnpm resolves it against the workspace root, landing the store two directories above the repository and creating a second, divergent store.
evidence:
apps/core-app/.npmrc:3
  store-dir=../../.pnpm-store

Empirically verified in this checkout (repo root = /Users/talexdreamsoul/Workspace/Projects/talex-touch):
  $ pnpm store path                       -> /Users/talexdreamsoul/Workspace/Projects/talex-touch/.pnpm-store/v10
  $ pnpm -C apps/core-app store path      -> /Users/talexdreamsoul/Workspace/.pnpm-store/v10
failure_scenario: Author intended ../../.pnpm-store (relative to apps/core-app) to point at <repo>/.pnpm-store, but pnpm resolves it relative to the workspace root, yielding <repo>/../../.pnpm-store. Any pnpm command run with cwd inside apps/core-app (the repo does this constantly: `pnpm -C "apps/core-app" exec ...` in package.json quality:pr, test:targeted and lint-staged) uses a completely different store from the root install. Adding a dependency from that directory then fails with ERR_PNPM_UNEXPECTED_STORE against the root node_modules, and the workaround is to pass --store-dir explicitly.
recommendation: Delete the per-package store-dir override, or make both .npmrc files point at one absolute/normalized location.

title: Root .npmrc puts the pnpm content-addressable store inside the git checkout
summary: store-dir is a bare relative path, so the pnpm store is created inside the repository working tree and, in CI, inside the actions/checkout directory that setup-node then caches.
evidence:
.npmrc:10
  store-dir=.pnpm-store

$ pnpm store path
/Users/talexdreamsoul/Workspace/Projects/talex-touch/.pnpm-store/v10

.gitignore:38
  .pnpm-store/
failure_scenario: Every workflow uses `actions/setup-node@v7` with `cache: pnpm`, which calls `pnpm store path` and caches whatever it returns - here a directory inside the checkout. The store is therefore restored into the working tree before install and re-uploaded after, so the cache key covers files the build also writes to, and any workspace-wide cleanup (build-and-release.yml runs several `rm -rf` sweeps under GITHUB_WORKSPACE) can delete the store that node_modules hardlinks point into. It also means the store is per-clone rather than shared, so a fresh clone re-downloads every package.
recommendation: Point store-dir at a path outside the repository (e.g. ~/.pnpm-store) or drop the setting and let pnpm use its default.

title: lint and lint-staged target a workers/ directory that does not exist in the repo
summary: Both the root lint script and the lint-staged config include workers/** globs, but there is no workers/ directory anywhere in the repository, so the config is dead.
failure_scenario: The glob only survives because --no-error-on-unmatched-pattern is passed. If Cloudflare Worker sources are later added under a different path (the Worker config in wrangler.toml points at apps/nexus/dist), they silently get no lint coverage while the config reads as though they do; conversely nobody notices the stale glob because it never errors.
recommendation: Remove the workers/** globs, or move the Worker sources under workers/ if that was the intent.

title: lint-staged lets ESLint warnings through for apps/core-app only
summary: Every lint-staged entry passes --max-warnings=0 except the apps/core-app entry, so warnings in the largest package pass the pre-commit hook while identical warnings elsewhere block it.
failure_scenario: A developer commits core-app code that produces ESLint warnings; the pre-commit hook passes. CI then runs `pnpm quality:pr` -> `lint:changed`, and if that path applies --max-warnings=0 the same change fails in CI, after the commit is already pushed. The inconsistency also means core-app is the one package where warning-level rules have no enforcement at all.
recommendation: Add --max-warnings=0 to the apps/core-app lint-staged command to match every other entry.

title: lint-staged skips five workspace packages, so their code never hits the pre-commit hook
summary: The lint-staged map enumerates packages by hand and omits tuff-core, tuff-cli, tuff-cli-core, intelligence-uikit and pi-extension-tuff, all of which exist under packages/.
evidence:
package.json:213-252 lint-staged keys under packages/: packages/test, packages/tuff-intelligence, packages/tuffex, packages/unplugin-export-plugin, packages/utils

$ ls packages/
intelligence-uikit  pi-extension-tuff  test  tuff-analyse  tuff-business  tuff-cli  tuff-cli-core  tuff-core  tuff-intelligence  tuff-native  tuffex  unplugin-export-plugin  utils
failure_scenario: Editing packages/tuff-cli/src/**.ts and committing runs no ESLint at all, because no lint-staged glob matches. tuff-core, tuff-cli and unplugin-export-plugin are published to npm by .github/workflows/package-tuff-cli-publish.yml, which also runs no lint step - so unlinted code in those three packages can go straight from commit to a published npm release.
recommendation: Replace the hand-maintained per-package map with a single packages/**/*.{...} entry, or add the missing packages.

title: CI never runs on master: the only quality workflow triggers on pull_request alone
summary: ci.yml (lint, targeted tests, typecheck, docs verification) is wired exclusively to pull_request, so nothing validates the default branch after a merge or a direct push.
evidence:
.github/workflows/ci.yml:3-7
  on:
    pull_request:
      branches:
        - main
        - master
failure_scenario: Two PRs that each pass CI independently are merged in sequence and their combination breaks typecheck or a test (a semantic conflict PR-level CI cannot see). No workflow runs on the merge commit, so master stays broken until someone opens the next PR - and that PR's CI failure looks like it was caused by the new PR. A direct push to master (which the branch protection would have to forbid separately) is never checked at all.
recommendation: Add a `push: branches: [master, main]` trigger to ci.yml.

title: No timeout-minutes on any release or CI job except one
summary: Across all 18 workflows only windows-everything-production.yml sets timeout-minutes; the three-platform Electron release matrix, the Rust matrix and every publish job can hang for the 6-hour runner default.
evidence:
$ grep -rn "timeout-minutes" .github/workflows/
.github/workflows/windows-everything-production.yml:35:    timeout-minutes: 60

.github/workflows/build-and-release.yml:48-50
  build-and-release:
    name: Build and Release Tuff App
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
(no timeout-minutes)
failure_scenario: macOS notarization waits on an Apple service that stops responding, or electron-builder blocks on a download from the npmmirror mirror. The job sits idle until GitHub's 6-hour default kills it, once per matrix leg on three runners (macOS minutes bill at 10x), and `concurrency.cancel-in-progress: false` means a follow-up tag push queues behind it rather than superseding it.
recommendation: Set a realistic timeout-minutes on each job (e.g. 90 for the build matrix, 20 for publish jobs).

title: release-drafter fires twice for one merge with contents: write and no concurrency group
summary: The workflow triggers on both push to main/master and pull_request_target closed, so merging a PR starts two concurrent runs that both mutate the same draft release, and there is no concurrency group to serialize them.
evidence:
.github/workflows/release-drafter.yml:3-18
  on:
    push:
      branches:
        - main
        - master
    pull_request_target:
      types:
        - closed

  permissions:
    contents: write
    pull-requests: read

  jobs:
    update-release-draft:
      if: github.event_name == 'push' || (github.event_name == 'pull_request_target' && github.event.pull_request.merged == true)
(no concurrency: block)
failure_scenario: Merging a PR into master emits both a push event and a pull_request_target closed(merged) event. The `if` admits both, so two release-drafter runs start within seconds of each other. Both read the existing draft, both compute a body, and the slower one overwrites the faster one - or, when neither sees a draft yet, both call createRelease and the repo ends up with two duplicate draft releases for the same version.
recommendation: Drop one trigger (push alone is sufficient) and add a concurrency group with cancel-in-progress: false.

title: release-drafter config uses a filter-by-labels key that is not a release-drafter option
summary: The label gate that pr-flags.yml exists to feed is written as filter-by-labels.include, which is not part of release-drafter's option set; the documented key for an allowlist is include-labels (a flat list), as the adjacent exclude-labels shows.
evidence:
.github/release-drafter.yml:5-9
  filter-by-labels:
    include:
      - needs-release-note
  exclude-labels:
    - skip-changelog
failure_scenario: pr-flags.yml (.github/workflows/pr-flags.yml:53-66) exists solely to add the needs-release-note label when a contributor ticks the PR-template checkbox, and this config is the consumer of that label. Because the key does not match release-drafter's schema, the allowlist never takes effect: either the option is ignored and every merged PR lands in the draft release notes regardless of the checkbox, or the config fails schema validation and the action errors on every run. Either way the opt-in release-note gate does not work.
recommendation: Replace with `include-labels:` followed by the flat list, and confirm against the release-drafter option reference.
