failure_scenario: A plugin drives the storage IPC (plugin-storage-transport-service.ts:492 -> plugin.savePluginFile(fileName, payload?.content)) with 100 distinct file names of 9MB each. Every write passes the per-file check and the plugin ends up occupying ~900MB of the user's disk, while getStorageStats() reports usagePercent in the thousands. The sibling API plugin-business-file-storage.ts enforces MAX_TOTAL_BYTES/MAX_FILES for exactly this reason; this path does not.
recommendation: Track the directory total (as plugin-business-file-storage does) and reject writes that would push the plugin over the quota, plus a file-count cap.

title: Replacing a system notification untracks the new one via the old notification's close event
summary: showSystemNotification() closes any existing notification with the same id and then registers the replacement under that id. The old notification's 'close' handler fires asynchronously and deletes the map entries by id — by then those entries belong to the new notification.
failure_scenario: A plugin or module updates a progress notification by re-sending the same id. dismissSystemNotification closes toast #1 and the new toast #2 is registered; when the OS delivers #1's 'close' event it removes #2 from systemNotifications/systemRequests. A later dismiss for that id then finds nothing and silently no-ops, leaving toast #2 on screen with no way to close it programmatically. On a platform where Notification.isSupported() is false the same path leaves systemRequests entries that no close event will ever remove.
recommendation: Capture the notification instance in the close handler and only delete when the map still holds that same instance.

title: Shortcut re-registration dereferences shortcut.meta after guarding it with ?., losing all shortcuts
summary: reregisterAllShortcuts() reads shortcut.meta with optional chaining (so a missing meta reaches the branch) and then assigns through it without a guard. The whole function runs after globalShortcut.unregisterAll() with no try/catch around the loop, so the TypeError leaves every global shortcut unregistered.
failure_scenario: A TRIGGER shortcut persisted without a meta object (an older schema, a hand-edited shortcut store, or any partially written record — the file's own ~10 uses of `shortcut.meta?.` show this is expected at runtime) reaches line 488: `undefined !== triggerKind` is true, so line 489 throws 'Cannot set properties of undefined'. The exception escapes reregisterAllShortcuts, which has already called globalShortcut.unregisterAll(), so no shortcut is re-registered — including Cmd/Ctrl+E for CoreBox — until the app restarts.
recommendation: Normalize meta (`shortcut.meta ??= {...}`) before writing, and wrap the per-shortcut body in try/catch so one bad record cannot take down every shortcut.

title: MCP session can be cached as open after the transport closed during connect
summary: openSession() installs client.onclose before awaiting connect, but the handler reads a `session` variable that is only assigned after the await. A close that arrives during connect finds session === null, does nothing, and the freshly built session object is then returned and cached with closed: false.
failure_scenario: A stdio MCP server completes the initialize handshake and then exits immediately (bad config, missing dependency printed to stderr). onclose fires while session is still null, so nothing is removed; connectProfile then stores the dead session in this.sessions with closed: false. Every later listTools/callTool passes the `if (session.closed)` guard in withSessionRpc and fails against a dead transport, and no reconnect is attempted because the cache still looks healthy.
recommendation: Build the session object before connect (or set a `closedDuringConnect` flag in the handler) and re-check it after connect resolves.

title: AI quota checks read a 10s usage cache nothing invalidates, so per-minute limits do not bind
summary: checkQuota() compares the configured limits against getCurrentUsage(), which serves a snapshot cached for 10 seconds. Nothing invalidates that entry when a request is recorded — clearCache() has no production caller — so every check inside a 10s window sees the same counters.
failure_scenario: A plugin with requestsPerMinute: 10 fires 500 calls in two seconds. The first checkQuota populates the cache with requestsThisMinute: 0; the remaining 499 all read that same cached zero and are admitted (intelligence-sdk.ts:870 gates the real invoke on this result). Even after the cache expires the next snapshot only reflects rows already flushed to intelligence_audit_logs, so the limit is never actually enforced against a burst.
recommendation: Invalidate (or decrement into) the usage cache when an audit entry is recorded, and hold an in-memory counter of in-flight requests so concurrent checks do not all read the same snapshot.

title: Audit flush failure reschedules every 200ms against an unbounded pending buffer
summary: flushBatch() requeues the batch and returns false on any DB error; flushToDB()'s finally then reschedules with the default 200ms delay. pendingLogs has no cap (only memoryLogs is trimmed), so a persistently failing write turns into a tight retry loop over a growing array.
failure_scenario: The database becomes unwritable (disk full, a corrupt aux file, or the write scheduler rejecting during shutdown). Every 200ms the logger re-serializes up to 20 entries with JSON.stringify, fails, unshifts them back, and reschedules — five times a second, forever — while new AI calls keep pushing onto pendingLogs. Error logging is throttled to once a minute, so the loop is invisible in logs while CPU burns and memory grows.
recommendation: Back off exponentially after a failed flush and cap pendingLogs (drop oldest, as memoryLogs already does) so the buffer cannot grow without bound.

title: Usage-stats upsert errors swallowed inside the audit transaction, so quota counters drift
summary: updateUsageStats() runs inside the same transaction as the audit-log insert, but wraps each bucket's upsert in its own try/catch. A swallowed error lets the transaction commit with the audit rows written and the aggregate counters not advanced.
failure_scenario: One bucket's onConflictDoUpdate fails (a constraint change, a NULL avgLatency producing a bad expression, or a transient error). The catch logs at most once per minute and the transaction still commits, so intelligence_usage_stats for that caller/period permanently under-counts. intelligence-quota-manager.getCurrentUsage() reads exactly that table for requestsToday/requestsThisMonth, so the caller's daily and monthly quotas are enforced against the wrong numbers for the rest of the period.
recommendation: Let the error propagate so the transaction rolls back and the batch is requeued, or record the failed bucket for replay instead of dropping it.

title: Chunked download merges straight into the destination file with no temp-and-rename
summary: mergeChunks() opens the final output path with 'w' (truncating anything already there) and writes each chunk into it. A failure or crash partway through leaves a truncated file at the real filename, and unlike the single-stream path the partial file is never removed.
failure_scenario: A user re-downloads a multi-GB file into a folder that already holds a good copy under the same name. The merge truncates that copy, writes a few chunks, and then hits ENOSPC (the chunks plus the merged output need double the space) or the app is quit. The original file is destroyed and a partial file with the correct name is left behind — nothing in mergeChunks unlinks it, and cleanupChunks/cleanupTaskTempDir after the try block are skipped on the throw, so the temp chunks leak too.
recommendation: Merge into `${outputPath}.part` and fs.rename() onto the destination only after the last chunk is written; unlink the partial file in a catch.

title: File clipboard formats are wiped by the clipboard.write() that follows, so pasting files fails
summary: Both file-apply paths write the file-URL pasteboard formats with writeBuffer and then call clipboard.write({ text }). Electron's clipboard.write() replaces the whole clipboard, so the three file formats written immediately before it are discarded and only the plain-text path survives.
failure_scenario: A user picks a files entry from clipboard history and triggers apply/auto-paste (handleApplyRequest -> applyToActiveApp -> writeItemToClipboard). The three file formats are written and then cleared by clipboard.write, so the target app receives only text — pasting into Finder/Explorer or a file drop zone yields the literal path string instead of the file, and a multi-file selection collapses to resolvedPaths[0] because only the first path is put in the text flavor.
recommendation: Write the plain-text flavor first (or pass it in the same clipboard.write call) and add the file-URL buffers afterwards with writeBuffer, since writeBuffer appends to the current clipboard while write() resets it.

title: Clipboard URL recommendation opens the SHA-256 hash instead of the real URL
summary: getClipboardUrlCandidates treats ContextSignal.clipboard.content as the URL, but ContextProvider stores a privacy hash there (`crypto.createHash('sha256')...slice(0,16)`). The generated "打开 URL" card carries the hash as its subtitle, item id and open-url payload.
evidence:
if (!context.clipboard?.meta?.isUrl || !context.clipboard.content) return []

const url = context.clipboard.content

return [{ sourceId: '__builtin_clipboard_url__', itemId: `clipboard-url-open:${url}`, ... pluginCandidate: { subtitle: url.length > 60 ? ... : url, action: 'open-url', data: { url } } }]
failure_scenario: Copy https://github.com/talex-touch/talex-touch and open CoreBox within 30s. ContextProvider.getClipboardContext sets content = hashContent(url) = e.g. '9f2c1a...'. The recommendation grid renders a card titled '打开 URL' with subtitle '9f2c1a4b8e7d3f01', and pressing Enter dispatches open-url with data.url = '9f2c1a4b8e7d3f01' — never the copied link.
recommendation: Carry the real URL on a separate non-hashed field of the clipboard context (or re-read the clipboard at candidate-build time) and keep `content` as the privacy hash.

title: Corrupt item_time_stats JSON crashes the whole recommendation request
summary: getTimeBasedTopItems calls raw JSON.parse on three text columns with no try/catch, inside the un-guarded getCandidates chain. One malformed row aborts recommend() entirely, even though item-time-stats-buckets.ts already ships a tolerant parser (parseStoredTimeBuckets).
evidence:
const parsed: ParsedItemTimeStats = {
  sourceId: raw.sourceId,
  itemId: raw.itemId,
  hourDistribution: JSON.parse(raw.hourDistribution),
  dayOfWeekDistribution: JSON.parse(raw.dayOfWeekDistribution),
  timeSlotDistribution: JSON.parse(raw.timeSlotDistribution),
  lastUpdated: raw.lastUpdated
}
failure_scenario: A single item_time_stats row with a truncated hour_distribution (partial write / disk-full during the additive flush) makes JSON.parse throw SyntaxError. getTimeBasedTopItems rejects -> getCandidates rejects -> recommend() rejects -> handleGetRecommendations in search-core.ts:2023 returns `{items:[], error}` and the CoreBox recommendation grid is permanently empty until the row is deleted.
recommendation: Route both this and TimeStatsAggregator.parseTimeStats through parseStoredTimeBuckets, which already tolerates legacy/short/corrupt payloads.

title: Items never used on today's weekday outrank items used below average
summary: calculateTimeRelevanceScore gives dayFactor = 1 (the neutral value) when the item was never executed on the current weekday, but a below-average weekday count yields a factor < 1. Absence of evidence therefore scores higher than weak evidence.
evidence:
const dayUsage = itemTimeStats.dayOfWeekDistribution[currentTime.dayOfWeek] ?? 0
const avgDayUsage = itemTimeStats.dayOfWeekDistribution.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / 7
const dayFactor = dayUsage > 0 ? dayUsage / (avgDayUsage || 1) : 1
failure_scenario: On a Monday, item A has dayOfWeekDistribution[1] = 0 (never used on Mondays, avg 10/day) -> dayFactor 1. Item B has dayOfWeekDistribution[1] = 2 (avg 10) -> dayFactor 0.2. With equal slot ratios, A scores 5x B, so a never-used-on-Monday app is ranked above one the user actually does use on Mondays.
recommendation: Use dayUsage / (avgDayUsage || 1) unconditionally, or clamp the zero case to a small floor below 1 rather than to the neutral 1.

title: Renderer-reported exposure list is inserted unbounded before the 500-entry prune
summary: recordExposure prunes to EXPOSURE_MAX_ENTRIES before inserting, then inserts every reported key with no cap. The size limit is only applied on the next call, so one oversized IPC report grows the map without bound and also fires 4 aux DB writes.
failure_scenario: The renderer transport handler at search-core.ts:2049 passes `data?.itemKeys ?? []` straight through with no length check. A buggy or compromised renderer reporting 1,000,000 keys inserts 1,000,000 Map entries in the main process, held for the 10-minute TTL, before any prune runs.
recommendation: Slice itemKeys to EXPOSURE_MAX_ENTRIES (or the largest k bucket) at entry, and prune after insertion rather than before.

title: stopBackgroundRefresh leaves the jitter timer armed, so a refresh runs after teardown
summary: startBackgroundRefresh schedules the actual refresh through an untracked setTimeout inside the polling callback. stopBackgroundRefresh only unregisters polling tasks and the migration timer, so a pending jitter timer still fires a full recommendation pass after shutdown.
failure_scenario: The polling tick fires, arms a jitter timer of up to 15s, and SearchEngineCore.destroy() runs stopBackgroundRefresh() 2s later. The timer still fires and runBackgroundRefresh executes recommend({forceRefresh:true}), issuing reads and cache writes against a database handle that is being closed — surfacing as a post-shutdown rejection or a LibSQL 'client is closed' error.
recommendation: Store the jitter timeout handle on the instance and clearTimeout it in stopBackgroundRefresh, alongside resetting refreshInFlight.

title: getTimeBasedTopItems loads the whole item_time_stats table and re-queries every key
summary: Every uncached recommend() reads all of item_time_stats into memory, then passes one key per row to getUsageStatsBatch, which builds two inArray() lists of that size. The work grows linearly with lifetime item count and there is no LIMIT anywhere.
failure_scenario: A user who has executed 20,000 distinct items accumulates 20,000 item_time_stats rows. Each cold recommend() JSON.parses 20,000 rows (yielding only every 50) and issues a single SELECT with two 20,000-element IN lists; past SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER (32,766 total bound parameters) the query fails outright with 'too many SQL variables', and below it the statement still scans a 20,000 x 20,000 candidate cross-product.
recommendation: Add a bounded query (ORDER BY last_updated DESC LIMIT N) for the time-based dimension and chunk the usage-stats batch lookup.

title: getFocusContext shells out to `defaults` with no timeout on every recommendation
summary: Each getCurrentContext() spawns a `defaults read com.apple.ncprefs dnd_prefs` child process with no timeout and no caching. getCurrentContext runs on every recommend(), which is on the CoreBox-open path.
evidence:
const { stdout } = await execFileAsync('defaults', ['read', 'com.apple.ncprefs', 'dnd_prefs'])
const enabled = /\buserPref\s*=\s*1\b|\benabled\s*=\s*1\b/i.test(stdout)
failure_scenario: On macOS the process spawn plus preference read costs tens of milliseconds on every CoreBox open, inside the awaited Promise.all of getCurrentContext. Worse, execFileAsync is called without `timeout`, so if `defaults` blocks (cfprefsd contention / very large ncprefs plist) getCurrentContext never resolves and recommend() hangs forever — the grid stays empty with no error logged.
recommendation: Pass `{ timeout: 500 }` to execFileAsync and cache the DND result for the length of the recommendation cache window.

title: TimeStatsAggregator.parseTimeStats throws on any non-JSON distribution column
summary: parseTimeStats JSON.parses three columns unguarded and is reached from the public getItemTimeStats / getItemTimeStatsBatch API. The tolerant parser in the sibling item-time-stats-buckets.ts is not used here.
failure_scenario: A row whose time_slot_distribution is an empty string (written by a legacy code path, or truncated) makes JSON.parse('') throw 'Unexpected end of JSON input'. getItemTimeStatsBatch rejects and every caller loses its whole batch rather than one row.
recommendation: Delegate to parseStoredTimeBuckets from item-time-stats-buckets.ts, which already returns zero-filled buckets on parse failure.

title: Search-flush drop detection matches on the substring 'dropped' in the error message
summary: flushSearchQueue distinguishes an intentional scheduler drop from a real failure by string-matching the message. Any unrelated error whose text contains 'dropped' silently discards the whole batch instead of merging it back.
failure_scenario: A LibSQL/driver error such as 'connection dropped' or a transaction abort worded with 'dropped' is classified as a deliberate pressure drop. Up to 2,000 aggregated search events (searchCount plus lastSearched for every displayed item) are thrown away and logged only at debug level, so recommendation frequency scores silently lose a flush window.
recommendation: Have scheduleDbWrite reject with a typed/sentinel error (e.g. a DbWriteDroppedError class) and test with instanceof instead of message text.

title: UsageStatsQueue.clear() leaves in-flight flags set, so a racing flush restores cleared data
summary: clear() empties both queues and cancels the timers but leaves searchFlushing/actionFlushing untouched. An in-flight flush that fails afterwards merges its snapshot back into the queue that was explicitly cleared.
failure_scenario: flushActionQueue() is awaiting scheduleDbWrite when a privacy/retention reset calls clear(). The write then fails; the catch runs mergeBack(records, false) and re-adds every execute/cancel aggregate the user just asked to erase, and schedules a flush that persists them.
recommendation: Add a generation counter (or an `aborted` flag set by clear()) that mergeBack checks before restoring a snapshot.

title: Usage-stats cache never memoises misses, so no-history items re-query on every keystroke
summary: getUsageStatsBatchCached only caches rows the database returned. Keys with no item_usage_stats row are recomputed as misses on every call, so the DB round trip never shrinks for fresh items.
failure_scenario: A file search returns 50 results the user has never executed. injectUsageStats runs on every debounced keystroke; each call finds 50 cache misses and issues a getUsageStatsBatch with 100 bound parameters that returns zero rows, on the interactive search path.
recommendation: Store a negative-cache marker (or an explicit tombstone entry) for keys the batch query did not return, with a shorter TTL.

title: TimeStatsAggregator holds a write transaction open across event-loop turns
summary: The rebuild's transaction body awaits setImmediate every 20 upserts. Yielding inside an open SQLite write transaction keeps the WAL writer lock held while unrelated main-process work runs, widening the SQLITE_BUSY window for the search-index worker thread.
failure_scenario: With 5,000 items the rebuild yields 250 times inside one transaction. Each yield lets other main-process I/O run while the writer lock is still held, so the search-index worker's concurrent writes hit SQLITE_BUSY for the full duration of the rebuild instead of for one short transaction.
recommendation: Chunk the upserts into separate scheduleDbWrite transactions and yield between chunks, the pattern backfillTrendDay already uses.

title: Time-stats rebuild loads every execute log into memory with no bound
summary: aggregateTimeStats selects every row of usage_logs with action='execute' via .all() and materialises the full array before aggregating. The user-triggered repair path forces this regardless of table size.
evidence:
const logs = await db
  .select({ sourceId: schema.usageLogs.source, itemId: schema.usageLogs.itemId, timestamp: schema.usageLogs.timestamp })
  .from(schema.usageLogs)
  .where(eq(schema.usageLogs.action, 'execute'))
  .orderBy(desc(schema.usageLogs.timestamp))
  .all()
failure_scenario: A long-lived install with a raised retention window accumulates ~2M execute logs. The IPC handler CoreBoxEvents.recommendation.aggregateTimeStats (search-core.ts:2039) forces the rebuild, materialising ~2M row objects plus a Map of per-item bucket arrays in the main process before a single yield to the event loop.
recommendation: Aggregate with a GROUP BY in SQL, or page through the logs with LIMIT/OFFSET and fold into the buckets incrementally.

title: Semantic profile tokenizer drops every non-ASCII character, blanking CJK app names
summary: splitIdentifier replaces everything outside [a-zA-Z0-9] with whitespace, so identifiers written in Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Cyrillic or accented Latin contribute zero tokens to a candidate's semantic profile.
evidence:
return value
  .replace(/([a-z])([A-Z])/g, '$1 $2')
  .replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9]+/g, ' ')
  .split(/\s+/)
  .map((part) => part.trim().toLowerCase())
  .filter((part) => part.length > 1 && !STOP_TOKENS.has(part))
failure_scenario: A candidate with itemId '/Applications/微信.app' yields only the token 'applications' ('app' is a stop token) — the app name is erased. buildCandidateSemanticProfile then produces a profile indistinguishable from every other CJK-named app, so calculateLocalSemanticScore (weight 6e5, the largest non-context term) scores 网易云音乐, 微信 and 迅雷 identically for every context.
recommendation: Use a Unicode-aware split (e.g. /[^\p{L}\p{N}]+/u) so CJK and accented names produce real tokens, matching the charset widening already applied to the search keyword path.

title: Unbounded plugin manifest priority can pin a feature above exact app title matches
summary: getKindBias adds the plugin-supplied `feature.priority` (typed `priority?: number` in the manifest, never clamped) to the kind bias, which is then multiplied by KIND_SCORE_MULTIPLIER = 300. Nothing bounds the value.
failure_scenario: A plugin declares `"priority": 100000` on a feature. plugin-features-adapter.ts:482 copies it verbatim into meta.priority, and calculateSortScore adds 100000 * 300 = 3e7 — larger than APP_EXACT_TOKEN_INTENT_BONUS (6.2e6) and larger than the maximum realistic match contribution (1000 * 20000 * 1.5 = 3e7). The plugin's feature outranks an exact-title app match for every query it recalls on, contradicting the comment that priority is 'only a soft bias'.
recommendation: Clamp metaPriority to a documented range (e.g. 0..100) when reading the manifest, so a plugin cannot exceed the intent-bonus tiers.

title: lookupByKeywordPrefix leaves LIKE wildcards in the user query unescaped
summary: The prefix pattern is built by string concatenation with no wildcard escaping and no ESCAPE clause, unlike the sibling lookupBySubsequence which escapes via buildSubsequenceLikePattern.
failure_scenario: Typing '%' in CoreBox produces the pattern '%%', which matches every keyword row for the provider; the search returns up to 200 arbitrary unrelated apps as 'prefix matches'. Typing 'a_c' matches 'abc', 'a1c' and so on, silently widening recall beyond what the user typed. lookupBySubsequence in the same class already escapes with SQLITE_LIKE_WILDCARD_REGEX plus an ESCAPE clause, so the two paths disagree on the same input.
recommendation: Reuse the existing wildcard escaping (SQLITE_LIKE_WILDCARD_REGEX + `ESCAPE ${SUBSEQUENCE_LIKE_ESCAPE_CHAR}`) for the prefix pattern.

title: Query completion suggestions run an unescaped, unlimited LIKE on every keystroke
summary: getSuggestions builds the LIKE pattern from raw user text with no wildcard escaping and calls .all() with no LIMIT; the `limit` argument is only applied in JS after every matching row has been loaded and scored.
evidence:
const results = await db
  .select()
  .from(schema.queryCompletions)
  .where(sql`${schema.queryCompletions.prefix} LIKE ${`${prefix}%`}`)
  .all()
failure_scenario: Typing '%' makes the pattern '%%', matching every row of query_completions. injectCompletionWeights calls this on each debounced keystroke of the interactive search path, so the full table is materialised and exp()-scored in JS per keystroke. On a long-lived install with tens of thousands of completion rows this blocks the main process on the hot search path.
recommendation: Escape LIKE metacharacters with an ESCAPE clause and push the ordering plus LIMIT into SQL instead of loading every match.

title: cleanupOldCompletions reports success and a zero count even when the delete is dropped
summary: The delete is scheduled with dropPolicy 'drop', so it can be discarded under write pressure, yet the method unconditionally logs 'Cleaned up old completions' and hard-codes a return of 0 rows — callers cannot distinguish 'nothing expired' from 'the delete never ran'.
evidence:
await scheduleDbWrite(
  'query-completions.cleanup',
  () => db.delete(schema.queryCompletions).where(sql`${schema.queryCompletions.lastCompleted} < ${expirationDate}`),
  { dropPolicy: 'drop', maxQueueWaitMs: 10_000 }
)

timer.end('info')
log.info('Cleaned up old completions', { meta: { cutoffDate: expirationDate.toISOString() } })

return 0
failure_scenario: Maintenance runs while the indexing write queue is saturated. scheduleDbWrite drops the task after 10s, so no rows are deleted, but the log line claims a successful cleanup and the return value (0) is identical to a genuine no-op. Retention past 90 days silently never happens and no signal reaches the operator.
recommendation: Return the delete's rowsAffected and surface the dropped case (either rethrow or log at warn) instead of a hard-coded 0.

title: Recommendation score matching falls back to substring comparison across bundle ids
summary: findScoredByPartialMatch resolves an app item to a scored candidate with a two-way `includes` test whenever either identifier is not a path, so one app can inherit a different app's usage score, badge and _originalItemId.
failure_scenario: The user has both Chrome and Chrome Canary. The rebuilt item for Chrome has id 'com.google.Chrome' (appIdentity form from buildProcessedAppItem), and a scored candidate exists for 'com.google.Chrome.canary'. `s.itemId.includes(itemId)` is true, so Chrome is enriched with Canary's score and, via meta._originalItemId/_originalSourceId, is deduped and pin-matched as Canary. The same happens for com.microsoft.VSCode vs com.microsoft.VSCode.exploration.
recommendation: Require exact identifier equality, or compare against the item's known identity set (path, bundleId, appIdentity) rather than substring containment.

title: Bare itemId lookup shadows the source-qualified key when enriching rebuilt items
summary: mergeAndEnrichItems registers each scored candidate under both its bare itemId and its sourceId:itemId key, then queries the bare key BEFORE the qualified one. Two candidates sharing an itemId across sources collapse to whichever was inserted last.
failure_scenario: item_usage_stats still carries both spellings of the app source ('application' and 'app-provider' — the split usage-source-identity-migration exists to repair). Both candidates keep the same itemId (the app path) and both survive deduplicateCandidates, which keys on sourceId:itemId. scoreMap.get(item.id) then returns whichever candidate appeared later in the candidate list, so the rebuilt app is enriched with an arbitrary one of the two scores rather than the correct or the higher one, and meta._originalSourceId records the arbitrary source.
recommendation: Query the sourceId-qualified key first and keep the bare-itemId entry only as a last-resort fallback.

title: Gather controller promise is rejected but never consumed, producing an unhandled rejection
summary: createGatherController rejects its `promise` on any failure of the gather callback, but the only consumer (SearchSession.attachGather) stores the controller and uses just .abort() and .signal. Nothing ever attaches a rejection handler to IGatherController.promise.
failure_scenario: A fast-layer provider's late result triggers `await dispatcher.emit(...)` (search-gather.ts:388) after createGatherUpdateDispatcher has entered its 'failed' state; emit rejects, the worker rejects, Promise.all(workers) rejects, runFastLayer throws, and the controller callback's `.catch(reject)` rejects the never-consumed `promise`. Under Node's default --unhandled-rejections=throw this terminates the Electron main process.
recommendation: Either attach a handler in attachGather (e.g. `void controller.promise.catch(...)` logging into the session) or stop rejecting the promise and surface failures only through the onUpdate callback.

title: searchFirstResultMetrics entries leak when a session fails or telemetry is off
summary: The per-session metrics map is cleaned up only on normal completion/cancel and inside queueExecuteTelemetry, where the delete sits AFTER the isTelemetryEnabled() early-return. finalizeWithError never deletes at all.
failure_scenario: With telemetry disabled (the privacy default), every search whose gather pipeline hits finalizeWithError leaves its SearchFirstResultMetrics entry — sessionId, durations and a copy of stageDurations — in the map permanently. A provider that fails repeatedly (e.g. a plugin throwing on every query) grows the map by one entry per keystroke for the process lifetime.
recommendation: Move the delete above the telemetry gate and add a delete to finalizeWithError, or key cleanup off session completion rather than off the telemetry path.

title: Fast-layer timeout guard is dead code because didTimeout is overwritten after the race
summary: The timer only sets didTimeout when providers are still outstanding, but line 616 unconditionally reassigns didTimeout from the race outcome, so the `completed < total` guard has no effect.
failure_scenario: All fast providers finish at ~79ms with fastLayerTimeoutMs = 80. The timer fires with completed === total (guard correctly skips) but still resolves 'timeout'; if that settles the race first, didTimeout becomes true anyway. createLayeredSearchController then computes hasPendingAfterFast = true, withholds isDone from the fast-layer emit, and forces an extra `await fastLayerOutcome.completion` plus a second dispatcher round trip even though the search is already complete.
recommendation: Drop the post-race reassignment and let the guarded timer callback be the single writer of didTimeout.

title: upsertScanProgress builds one unbounded multi-row VALUES statement
summary: The legacy (non source-scoped) branch emits a single INSERT with two bound parameters per path and no chunking, while normalizeScanProgressUpsert only dedupes and validates — it applies no size cap. The sibling persistChunk in the same class does chunk.
evidence:
await this.db.run(sql`
  INSERT INTO scan_progress (path, last_scanned)
  VALUES ${sql.join(
    normalizedUpsert.paths.map(
      (entryPath) => sql`(${entryPath}, ${normalizedUpsert.lastScanned.getTime()})`
    ),
    sql`, `
  )}
  ON CONFLICT(path) DO UPDATE SET
    last_scanned = excluded.last_scanned
`)
failure_scenario: A caller (the worker's 'upsertScanProgress' message handler forwards whatever paths array it receives) passes more than ~16,383 completed paths after a large recursive scan. The statement exceeds SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER and fails with 'too many SQL variables', so the entire progress batch is lost atomically and the scan re-walks those roots on the next run.
recommendation: Chunk the VALUES list (e.g. 500 paths per statement) the way persistChunk already does, or cap paths in normalizeScanProgressUpsert.

title: Diversity filter caps the recommendation grid at 5 items when all candidates share a source type
summary: applyDiversityFilter stops accepting a source type once its count reaches ceil(limit*0.4) AND the result has reached limit/2. For a single-type candidate pool both conditions latch simultaneously, so the loop terminates at exactly limit/2 items and never reaches `limit`.
failure_scenario: With the default limit of 10 (search-core.ts:2012 and the empty-query path's `recommend({limit: 10})`), maxPerType is 4 and the half-mark is 5. Every candidate from item_usage_stats for an app carries sourceType 'application', and getCandidates already filters files out, so a typical user's pool is homogeneous. Items 1-5 are pushed (item 5 passes because result.length is still 4), then item 6 onward hits currentCount 5 >= 4 and result.length 5 >= 5 and is skipped forever. The grid renders 5 recommendations instead of 10, and 'more diverse' types never appear because there are none.
recommendation: Do a second pass that backfills from the skipped items once the diverse pass is exhausted, so the cap only reorders rather than truncates the result.

title: Lowering maxCachedViews never shrinks the plugin view cache toward the new cap
summary: updateConfig changes the cap but evicts nothing, and set() only ever evicts a single LRU entry before inserting, so the cache size is net-unchanged. With the cap at 0 the cleanup polling task is also unregistered while set() keeps caching.
failure_scenario: A user lowers the cached-view setting from 4 to 0 to reclaim memory. ensureCleanupTask unregisters 'core-box.view-cache.cleanup', but set() has no cap check of its own: the next plugin view evicts one entry and inserts itself, leaving a live WebContentsView (a full renderer process) resident with no stale-cleanup task to ever reclaim it. Lowering 4 to 1 likewise leaves the cache pinned at 4 WebContentsViews indefinitely.
recommendation: Evict down to the new cap inside updateConfig, and make set() a no-op (or immediately close) when maxCachedViews is 0.

title: Plugin recommendation providers are polled sequentially with an uncleared timeout each
summary: getPluginCandidates awaits each provider inside a for-of loop, so the 200ms PLUGIN_PROVIDER_TIMEOUT_MS budget is per provider rather than shared, and the setTimeout that arms each race is never cleared when the provider wins.
failure_scenario: Six plugins register recommendation providers and each takes the full 200ms (or hangs to the timeout). getCandidates blocks for 1.2s on every uncached recommend(), which is the CoreBox empty-query path — the user sees an empty grid for over a second on every open. Each iteration also leaves an unreferenced 200ms timer pending even when the provider resolved immediately.
recommendation: Run the providers with Promise.allSettled so the timeout budget is shared, and clear the race timer in a finally block.

title: forceRefresh still pays for the DB recommendation-cache read it will discard
summary: recommend() awaits getCachedRecommendations unconditionally and only afterwards checks options.forceRefresh, so a forced refresh performs a cache-key build, a SELECT on recommendation_cache, a JSON.parse of the stored item list and a dedupe pass whose result is thrown away.
failure_scenario: The 15-minute background refresh calls recommend({forceRefresh: true}). Each run issues an extra aux+primary lookup (getRecommendationCache falls back to the primary db when the aux row is missing) and JSON.parses a serialized list of up to 10 fully-rendered TuffItems before discarding it. The same waste applies to every user-triggered refresh from the CoreBox IPC handler.
recommendation: Guard the call: `const cached = options.forceRefresh ? null : await this.getCachedRecommendations(...)`.

title: Router unsubscribe strands pending coalesced watch deltas instead of flushing them
summary: unsubscribe() detaches every event-bus handler and then calls queue.dispose(), which only clears the debounce timer — its own doc says pending entries stay queued 'for the next flush', but no further enqueue can happen because the handlers are gone.
failure_scenario: A user drags an app into /Applications and quits Touch within the 400ms APP_WATCH_COALESCE_WINDOW_MS. SearchEngineCore.destroy() calls indexedSourceEventRouter.unsubscribe(), the debounce timer is cleared before it fires, and the coalesced 'add' is discarded with no reconcile marker — the index stays stale until the next startup scan re-walks the source.
recommendation: Call flushSoon() (and await the resulting task chain) before dispose(), or have dispose() drain the pending map.

title: Frequent/recent candidate queries full-scan and sort item_usage_stats on every cold recommend
summary: getFrequentItems orders by execute_count and getRecentItems orders by last_executed, but item_usage_stats declares only its composite primary key and a retention expression index — neither ordering column is indexed, so both queries are a full scan plus a temp B-tree sort.
failure_scenario: item_usage_stats grows by one row per distinct item ever searched or executed, and recordDisplayedResults enqueues a 'search' increment for the top 10 results of every query — so the table reaches tens of thousands of rows quickly. Each cold recommend() (CoreBox empty query, plus the 15-minute background refresh) runs two full scans with SELECT * plus a sort to return 30 and 20 rows respectively, on the main process's DB connection.
recommendation: Add descending indexes on execute_count and last_executed (or a single covering index) so both LIMIT queries can be served from an index scan.

title: Searches arriving after teardown are accepted because both shutdown guards are ineffective
summary: SearchSessionRegistry.destroy() nulls its own destroyPromise in a finally block, so the 'registry is shutting down' guard only holds during the drain. SearchEngineCore.startSearch never checks this.destroying either, so a late request creates a live session against torn-down services.
failure_scenario: SearchEngineCore.destroy() sets destroying = true and drains the registry; the drain completes and destroyPromise resets to null. A renderer search stream that arrives afterwards (the CoreBox window outlives the module teardown ordering) reaches startSearch, which has no destroying check, creates a session and runs providers whose dbUtils/indexWriter handles are already closed — surfacing to the user as a stream error instead of a clean 'engine unavailable'.
recommendation: Keep destroyPromise (or a separate `destroyed` flag) latched after the drain, and add a `this.destroying` guard at the top of startSearch.

title: Prerendered docs pages ship canonical/hreflang/og:url pointing at http://localhost
summary: The docs SEO head is built from `useRequestURL().origin`. During Nitro prerender there is no real request host, so every one of the ~482 prerendered HTML files bakes in `http://localhost` for rel=canonical, og:url, all hreflang alternates and the JSON-LD `url`/`@id`. There is no site-url/baseURL fallback anywhere in nuxt.config.ts.
evidence:
app/pages/docs/[...slug].vue:42 `const requestUrl = useRequestURL()`
app/pages/docs/[...slug].vue:1051 `origin: requestUrl.origin,`
app/utils/docs-seo.ts:43 `const canonicalUrl = resolveDocsAbsoluteUrl(input.origin, canonicalLocalePath)`
Built output dist/en/docs/index.html: `<link rel="canonical" href="http://localhost/en/docs">`, `<meta property="og:url" content="http://localhost/en/docs">`, `hreflang="zh-CN" href="http://localhost/zh/docs"`
failure_scenario: `pnpm -C apps/nexus build` prerenders 496 HTML files; 482 of them contain `rel="canonical" href="http://localhost..."` (verified by `grep -rl 'rel="canonical" href="http://localhost' dist --include='*.html' | wc -l`). Once deployed, a crawler fetching https://<site>/en/docs is told the canonical URL lives on http://localhost, so the page is dropped from the index and every hreflang alternate resolves to an unreachable host.
recommendation: Resolve the origin from a configured public site URL (runtimeConfig.public.siteUrl / AUTH_ORIGIN) and only fall back to useRequestURL() when a real request host exists.

title: Web Push handler SW is registered at the same scope as the PWA SW and gets replaced
summary: `/notification-sw.js` is registered with no `scope` option, so it claims scope `/`. The @vite-pwa/nuxt worker `/sw.js` is configured with `scope: '/'` too and re-registers on every page load because `registerType: 'autoUpdate'`. A service-worker registration is keyed by (origin, scope), so the two scripts overwrite each other; whichever registered last owns the scope.
evidence:
app/pages/dashboard/notifications.vue:234 `return await navigator.serviceWorker.register('/notification-sw.js')`
app/config/pwa.ts:5-12 `const scope = '/'` … `registerType: 'autoUpdate', scope, base: scope,`
Built bundle contains both: `navigator.serviceWorker.register("/notification-sw.js")` and the vite-pwa `register(c.sn,c.nn)` with `scope:"/"`.
failure_scenario: A user enables Web Push on /dashboard/notifications: `notification-sw.js` takes scope `/` and `pushManager.subscribe()` stores a subscription on that registration. On the next page load the PWA plugin re-registers `/sw.js` at scope `/`, replacing the script. The push subscription survives on the registration but is now served by the generated `sw.js`, which has no `push` listener (public/notification-sw.js:1 is the only `addEventListener('push', ...)` in the repo), so every delivered push is silently dropped and no notification is ever shown.
recommendation: Register the push handler under a dedicated scope (e.g. `/push/`) or move the `push`/`notificationclick` listeners into the vite-pwa worker via `injectManifest`/`importScripts`.

title: Docs "Edit this page" link points at a GitHub repo that is not this project
summary: The edit-on-GitHub URL is built from a hard-coded `AJLoveChina/talex-touch` slug. The repository's own remote is `https://github.com/talex-touch/tuff.git`, and every other GitHub reference in app/ and content/ uses `talex-touch/tuff`.
evidence:
app/pages/docs/[...slug].vue:1366 `const GITHUB_REPO = 'AJLoveChina/talex-touch'`
app/pages/docs/[...slug].vue:1371 `return `https://github.com/${GITHUB_REPO}/edit/master/apps/nexus/content${path}.mdc``
`git remote -v` → `origin https://github.com/talex-touch/tuff.git`
failure_scenario: A reader opens any docs page and clicks the "Edit this page" affordance rendered at app/pages/docs/[...slug].vue:2023. The browser navigates to https://github.com/AJLoveChina/talex-touch/edit/master/apps/nexus/content/docs/guide/start.en.mdc, which is not this project's repository, so the contributor gets a 404 instead of the editor. The link is present on all ~230 docs pages.
recommendation: Set GITHUB_REPO to `talex-touch/tuff` (or read it from runtimeConfig so it cannot drift again).

title: /dashboard/notifications renders hard-coded Chinese for English users (23 missing keys)
summary: The page calls `t('dashboard.notifications.*', '<Chinese default>')` for its title, description, filters, empty states, buttons and relative-time labels, but the `notifications` block in i18n/locales/route/en/dashboard.ts only defines `unreadBadgeLabel`, `browser.*` and `errors.*`. vue-i18n falls back to the second argument, so the Chinese literal is what renders.
evidence:
app/pages/dashboard/notifications.vue:420 `{{ t('dashboard.notifications.title', '通知中心') }}`
app/pages/dashboard/notifications.vue:423 `{{ t('dashboard.notifications.description', '查看浏览器通知与平台投递记录。') }}`
app/pages/dashboard/notifications.vue:555 `filter === 'unread' ? t('dashboard.notifications.emptyUnread', '暂无未读通知') : t('dashboard.notifications.emptyAll', '暂无通知')`
i18n/locales/route/en/dashboard.ts:630 `notifications: {` … block contains no `title`, `description`, `emptyAll`, `markRead`, `unread`, `filters`, `refresh`, `markAllRead` keys.
failure_scenario: An English-locale user opens /dashboard/notifications. Because `dashboard.notifications.title` does not exist in either the en or zh chunk, the heading renders as 通知中心, the filter chips as 未读/全部, and the buttons as 标记已读 — 23 such sites on this page alone.
recommendation: Add the missing `dashboard.notifications.*` keys to both locale chunks and drop the inline Chinese defaults.

title: /dashboard/team renders hard-coded Chinese for English users (40 missing keys)
summary: 40 `t(key, '<Chinese default>')` call sites on the team page reference `dashboard.team.*` keys that exist in neither i18n/locales/route/en/dashboard.ts nor the zh chunk, so the Chinese default is what every locale sees.
evidence:
app/pages/dashboard/team.vue:242 `t('dashboard.team.success.teamCreated', '团队创建成功')`
app/pages/dashboard/team.vue:506 `t('dashboard.team.pending', ...)`
app/pages/dashboard/team.vue:575 `t('dashboard.team.modal.createTitle', ...)`
None of `dashboard.team.success.*`, `dashboard.team.errors.*`, `dashboard.team.modal.*` resolve against the merged en message tree (en.ts + route/en/dashboard.ts + route/en/landing.ts).
failure_scenario: An English user creates a team on /dashboard/team; the success toast reads 团队创建成功 and the invite dialog title, pending state and error toasts are all Chinese. Verified programmatically: 40 missing-key sites with CJK defaults in this file.
recommendation: Add the `dashboard.team.*` subtree to both locale chunks; keep English text out of Chinese defaults.

title: 91 i18n call sites across 12 files fall back to Chinese literals in every locale
summary: A repo-wide scan of `t('<key>', '<default>')` against the merged English message tree (i18n/locales/en.ts + route/en/dashboard.ts + route/en/landing.ts) finds 91 call sites whose key is absent and whose default contains CJK. Beyond team.vue (40) and notifications.vue (23) the remaining 28 sit on auth-critical pages.
evidence:
app/pages/device-auth.vue:49 `t('auth.deviceAuthLongSessionWindow', '长期授权需要在重新登录后的 10 分钟内确认。')`
app/pages/reset-password.vue:34 `t('auth.resetTokenMissing', '重置链接无效')`
app/pages/verify.vue:29 `t('auth.verifyMissing', '缺少验证信息')`
app/pages/dashboard.vue:30 `t('auth.redirecting', '正在跳转登录...')`
app/pages/dashboard/assets.vue:1290 `t('common.retry', '重试')`
app/components/dashboard/DashboardNav.vue:257 `t('dashboard.sections.menu.risk', '风控控制面')`
failure_scenario: An English user hits an expired password-reset link on /reset-password: the error banner reads 重置链接无效. Same for the device-authorization flow (12 sites), email verification (4 sites) and the generic Retry/Collapse buttons — none of these keys exist in any locale file, so no translation can ever apply.
recommendation: Add the missing keys to both locale chunks; add a CI check that fails when a `t()` key is absent from en.ts.

title: Release links on /updates point at a non-existent talex-touch/tuff-nexus repo
summary: Five release entries link to `github.com/talex-touch/tuff-nexus/releases/tag/...`. The project repository is `talex-touch/tuff`; `tuff-nexus` is the package name (@talex-touch/tuff-nexus), not a GitHub repo, and no other reference in the codebase uses that slug for a URL.
evidence:
app/data/updates.ts:85 `href: 'https://github.com/talex-touch/tuff-nexus/releases/tag/v2.0.0-preview',`
app/data/updates.ts:100,115,130,145 — same slug for v2.0.0-dev.5, v1.2.0, v1.1.0, v1.0.0
`git remote -v` → `https://github.com/talex-touch/tuff.git`
failure_scenario: A visitor on /updates clicks the release-notes link for any of the five listed versions and lands on a GitHub 404 because the `tuff-nexus` repository does not exist under the talex-touch org.
recommendation: Point the hrefs at `talex-touch/tuff` releases, or at the in-app /updates detail route.

title: Extension docs link to an AkraTech/talex-touch repo that is not the project repo
summary: Both locale variants of the unplugin-export-plugin doc link plugin examples and the CHANGELOG to `github.com/AkraTech/talex-touch`, a slug used nowhere else in the repo. Every other content link uses `talex-touch/tuff`.
evidence:
content/docs/dev/extensions/unplugin-export-plugin.en.mdc:401 `- [touch-image](https://github.com/AkraTech/talex-touch/tree/main/plugins/touch-image) - Image processing plugin`
content/docs/dev/extensions/unplugin-export-plugin.zh.mdc:409 `查看 [CHANGELOG.md](https://github.com/AkraTech/talex-touch/blob/main/packages/unplugin-export-plugin/CHANGELOG.md) 获取版本更新信息。`
failure_scenario: A plugin developer reading /en/docs/dev/extensions/unplugin-export-plugin clicks any of the three example-plugin links or the CHANGELOG link and gets a GitHub 404, because the repo lives at talex-touch/tuff and the plugins are under `plugins/` there.
recommendation: Rewrite the six links to `talex-touch/tuff` paths.

title: system.executeCommand / system.openApp pass unvalidated input to shell.openPath
summary: Two transport handlers forward a caller-supplied string straight into shell.openPath() with no path allowlist, no extension check, and no caller-identity check. shell.openPath executes .app/.exe/.sh/.command targets rather than merely revealing them. The same file validates showInFolder with fs.stat (lines 49-76), so the validation capability exists but was not applied to the two most dangerous entry points.
failure_scenario: A compromised renderer (reachable via the wide-open CSP) or any plugin UI view (reachable because transport handlers are registered on the plugin channel too) sends AppEvents.system.executeCommand with command='/Applications/Calculator.app' or a dropped payload path. The main process launches it. Combined with the arbitrary-file-write in addon-opener.ts, this yields write-then-execute local code execution.
recommendation: Delete executeCommand or restrict it to pre-registered command IDs. Constrain openApp to entries from the existing app index / launch-plan layer. Require context.plugin === undefined on both so only the host renderer can call them. Violates Electron security checklist items 14 and 17.

title: Every transport handler is registered on both MAIN and PLUGIN channels with no default deny
summary: TuffMainTransport.on() registers the identical channelHandler on BRIDGE_CHANNEL.MAIN and BRIDGE_CHANNEL.PLUGIN. The plugin-view preload exposes $channel.send(eventName, payload) (src/preload/plugin-view.ts:71) whose implementation (src/preload/plugin-view-channel.ts:254) applies no event-name allowlist. Checking context.plugin is voluntary per handler; common.ts:1181-1185 does it for temp files, but the shell, window, and debug handlers do not.
failure_scenario: A malicious or compromised plugin's UI view calls $channel.send('system:execute-command', {command: '/path/to/payload'}). Because the handler is also bound to the plugin channel and never inspects context.plugin, the main process honours it. The window-level sandbox (sandbox:true, contextIsolation:true, per-plugin partition, navigation policy) is fully bypassed at the IPC layer.
recommendation: Add a required audience discriminator to transport.on() ('host' | 'plugin' | 'both') and only bind PLUGIN-channel handlers for events that opt in. Add an event-name allowlist inside plugin-view-channel.ts as defence in depth. Violates Electron security checklist item 17.

title: Renderer CSP is effectively disabled (script-src * with unsafe-inline and unsafe-eval)
summary: The only CSP in the project is this meta tag. There is no session.defaultSession.webRequest.onHeadersReceived injecting a CSP header anywhere in the repo. script-src * permits script loading from any remote origin, and unsafe-inline plus unsafe-eval permit arbitrary inline execution.
failure_scenario: Any injection point that reaches the renderer DOM (Markdown rendering, plugin-supplied rich text, AI-returned content, a remote image URL that is actually a script) executes attacker JS. That JS holds window.electron.ipcRenderer (preload/index.ts:139), so it can call system.executeCommand and reach local code execution. The CSP is the only barrier and it is absent.
recommendation: Tighten to default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; connect-src 'self' plus the known backend origins (ws://localhost:* in dev only); img-src 'self' data: blob: tfile:. Deliver it via session.defaultSession.webRequest.onHeadersReceived rather than a meta tag, since meta CSP does not cover worker contexts. Violates Electron security checklist items 6 and 7.

title: Plugin install handlers build temp paths from an unsanitized IPC-supplied name (path traversal / arbitrary file write)
summary: Both name and buffer come from the IPC payload. name is interpolated into path.join with no sanitisation before fs.writeFile. The same pattern repeats at line 285 in dropPluginHandler.
failure_scenario: A caller sends name='../../../Library/LaunchAgents/com.evil.plist' with a matching buffer. path.join resolves out of os.tmpdir() and writes a fully attacker-controlled file to a persistence location. On macOS a LaunchAgent write is equivalent to persistent code execution; equivalent targets exist on Windows (Startup folder) and Linux (~/.config/autostart).
recommendation: Apply path.basename(name) then filter to [^a-zA-Z0-9._-], and assert path.resolve(tempFilePath).startsWith(path.resolve(os.tmpdir())) before writing. Better: ignore name entirely for the filename, use randomUUID(), and keep name only for logging.

title: will-navigate forwards any URL to shell.openExternal with no scheme allowlist, and the confirm branch never confirms
summary: Every TouchWindow forwards any attempted navigation to the OPEN_EXTERNAL_URL bus. The consumer (channel/common.ts:1086-1095) resolves 'open' for file: and 'confirm' for every other protocol, and the 'confirm' branch just logs a debug line and calls shell.openExternal anyway. The repo already has validateExternalUrl() in src/main/utils/external-url-policy.ts with an http/https/mailto/tel/tuff allowlist, used correctly in a dozen other call sites, but not here.
failure_scenario: Injected renderer content sets location.href to a hostile scheme URI (smb://, search-ms:, vscode://, or any registered OS handler). The main process passes it unfiltered to shell.openExternal, invoking the OS handler. Users never see the confirmation prompt the code's own naming promises.
recommendation: Replace both shell.openExternal(url) calls in createOpenUrlHandler with openValidatedExternalUrl(url, { opener: shell.openExternal }). Either make the 'confirm' branch actually show dialog.showMessageBox or merge it into 'open' and rename, so the code stops misreporting its own behaviour. Violates Electron security checklist items 13 and 14.

title: ipcMain.handle registrations never validate event.senderFrame
summary: Every transport event opens a global ipcMain.handle channel. The handler puts event.sender into context (lines 701-708) but never checks event.senderFrame.url or whether the sender belongs to a trusted window. The parallel channel-core.ts path does resolve identity via resolvePluginRegistrationByWebContents; the invoke path has no equivalent constraint.
failure_scenario: Any webContents in the process that can guess or read an event name invokes a privileged main-process handler directly through ipcRenderer.invoke, bypassing whatever identity resolution the channel-core path performs.
recommendation: Add a shared guard at the top of the ipcMain.handle callback that validates event.senderFrame origin against the app's own file:// entry or the dev-server origin, and routes plugin-partition senders through the same audience check proposed for the double-channel registration issue. Violates Electron security checklist item 17.

title: Preload bridges the entire electronAPI including raw ipcRenderer into the renderer world
summary: @electron-toolkit/preload's electronAPI is a generic wrapper that bridges ipcRenderer send/on/invoke/sendSync wholesale. The renderer consumes it directly at apps/core-app/src/renderer/src/modules/channel/channel-core.ts:12 (const ipcRenderer = window.electron.ipcRenderer), so this is a live dependency, not dead surface.
evidence:
contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld('electron', electronAPI)
    contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld('api', api)
failure_scenario: Any script executing in the renderer world (trivially reachable given script-src *) can send to any IPC channel name. contextIsolation is still on, but its benefit is largely neutralised because the bridged surface is the full IPC primitive rather than a narrow typed API, leaving preload no place to enforce an event allowlist.
recommendation: Stop exposing electronAPI. Keep ipcRenderer private inside preload and expose only the typed transport domain methods through contextBridge. Violates the intent of Electron security checklist items 2 and 3 (expose a minimal API surface).

title: Privileged transport MessagePort is transferred with wildcard targetOrigin
summary: After the main process hands a transport MessagePort to preload, preload re-posts it into the page world with '*' as targetOrigin. The receiving side (subscribeTransportPortHandoff, lines 144-147) only checks event.source === targetWindow, which injected page scripts trivially satisfy.
evidence:
targetWindow.postMessage(
        { marker: TRANSPORT_PORT_HANDOFF_MARKER, payload } satisfies TransportPortHandoffMessage,
        '*',
failure_scenario: An injected script registers a message listener and receives the transferred MessagePort, gaining the high-privilege streaming transport channel directly. This bypasses any gating preload might apply, and the port remains usable for the lifetime of the page.
recommendation: Use window.location.origin (with the 'file://' special case already implemented in this repo's sendPreloadEvent) instead of '*'. Better still, consume the port inside preload and expose only wrapped methods, never transferring the raw port into the page world.

title: tuff://auth/callback deep link sets the session token with no state/nonce binding (login CSRF)
summary: The app registers itself as the tuff: protocol client (addon-opener.ts:194). The auth/callback deep-link handler pulls token and app_token straight from query params and passes them to applyExternalAuthCallback, which lands at auth/index.ts:1186 as await setAuthToken(resolvedToken) after only a non-empty check. The real login flow is device-code based (auth/index.ts:255-284); this path bypasses that binding entirely.
evidence:
const token = url.searchParams.get('token') || ''
      const appToken = url.searchParams.get('app_token') || ''
        void applyExternalAuthCallback(token, appToken)
failure_scenario: A hostile web page navigates the user's browser to tuff://auth/callback?token=<attacker_token>. The main process silently swaps the user's session to the attacker's account. Everything the victim subsequently does in the app (sync, AI conversations, stored credentials) is written under the attacker's account, where the attacker can read it.
recommendation: Generate a single-use state value when constructing the authorize URL, hold it in main-process memory, and reject any callback whose state is missing, mismatched, or expired. Apply the same binding to the auth/stepup handler at lines 66-77.

title: No permission handler is installed on session.defaultSession
summary: This is the only setPermissionCheckHandler / setPermissionRequestHandler pair in the repo, and it is scoped to the per-plugin session. session.defaultSession, shared by the main window, CoreBox, Assistant, Screenshot and OmniPanel windows, has no handler at all. Electron's default is to approve permission requests.
failure_scenario: Script running in the main renderer silently obtains camera, microphone, geolocation or clipboard-read permission with no prompt and no policy. The macOS entitlements plus NSCameraUsageDescription / NSMicrophoneUsageDescription in electron-builder.yml mean the OS-level grants are already in place, so the Electron layer is the only remaining gate and it is open.
recommendation: Install an explicit allowlist handler on defaultSession: permit only what the product needs (media for the voice assistant, clipboard-read), deny everything else, and constrain the requesting origin to the app's own entry URL. Violates Electron security checklist item 4.

title: Plugin channel key is passed through renderer process command-line arguments
summary: The plugin's _uniqueChannelKey is packed into the bootstrap argument and handed to buildWindowWebPreferences as additionalArguments, which become real command-line arguments of the renderer process.
failure_scenario: Any unprivileged process on the machine reads the key from the process table (ps -ww on macOS/Linux, WMI on Windows). Because resolveChannelCallerIdentity accepts a self-declared uniqueKey as an identity source when the sender is not a registered plugin webContents, this key is a bearer credential, not inert config.
recommendation: Deliver the key over MessageChannelMain after did-finish-load, or transfer the port itself. Keep additionalArguments limited to non-sensitive metadata such as bridgeVersion and plugin name.

title: Caller identity can be self-declared via uniqueKey when the sender is not a registered plugin view
summary: When the sender misses the webContents registry lookup, the function falls back to trusting the key carried in the message itself and returns that plugin's name. It does not populate pluginIdentity, so the strict check in main-transport.ts:607-617 still rejects, but every handler that reads only data.plugin is fooled.
evidence:
const declaredIdentity = input.resolveIdentity(input.declaredKey)
  return declaredIdentity ? { pluginName: declaredIdentity.name } : {}
failure_scenario: Any webContents holding a plugin key (readable from the process table per the additionalArguments issue) impersonates that plugin on the PLUGIN channel. Handlers that gate on the plugin name string alone -- storage namespacing, quota accounting, permission lookups -- attribute the caller's actions to the impersonated plugin.
recommendation: Remove the fallback. Identity should come only from resolvePluginRegistrationByWebContents(senderId); declaredKey should be used solely as a consistency check that causes rejection on mismatch, never as an identity source.

title: debug.openDevTools is reachable in packaged builds with no caller check
summary: The handler has neither an app.isPackaged guard nor a context.plugin check, and per the double-channel registration issue it is bound to the plugin channel as well. Note that touch-app.ts:372-378 deliberately disables Ctrl+R in packaged builds, so the intent to restrict debug affordances in production exists but was not applied here.
failure_scenario: A plugin view calls debug.openDevTools and opens DevTools on the main application window in a released build. DevTools executes arbitrary JS in the main renderer and exposes all in-memory renderer state, including auth tokens -- a clean privilege-escalation step out of the plugin sandbox.
recommendation: Return early when app.isPackaged, or at minimum require context.plugin === undefined and gate on an explicit developer-mode setting.

title: A malformed IPC payload throws out of the ipcMain.on listener with no production uncaughtException handler
summary: __parse_raw_data throws when the payload has no header object, and its only caller __handle_main (lines 288-289) invokes it with no try/catch. The exception propagates out of the EventEmitter as an uncaught main-process exception. The repo's only process.on('uncaughtException') is in utils/dev-process-manager.ts:50, and that file returns early when app.isPackaged (lines 38-40), so production has no handler.
evidence:
channelLog.error('[Channel] Invalid message payload', { error: e, payload: arg })
    throw new Error('Invalid message!')
failure_scenario: Any renderer or plugin view calls ipcRenderer.send('@main-process-message', 'x'). The main process terminates. This is a one-line denial of service from the least-privileged context in the app, and it takes unsaved state with it.
recommendation: Wrap __handle_main in try/catch, log and drop unparseable messages, and reply with an ERROR code for sync requests. Separately, register a production uncaughtException handler in precore.ts to match the existing unhandledRejection handler at line 40.

title: tfile and stream schemes are registered with bypassCSP: true
summary: The tfile scheme is registered privileged with bypassCSP. The stream scheme gets the same treatment at src/main/service/protocol-handler.ts:5 despite having no protocol.handle implementation anywhere -- that file only registers a 410 responder for the retired atom scheme.
evidence:
stream: true,
      bypassCSP: true,
      corsEnabled: true
failure_scenario: Resources loaded through tfile: ignore the page CSP entirely. Even after the renderer CSP is tightened, tfile: remains an unclosed bypass, and the file-protocol module resolves it to local files under a home-directory-level allowlist. The stream registration grants CSP-bypass privilege to a scheme with no handler, which is pure latent attack surface.
recommendation: Drop bypassCSP from tfile and instead list tfile: explicitly in the CSP img-src / media-src directives (index.html already does this, making bypassCSP redundant). Delete the stream scheme registration outright.

title: macOS builds are unsigned, un-notarized, and only produce a dir target
summary: Three problems coincide: notarize:false and gatekeeperAssess:false with forceCodeSigning:false at both mac scope (line 125) and top level (line 160); hardenedRuntime:true which is inert without signing; and mac.target of dir only, arm64 only, which is neither distributable nor consumable by the configured publish:github provider. The dmg: key is an empty value.
evidence:
notarize: false
  gatekeeperAssess: false
  forceCodeSigning: false
failure_scenario: Every macOS user who downloads a release hits a Gatekeeper block and must right-click-open or run xattr -d to launch it, training them to bypass OS security warnings on this app. Intel Mac users get no artifact at all, and the release pipeline has nothing publishable to upload.
recommendation: Set notarize:true and forceCodeSigning:true in the release profile, wire CSC_LINK / APPLE_ID CI secrets, change target to dmg plus zip (electron-updater needs zip on macOS), and add x64 or universal. If this is intentionally a local debug configuration, split it into a separate electron-builder.dev.yml so it cannot ship by accident.

title: Windows update code-signature verification is disabled
summary: verifyUpdateCodeSignature:false turns off publisher-signature verification of downloaded Windows update packages. The app does ship its own sha256 checking (update-system.ts:548-549) and a release-signing public key (electron-builder.yml:71-72), but disabling the platform check removes an independent layer.
evidence: verifyUpdateCodeSignature: false
failure_scenario: An attacker who can serve or tamper with an update artifact (compromised release asset, MITM against a non-pinned endpoint, or a flaw in the in-house verification code) gets their installer executed with no OS-level publisher check to catch it. Update integrity rests entirely on one in-house implementation.
recommendation: Remove the line once a Windows code-signing certificate is available (the default is true). While it stays, document the weakening in the release notes and confirm the in-house signature check hard-fails rather than warning and continuing.

title: loadModule returns false for three distinct reasons and the startup loader treats all of them as fatal
summary: loadModule returns false when the module is already loaded (lines 358-360), when it is skipped by an env flag (lines 363-372), and when a lifecycle phase actually fails. loadStartupModules cannot distinguish them and throws for any false on a non-optional module (startup-module-loader.ts:57), which index.ts catches and turns into app.quit(). No module currently declares env, so this is latent, but isModuleEnvEnabled (lines 867-873) clearly exists to be used.
failure_scenario: The first developer to add env: ['TUFF_SOMETHING'] to a module ships an app that quits during startup on every machine where that environment variable is unset. The failure presents as a silent exit with a generic 'Required module failed to load' message that names the module but not the real cause.
recommendation: Change loadModule to return a discriminated result ({ status: 'loaded' | 'already-loaded' | 'skipped-by-env' | 'failed' }) and have loadStartupModules throw only for 'failed'.

title: 35 of 36 foreground modules are mandatory; any single init failure quits the app
summary: The foreground module list at lines 171-210 contains 36 modules and only the tray is optional. Any non-optional module returning false makes loadStartupModules throw, which the catch block at lines 390-402 converts into setQuitIntent('startup-failure') plus app.quit().
evidence: const optionalModulesToLoad = new Set([trayManagerModule])
failure_scenario: voiceModule, terminalModule, downloadCenterModule, syncModule or screenshotSessionModule fails to init because of a full disk, a native dependency that will not load on that OS build, or a network timeout. The entire launcher refuses to start, even though the user only wanted to search for a file. The blast radius of a peripheral feature equals total unavailability.
recommendation: Split the list into core (database, storage, shortcut, CoreBox, plugin) and enhancement tiers. Put voice, terminal, download, sync, screenshot and AI in the optional set so failures degrade and surface through the existing analytics message store instead of aborting startup.

title: Single-instance guard's quit does not preempt the whenReady bootstrap
summary: setupSingleInstanceGuard returns false for a duplicate instance (single-instance-guard.ts:56-57) but precore.ts discards the return value, and index.ts's whenReady callback (line 227) has no corresponding check. The app.quit() it issues is then intercepted by precore's own before-quit handler at line 302, which calls event.preventDefault() and runs an async shutdown flow with an 8 second timeout.
failure_scenario: A second launch executes all of precore's side effects and, during the window before its deferred quit completes, whenReady may fire and begin loading databaseModule. Two processes then open the same libsql file concurrently, risking index corruption or lock contention. Marked low confidence because the exact interleaving depends on Electron's internal ready timing and I did not run it.
recommendation: Have the guard's return value set a module-level isDuplicateInstance flag, check it at the top of the whenReady callback and return immediately, and make the before-quit handler skip preventDefault for the duplicate-instance intent.

title: Dev-plugin install accepts an arbitrary filesystem path from the renderer
summary: Beyond a non-empty check there is no validation before installDevPluginFromPath reads and installs from the supplied path. The handler has no app.isPackaged guard, so it is live in release builds, and per the double-channel registration issue it is reachable from the plugin channel.
failure_scenario: A plugin view invokes the dev-install event pointing at a directory it has staged elsewhere on disk (for example via the temp-file API), causing the host to install a second attacker-authored plugin. That is lateral movement from one plugin's sandbox into a freshly registered plugin with its own permissions.
recommendation: Return DEV_ONLY when app.isPackaged, require context.plugin === undefined, and constrain the resolved path to a directory the user explicitly chose through dialog.showOpenDialog.

title: Window and plugin-view security profile parameters are unused, making the profile system decorative
summary: buildWindowWebPreferences takes a WindowSecurityProfile it never reads (underscore-prefixed), so 'app' and 'trusted-plugin-view' produce byte-identical preferences. The same pattern appears at plugin-view-host.ts:49. Callers such as plugin-view-controller.ts:250 compute securityProfile.effectiveProfile through real decision logic whose conclusion is then discarded.
failure_scenario: The current output happens to be safe (both profiles get the strictest baseline), but the API advertises a tiering that does not exist. A future change that relaxes the 'trusted-plugin-view' profile would silently apply to every window in the app, including the main window, because the parameter that was supposed to separate them is ignored.
recommendation: Either implement real tiering (e.g. additional hardening such as disableBlinkFeatures for plugin views) or delete the parameter and the WindowSecurityProfile type so the single-baseline reality is explicit in the code.

title: App-profile WebContentsViews get no navigation policy or window-open handler
summary: MetaOverlay constructs a WebContentsView and never installs navigation guards. The same gap exists in plugin-view-controller.ts:266 and division-box/session.ts, where navigationPolicy is null whenever plugin is absent, so installPluginViewNavigationPolicy is skipped. Plugin views by contrast get full coverage at plugin-window-policy.ts:534-548.
evidence: this.metaView = new WebContentsView({ webPreferences })
failure_scenario: Content in one of these views calls window.open and gets an uncontrolled new window created with default preferences, or navigates the view to an arbitrary URL. Unlike TouchWindow, which at least has the (flawed) will-navigate listener, these views have nothing at all.
recommendation: Extract an installAppViewNavigationPolicy() and apply it to every app-profile view: at minimum setWindowOpenHandler(() => ({ action: 'deny' })) plus a will-navigate handler restricted to the application's own entry URL. Violates Electron security checklist items 12 and 13.

title: Two window sites hand-roll webPreferences instead of using the central builder
summary: buildWindowWebPreferences is valuable precisely because it is the single entry point and strips caller overrides of managed keys. These two sites bypass it. The hand-written sets omit webSecurity:true, nodeIntegrationInSubFrames:false and webviewTag:false from the baseline. Second instance at box-tool/core-box/image-translate-pin-window.ts:390.
failure_scenario: Current Electron defaults happen to make the omissions safe, so nothing is broken today. The risk is drift: when a future hardening flag is added to SECURITY_BASE, these two windows silently do not receive it, and both load data: URLs with interpolated content, so they are exactly the windows that need the baseline most.
recommendation: Route both through buildWindowWebPreferences('app', {...}). Add an assertion to the existing source-contract test suite (plugin-window-boundary-contract.test.ts) that no literal 'webPreferences: {' appears under src/main outside the builder.

title: Global --max-old-space-size=512 caps the heap while the comment claims it raises it
summary: On 64-bit platforms V8's default old-space limit is well above 512MB (typically 2GB or more), so this flag lowers rather than increases it, contradicting the comment directly above. app.commandLine.appendSwitch('js-flags', ...) at line 207 applies to every child process, including renderers and utility processes.
evidence:
// Increase renderer process V8 heap limit (main process uses NODE_OPTIONS)
const v8JsFlags = ['--max-old-space-size=512']
failure_scenario: A renderer handling a large search index, a long AI streaming session, or bulk thumbnail work hits the 512MB ceiling and is killed. touch-window.ts:257 contains dedicated handling for details.reason === 'oom', suggesting this already happens in practice. The misleading comment means anyone investigating those OOMs will read this line and conclude the limit was already raised.
recommendation: Confirm whether 512 is deliberate. If it is a memory-budget decision, fix the comment so it stops misleading. If it is a mistake, remove the flag or raise it to a realistic value and set utility-worker limits separately.

title: app.quit() is not in a finally, so a throw in the before-quit flow leaves the app unquittable
summary: The before-quit handler unconditionally calls event.preventDefault() at line 302. Inside the async flow, touchEventBus.emitAsync is wrapped in try/catch but broadcastBeforeQuit() is not; it resolves the channel, builds a transport and broadcasts. Any throw there is swallowed by the outer .catch at line 343, leaving beforeQuitFlowDone false and app.quit() (line 341) never reached.
evidence:
broadcastBeforeQuit()
    mainLog.info('App quit requested')
failure_scenario: The channel or transport is in a bad state at shutdown (window already destroyed, key manager torn down). broadcastBeforeQuit throws, the quit is swallowed, and every subsequent quit attempt is preventDefault'ed again. The user cannot close the application through any normal path and must force-kill it.
recommendation: Move beforeQuitFlowDone = true and app.quit() into a .finally(), or wrap broadcastBeforeQuit() in its own try/catch. Add a backstop timer that calls app.exit() unconditionally after the timeout.

title: Preload message listeners accept cross-origin messages without any origin check
summary: Both this handler and the loading-overlay messageListener at lines 634-640 dispatch on ev.data fields alone, never checking ev.origin or ev.source, while running in the privileged preload context. The direct assignment form also clobbers any handler the page may have registered.
failure_scenario: A cross-origin frame posts { payload: 'removeLoading' } and dismisses the loading overlay early, or posts crafted PRELOAD_LOADING_CHANNEL events to inject text into the debug panel. Impact is currently cosmetic, but this is an unvalidated privileged-context message sink that will grow more dangerous if the handler ever gains capability.
recommendation: Switch to addEventListener('message', ...) and validate ev.source === window && ev.origin === window.location.origin before dispatching.

title: sendPreloadEvent falls back to a wildcard targetOrigin
summary: The function already handles the file: case correctly but retains a '*' fallback branch for the remaining case.
evidence:
: window.location.protocol === 'file:'
          ? 'file://'
          : '*'
failure_scenario: The loading-state payload is delivered to any cross-origin frame embedded in the page. The data itself is low value, but the wildcard is unnecessary exposure and mirrors the more serious wildcard in the transport port handoff.
recommendation: Remove the '*' branch; when the origin cannot be determined, skip the post and log a warning.

title: Sentry runs at 100% trace sampling in production
summary: tracesSampleRate is a flat 1.0 for both packaged and development builds. The adjacent environment field at line 750 does branch on app.isPackaged, so the infrastructure to differentiate exists but sampling does not use it.
evidence: tracesSampleRate: 1.0,
failure_scenario: Every transaction in a long-running desktop app with 36 modules is captured and uploaded, producing continuous CPU and network overhead on user machines and burning through the Sentry quota. Once the quota is hit, genuine error events get rate-limited and dropped, so the setting actively degrades the observability it is meant to provide.
recommendation: Drop production sampling to 0.01-0.1 while keeping 1.0 in development, branching on app.isPackaged or process.env.BUILD_TYPE.

title: Renderer-not-found dialog discloses full internal paths to the user
