summary: The detail string built at line 312 concatenates app.getAppPath(), __dirname, process.resourcesPath and every candidate path, then renders them in a user-facing modal. The identical information is already written to the log at lines 571-580.
failure_scenario: A user hitting a broken install screenshots the dialog for a support request and shares absolute paths that include their OS username and directory layout. The information is actionable only for developers, who already have it in the log file.
recommendation: Show a short user-facing message plus an 'Open log folder' button; keep the path detail in the log file only.

title: The snap build config is dead because Linux targets are AppImage and deb only
summary: The 16-line snap: block (lines 135-150) can never execute because linux.target at lines 129-132 lists only AppImage and deb. Line 149 still carries a Chinese comment about fixing an app-builder execution problem, indicating it was debugged at some point. The dmg: (line 128) and desktop: (line 150) keys are empty values.
evidence:
snap:
  confinement: strict
  grade: stable
failure_scenario: A maintainer reads the config, concludes snap is a supported distribution channel, and either promises it to users or spends time maintaining settings that never run. Empty keys additionally make the YAML harder to diff and validate.
recommendation: Either add snap to linux.target and verify the build, or delete the block entirely. Remove the empty dmg: and desktop: keys.

title: runStartupHealthCheck is dead production code
summary: The function is referenced only by its own test file. index.ts inlines the equivalent load-then-await-init sequence at lines 293-320, and its log line mainLog.time('Startup health check passed') at line 232 reinforces the impression that this module is what runs.
failure_scenario: A developer adding a new startup health check edits this file, sees green tests, and ships a change that never executes. The passing test suite actively conceals the fact that the module is unwired.
recommendation: Either have index.ts actually call runStartupHealthCheck, or delete the module together with its test.

title: Dev-mode protocol registration bakes --inspect into the OS handler
summary: In development the tuff: scheme is registered against the Electron binary with --inspect. The registration persists in the OS, and the guard at line 217 checks isDefaultProtocolClient before re-registering, so a stale dev registration can survive into packaged runs without being replaced.
evidence: app.setAsDefaultProtocolClient(APP_SCHEMA, electronPath, ['--inspect', appPath])
failure_scenario: On a developer machine, any web page containing a tuff:// link launches Electron with an open Node inspector port. Anything able to reach that port gets full main-process code execution.
recommendation: Drop --inspect from the registration; debugging ports belong in the dev launch script, not in a persistent OS protocol handler. Always removeAsDefaultProtocolClient then re-register in dev so dev and prod registrations cannot contaminate each other.

title: Plugin channel keys are opaque random bearer tokens with no expiry or rotation, not encryption
summary: CLAUDE.md describes plugin channels as using 'encrypted keys for additional security'. The implementation is a 16-byte random bearer token whose lifetime equals its entry in nameToKeyMap, with no TTL, no rotation, and no per-request binding.
failure_scenario: An engineer performing a security review reads the 'encrypted' claim, assumes the channel provides confidentiality or replay resistance, and skips the checks that would surface the command-line key leakage and the self-declared-identity fallback. The long-lived bearer nature amplifies both of those issues.
recommendation: Correct the documentation to 'per-activation random capability token'. Add a TTL and confirm every plugin-deactivation path actually calls the existing revokeKey.

title: The will-navigate guard is installed inside ready-to-show, leaving the first load unguarded
summary: ready-to-show fires only after the renderer's first paint, so the navigation listener does not exist during initial page load and early script execution. If a window never reaches ready-to-show (the did-fail-load path), the listener is never attached at all.
evidence:
this.window.once('ready-to-show', () => {
      this.window.webContents.addListener('will-navigate', (event: ElectronEvent, url: string) => {
failure_scenario: A navigation triggered during initial load bypasses the guard entirely. A window whose first load fails runs permanently with no navigation restriction. A security control should not depend on render timing.
recommendation: Move will-navigate (and the setWindowOpenHandler that should be added per the app-view navigation issue) into the constructor, registered as soon as webContents exists. Leave only the autoShow logic in ready-to-show.

title: No Linux branch for window effects while nearly every window sets transparent: true
summary: The platform chain handles darwin (vibrancy) and win32 (mica/acrylic fallback) and falls through with no else for Linux; window-effects.ts:2 likewise only tests win32. Seven of the eight window option sets in config/default.ts specify transparent: true, and electron-builder.yml configures AppImage and deb targets, so Linux is a shipped platform.
failure_scenario: On a Linux desktop without a compositor, or with one that handles ARGB visuals differently, transparent windows with no backgroundColor render fully black or fully invisible. The launcher becomes unusable and there is no fallback path to catch it.
recommendation: Add a Linux branch that sets an opaque backgroundColor, or detect compositor capability at runtime before enabling transparent. ScreenshotEditorWindowOption (config/default.ts:173-174) already demonstrates the transparent:false plus backgroundColor pattern.

title: Window lifecycle events including app close are reachable from the plugin channel
summary: These handlers are bound to the plugin channel like all transport handlers and never inspect context.plugin. The nearby system.getCwd / getPath / getPackage handlers (lines 1419-1447) are equally exposed and leak the working directory and application directory layout.
evidence:
transport.on(AppEvents.window.close, () => closeApp(touchApp)),
      transport.on(AppEvents.window.hide, () => touchApp.window.window.hide()),
      transport.on(AppEvents.window.minimize, () => touchApp.window.minimize()),
failure_scenario: A misbehaving plugin closes the entire application, or repeatedly hides the main window, denying service to the user. The path-disclosure handlers give a plugin the filesystem layout it needs to aim the shell.openPath and path-traversal issues precisely.
recommendation: Mark window.* and the system path/info handlers as host-only under the audience mechanism proposed for the double-channel registration issue.

title: _sendTo throws synchronously from a Promise-returning function
summary: _sendTo is declared to return Promise<unknown> and every other error path in the function (lines 672-690 and 746-768) returns a resolved error object. This one path throws synchronously instead.
failure_scenario: A caller written as channel._sendTo(...).catch(handler) cannot catch this error because it is thrown before the promise exists. The exception propagates up the call stack, and since the main process has no production uncaughtException handler, it can terminate the process.
recommendation: Return Promise.resolve({ code: DataCode.ERROR, data: { message: 'Invalid plugin name', reason: 'invalid_plugin', eventName } }) to match the function's other error paths.

title: clipboard-history: ships dev.enable+source+autoStart, prelude fetched from 127.0.0.1:3488
summary: The shipped official manifest commits a dev-mode block with enable/source true and a localhost dev address. plugin.ts loadPreludeScript() takes the remote branch whenever dev.enable && dev.source && dev.address, so the plugin's Prelude is fetched over HTTP from 127.0.0.1:3488 instead of the packaged file.
failure_scenario: End user installs the packaged app; clipboard-history loads with dev.enable=true so the runtime issues GET http://127.0.0.1:3488/index.js. Nothing listens on that port, the request fails and the plugin never loads. If any unrelated local process does listen on 3488, whatever body it returns is executed as the plugin Prelude. plugin-loaders.ts:249-255 only coerces the values (enable: rawDevConfig.enable === true) and there is no app.isPackaged guard anywhere on this path.
recommendation: Set dev.enable to false in the committed manifest and gate the remote-prelude branch on !app.isPackaged.

title: touch-intelligence: ships dev.enable+source, prelude fetched from 127.0.0.1:5174
summary: The AI plugin's committed manifest enables dev mode with source:true and a localhost address, so its 3000-line Prelude is loaded over the network from a dev server rather than from disk.
failure_scenario: In a packaged build the runtime resolves new URL('index.js', 'http://127.0.0.1:5174/') and GETs it with a 5s timeout (plugin.ts:1993-2007). On a user machine the fetch fails and the AI plugin - which owns intelligence.basic and the ai/@ai CoreBox prefix - silently fails to load; the local index.js sitting next to the manifest is never used.
recommendation: Set dev.enable to false before release and add a packaged-build guard.

title: touch-translation: ships dev.enable+source, prelude fetched from localhost:3733
summary: Committed manifest enables dev mode with source:true pointing at a localhost Vite address, diverting Prelude loading to the network in shipped builds.
failure_scenario: Packaged app loads touch-translation, hits the dev branch in plugin.ts:1992, GETs http://localhost:3733/index.js, times out after 5s and the translation plugin (network.internet + intelligence.basic + storage.plugin) fails to initialize. The bundled index.js is bypassed.
recommendation: Flip dev.enable to false in the committed manifest.

title: plugins:validate has no dev.enable check, so committed dev leakage passes the gate
summary: AGENTS.md prescribes `pnpm plugins:validate` as the manifest gate, but the validator never inspects the dev block. Running it against the current tree reports 24/24 passed while three manifests ship dev.enable:true with localhost addresses.
evidence:
Actual run output: `24/24 plugins passed validation.` / `All plugins validated successfully.` A grep for dev handling in the script returns only line 126-127, which is about a missing manifest, not the dev block:
  logWarn(pluginName, hasPackageJson ? 'manifest.json not found — skipping Surface-only plugin' : 'manifest.json not found — skipping')
failure_scenario: A contributor follows plugins/AGENTS.md:52 ('Manifest 校验：pnpm plugins:validate'), sees an all-green result, and ships clipboard-history / touch-intelligence / touch-translation with dev.enable:true. The prescribed gate cannot catch the exact class of defect it is cited for.
recommendation: Fail validation when a committed manifest has dev.enable true.

title: touch-image: no manifest.json in the repo, plugin cannot be loaded at all
summary: touch-image tracks no manifest.json. Its only manifest is dist/manifest.json, an untracked build artifact in the pre-SDK legacy schema with no id, no sdkapi, no permissions and no features.
failure_scenario: The loader only ever reads manifest.json (plugin-loaders.ts / official-plugin-seed.ts:75). With none present the plugin is skipped entirely — `node scripts/validate-plugins.mjs` prints `[touch-image] manifest.json not found — skipping Surface-only plugin`. Even if dist/manifest.json were used, checkSdkCompatibility blocks it: missing sdkapi returns compatible:false ('must declare sdkapi >= 251212').
recommendation: Add a real manifest.json in the current schema or remove the plugin from the workspace.

title: touch-music: no manifest.json, only a legacy init.json nothing reads
summary: touch-music ships init.json, a pre-manifest config format. No code in apps/ or packages/ reads init.json, and the plugin has no manifest.json, so it can never load.
failure_scenario: validate-plugins.mjs reports `[touch-music] manifest.json not found — skipping Surface-only plugin`. The plugin is dead weight in the workspace: it is built and linted by CI but the runtime can never register it, and the stale init.json misleads contributors into thinking it is configured.
recommendation: Either port touch-music to a current manifest.json or delete it along with init.json.

title: touch-image: package.json embeds talex-touch.plugin.dev.enable:true with 127.0.0.1:6001
summary: The committed package.json carries a talex-touch block that turns on dev mode and hardcodes a localhost address; this block is what the build copies into dist/manifest.json.
failure_scenario: Anyone building touch-image gets dist/manifest.json with dev.enable:true baked in, reproducing the same localhost-dev leakage as the three shipped manifests, and there is no validator step that inspects package.json talex-touch blocks.
recommendation: Set enable to false, or move the dev address into a git-ignored local override.

title: touch-music: five declared dependencies are never imported (xterm, wavesurfer, granim, milkdown)
summary: package.json declares xterm, xterm-addon-fit, wavesurfer.js, granim and @milkdown/theme-nord, none of which appear anywhere in src/, vite.config.js or index.html.
evidence:
plugins/touch-music/package.json dependencies include:
    "@milkdown/theme-nord": "^7.21.2",
    "granim": "^2.0.0",
    "wavesurfer.js": "^7.12.10",
    "xterm": "^5.3.0",
    "xterm-addon-fit": "^0.8.0"
Grepping each name across plugins/touch-music/src, vite.config.js and index.html returns 0 matches (only rgbaster, which is used, returns 1).
failure_scenario: pnpm install pulls a terminal emulator, a waveform renderer, a gradient library and a markdown editor theme into an example music plugin, inflating the workspace lockfile and install time with packages no code path can reach.
recommendation: Drop the unused dependencies from package.json.

title: touch-quick-actions: executes lock-screen/mute/shutdown inside onFeatureTriggered, the display callback
summary: The dynamic quick-action-* features run system.runAction directly from onFeatureTriggered instead of publishing an item and executing in onItemAction. onFeatureTriggered is re-entered on every input change while the feature is active, so the mutating system action fires repeatedly.
failure_scenario: apps/core-app/src/main/modules/plugin/adapters/plugin-features-adapter.ts:160-161 calls BOTH `await plugin.triggerFeature(feature, query)` and `await plugin.triggerInputChanged(feature, query)` on each input change, and both invoke onFeatureTriggered (plugin.ts:1008 and plugin.ts:1044). For lock-screen and mute-toggle the host requires no confirmation (plugin-system-capabilities.ts:40-41 `'lock-screen': {risk:'immediate', confirmation:'none'}`), so activating the feature locks the screen and every following keystroke locks it again. For shutdown/restart (confirmation:'double') the destructive confirmation dialog is re-raised on each keystroke. touch-system-actions uses the same system.runAction capability but correctly defers it to onItemAction.
recommendation: Publish an item from onFeatureTriggered and move runAction into onItemAction, as touch-system-actions does.

title: touch-quick-actions: onFeatureTriggered returns an action-result object, breaking the boolean|void contract
summary: onFeatureTriggered returns the object produced by runAction/blocked ({externalAction, success, status, reason, message}) but the lifecycle contract is boolean | void, where false means 'do not enter activation state'.
failure_scenario: plugin-features-adapter.ts:376 checks `typeof shouldActivate === 'boolean' && shouldActivate === false`. A returned object is never boolean, so even when runAction returns {status:'blocked', reason:'confirmation-denied'} the provider stays activated and CoreBox keeps the feature open with no items pushed - the user sees an empty active feature after declining a shutdown confirmation. plugins/touch-quick-actions/index.test.cjs:167-173 asserts on result.status/result.reason, codifying the wrong contract.
recommendation: Return true/false from onFeatureTriggered and surface action results through onItemAction.

title: touch-workspace-scripts: onFeatureTriggered throws to the host, tripping the auto-disable circuit breaker
summary: When the workspaceScripts capability is missing, onFeatureTriggered throws instead of publishing a degraded item. The throw is outside the try/catch that begins on the next line, so it escapes into the plugin host on every invocation.
failure_scenario: Every throw routes to plugin.ts:1022 `await this.handleRuntimeError('onFeatureTriggered', error)`, which pushes an issue and appends to a 60s sliding error window. plugin.ts:1376-1388: `if (this._runtimeStats.errorTimestamps.length > 10) { ... this.status = PluginStatus.CRASHED; await this.disable() }`. Because onFeatureTriggered fires on each input change (plugin.ts:1044), a user typing 'workspace scripts' with the capability unavailable produces >10 errors within seconds and the plugin is marked CRASHED and disabled, requiring manual re-enable.
recommendation: Publish the 'workspace scripts unavailable' info item instead of throwing, matching onItemAction.

title: All plugin manifests declare feature.platform in a shape IPlatform does not define, and it is never enforced
summary: Every manifest writes platform as {win32: boolean, darwin: boolean, linux: boolean}, but the IPlatform type is keyed win|darwin|linux with IPlatformInfo objects. The runtime never evaluates manifest feature.platform at all, so platform restrictions are silently inert.
evidence:
plugins/touch-window-presets/manifest.json:52-56 declares Windows-only support:
      "platform": {
        "win32": true,
        "darwin": false,
        "linux": false
      },

The type, packages/utils/plugin/index.ts:73-77:
  export type PlatformKey = 'win' | 'darwin' | 'linux'
  export type IPlatform = { [key in PlatformKey]?: IPlatformInfo }
with IPlatformInfo = { enable: boolean; arch: Arch[]; os: SupportOS[] } (line 67-71).

The host's own validator for runtime-registered features requires that shape: plugin-business-capabilities.ts:1052-1057 `exactRecord(requiredField(record, 'platform'), ['win', 'darwin', 'linux'])` then `exactRecord(platformRecord[key], ['enable', 'arch', 'os'])`.
failure_scenario: Grepping feature.platform across the main process finds only pass-through assignments (plugin.ts:803 and plugin.ts:1469); no code reads .win32, .win or .enable to filter features. touch-window-presets, touch-quick-actions, touch-system-actions, touch-window-manager and touch-browser-open all declare linux:false but their features still register and surface in CoreBox on Linux. They only avoid broken behaviour because each prelude re-checks the platform itself (e.g. touch-window-presets/index.js:192 `if (currentPlatform() !== 'win32')`); a plugin that trusts the manifest declaration gets no gating. Note touch-browser-open/index.js:125-133 builds the correct {win:{enable,arch,os}} shape for runtime-registered features, so the two shapes disagree inside one plugin.
recommendation: Pick one shape, enforce it in validate-plugins.mjs, and gate feature registration on it.

title: touch-batch-rename: missing permission SDK is reported as permission-denied, hiding the real reason
summary: hasPermission collapses 'permission SDK absent' and 'check threw' into the same false as 'permission genuinely denied', so both apply and undo report reason 'permission-denied'.
failure_scenario: If the permission facade is not injected (capability gated off) the user sees '缺少 fs.write 权限' and is told to grant a permission they may already hold, with no path to diagnose the real fault. plugins/AGENTS.md:27 requires the opposite: '返回结果保留具体 reason：permission-denied、permission-sdk-unavailable、permission-request-failed 等'.
recommendation: Return a discriminated result from hasPermission and map it to permission-sdk-unavailable / permission-request-failed / permission-denied.

title: touch-dictation: bare catch blocks discard every failure reason and plugin.voice is dereferenced unguarded
summary: The optional-chaining guard tests plugin.voice?.asrStream but the fallback calls plugin.voice.dictate without a guard, and the surrounding catch blocks take no error binding, so permission-denied, sdk-unavailable and transport failures all collapse into one generic message with no reason field.
failure_scenario: When the voice capability is not injected at all, plugin.voice is undefined; the guard on line 90 is satisfied (undefined !== 'function') and line 91 throws TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'dictate'). The bare catch swallows it and tells the user to check microphone permissions, which is unrelated to the actual fault. Unlike every sibling plugin, the returned object carries no `reason` or `status`, violating plugins/AGENTS.md:27 ('返回结果保留具体 reason'). onSpeakAction at line 157-168 has the identical pattern for plugin.voice.speak.
recommendation: Guard plugin.voice before use and bind the error to map PLUGIN_HOST_CAPABILITY_* codes to explicit reasons, as touch-snipaste's stableFailure does.

title: touch-browser-open: onInputChanged handler is dead code - the host never invokes the prelude hook
summary: The plugin implements onInputChanged to refresh search suggestions, but nothing in the main process ever calls the prelude's onInputChanged. It is declared on the lifecycle proxy and the wire allowlist yet has no call site.
failure_scenario: The handler and the activeSearch state it maintains never run. Suggestions still refresh only because plugin-features-adapter.ts:160-161 re-invokes onFeatureTriggered, so the dead path silently duplicates working logic. The `signal` parameter is also unreachable: the proxy forwards a single argument, so any plugin adopting the documented hook (packages/utils/plugin/index.ts:386) gets a handler that is never called.
recommendation: Either wire the lifecycle hook in the main process or drop it from the SDK surface and from this plugin.

title: discardActiveTurn() never marks the in-flight turn settled, so a stale turn clobbers the new one
summary: reset()/restore() call discardActiveTurn(), which nulls activeController/activeTurn but leaves the previous runTurn closure's `settled` flag false. The non-streaming `fallback()` path has no cancellation at all, so when its awaited sdk.text.chat resolves it runs complete() -> conclude(), which nulls activeTurn and sets streaming=false on whatever turn has since replaced it.
failure_scenario: Provider has no chatStream, so send() goes down `fallback()` (line 345) and awaits sdk.text.chat with no controller to cancel. While it is in flight the user clicks another thread in the sidebar -> route watcher -> conversation.restore() -> discardActiveTurn(). The user sends a new message in the restored thread. The old fallback resolves, sees `settled === false`, and runs conclude(): streaming.value=false and activeTurn=null while the NEW turn is still streaming. The Stop button stops cancelling, the composer re-enables mid-stream, and HomePage's persist watcher (keyed on isStreaming going false) writes a half-streamed thread to disk.
recommendation: Expose a per-turn `abort()` from runTurn that sets `settled = true` (and drops the assistant reference), and have discardActiveTurn call it instead of only nulling the module-level handles.

title: send() never resolves when a turn is cancelled via reset()/restore()
summary: runTurn ends with `await finished`, and `finished` is only resolved from conclude(). discardActiveTurn() cancels the StreamController but never calls conclude(), and the StreamController contract guarantees no further data/error/end callbacks fire after cancel(). The promise therefore stays pending forever.
failure_scenario: User sends a message, then navigates to plain /home while it streams. The route watcher calls conversation.reset() -> discardActiveTurn() -> activeController.cancel(). Per StreamController's documented contract ('After cancellation, no more data/error/end callbacks will be invoked', packages/utils/transport/types.ts:158) onEnd/onError never fire, so settle() is never called. `await finished` in runTurn and `await turn` at HomePage.vue:239 stay pending for the life of the window, retaining the whole runTurn closure (handlers, payload, assistant message, parts array) per cancelled turn.
recommendation: Have discardActiveTurn resolve the pending turn (call the same conclude/settle path) rather than only cancelling the transport controller.

title: Conversation route watcher has no in-flight guard: fast sidebar switches restore the wrong thread
summary: The async watcher on route.params.id awaits history.load(target) and then unconditionally assigns conversationId and calls conversation.restore(). Two overlapping invocations are not sequenced, so a slower earlier load overwrites a faster later one.
evidence:
if (target === conversationId) return

    const restored = await history.load(target)
    if (!restored) return
    conversationId = target
    conversation.restore(restored)
failure_scenario: User clicks conversation A then B in the sidebar within a few hundred ms. load(B) resolves first and restores B; load(A) resolves after and restores A while route.params.id is still B. The screen now shows A's messages under URL /home/c/B, and conversationId is A. The next settled turn persists A's thread plus the new turn, then router.replace('/home/c/A') fires because route.params.id !== conversationId — silently rewriting conversation A with content the user typed into what they believed was B.
recommendation: Capture a request token/sequence number before the await and bail if route.params.id has changed by the time load resolves.

title: history.load() rejection in the route watcher is an unhandled rejection with no UI recovery
summary: load() calls sdk.get(id) with no try/catch (unlike its sibling refresh(), which does catch). The only caller is HomePage's async route watcher, which also has no try/catch, so an IPC failure becomes an unhandled promise rejection and the view is left showing the previous thread.
failure_scenario: Main's conversation store is unavailable (DB locked, module not yet loaded, migration in progress). The user opens a stored conversation from the sidebar: sdk.get rejects, the watcher callback rejects, Vue logs an unhandled rejection, conversationId is never updated, and the URL says /home/c/<id> while the stream still renders the previous conversation. No error state is shown and there is no retry affordance.
recommendation: Wrap sdk.get in try/catch returning null (matching refresh()'s degrade-to-empty policy) and surface a load-failed state in HomePage.

title: Tool-confirmation approve/deny rejections are unhandled and permanently drop the request
summary: settle() advances the queue (dismissing the card) before awaiting sdk.decide, and has no catch. HomePage binds it straight to a template handler, so a rejected decide is both an unhandled rejection and an unrecoverable state — the card is gone and the gateway never got an answer.
failure_scenario: Agent tools are on and a tool asks for confirmation. The user clicks Allow; the IPC send fails (transport destroyed during a reload, gateway restarting). advance() has already cleared `pending`, so the TxToolConfirmation card unmounts, but the gateway never receives a decision. The assistant turn hangs on the blocked tool call with no card on screen and no error, and HomePage.vue:712 `@approve="agentTools.approve($event.remember)"` produces an unhandled rejection.
recommendation: Await decide before advancing, or catch and re-queue the request with a visible error so the user can retry.

title: DivisionBoxShell stays on the loading overlay forever when the initial state request fails
summary: isLoading is set true on mount and only cleared when getState resolves with an active state or a later stateChanged event says 'active'. The .catch() only logs, so a failed or non-success response leaves the shell permanently in its loading state with no error affordance.
failure_scenario: The DivisionBox session is torn down in main between window creation and the shell's getState call (or the transport send times out). The catch logs and returns; isLoading stays true and no stateChanged event for this sessionId ever arrives, so the user is left staring at 'Loading...' with no close path from within the shell.
recommendation: Clear isLoading in the catch and in the non-success branch, and render an error state with a retry/close action.

title: Search snapshot overwrites the established session id with an optional field, stranding loading=true
summary: The stream's `session` chunk sets currentSearchId correctly, then the snapshot handler unconditionally reassigns it from `initialResult.sessionId`, which is declared optional on TuffSearchResult. When that field is absent the id becomes null and every later chunk fails its `currentSearchId.value === chunk.sessionId` guard.
evidence: currentSearchId.value = initialResult.sessionId || null
failure_scenario: A provider returns a TuffSearchResult without `sessionId` (the field is `sessionId?: string` in packages/utils/core-box/tuff/tuff-dsl.ts:1485, and applyDetachedPayload at useSearch.ts:335 constructs exactly such a result). currentSearchId flips to null after the snapshot, so the later `update` chunks (line 996) and the `complete` chunk (line 1011) are both dropped by their session guards. applySearchEnd never runs, so `loading.value` is never set back to false: the CoreBox spinner runs forever, streaming results stop appearing, and CoreBox.vue:150 keeps `canSubmitFeaturePrompt` false so the send button stays disabled until the box is closed.
recommendation: Only reassign when the snapshot actually carries an id (`if (initialResult.sessionId) currentSearchId.value = initialResult.sessionId`), and set loading=false on the snapshot path as a backstop. Same fix needed at line 930 in applyRecommendationResult.

title: Store plugin cards are unreachable by keyboard — click-only <div> with no role or tabindex
summary: The entire plugin card is a plain <div> carrying the only affordance that opens plugin details. It has no role, no tabindex, and no keydown handler, so it is not focusable and does not respond to Enter/Space.
evidence:
<div
    class="store-item-card"
    :class="{ 'official-provider': item.providerTrustLevel === 'official' }"
    @click="handleOpen"
  >
failure_scenario: A keyboard-only or screen-reader user opens the plugin store and tabs through the grid. No card ever receives focus, and a screen reader announces each card as an unlabelled group rather than a control, so plugin detail pages cannot be opened at all without a mouse. The install button inside is focusable, meaning the only reachable action is installing a plugin whose details the user cannot read.
recommendation: Make the card a <button>/<a>, or add role="button", tabindex="0" and @keydown.enter/@keydown.space handlers.

title: Store source delete control is a click-only <div>, unreachable by keyboard
summary: The destructive 'remove source' affordance is a bare <div> with only @click, in both the list branches (lines 235-238 and 284-287). No role, tabindex, keydown handler, or accessible name.
evidence:
<div
                    :class="{ disabled: sources.length === 1 || item.readOnly }"
                    class="transition-cubic action-btn"
                    @click="deleteSource(item.id)"
                  >
failure_scenario: A keyboard user configuring plugin store sources tabs to the row: the enable/disable switch takes focus but the delete control never does, so a mis-added source cannot be removed without a mouse. A screen reader reads only the icon <div> with no accessible name, giving no indication that a destructive action exists there.
recommendation: Use <button type="button"> with :disabled and an aria-label for the delete affordance in both branches.

title: WidgetFrame shadow render mode can never mount: pre-flush watcher reads the template ref too early
summary: mountShadowApp() is driven by a default (pre-flush) watcher with immediate: true, but it needs shadowHost.value, which Vue only populates after the render that creates the `v-else-if="canRenderShadow"` div. ensureShadowRoot() therefore returns null and mountShadowApp bails, and nothing re-triggers the watcher afterwards.
failure_scenario: Pass render-mode="shadow" to WidgetFrame with a registered renderer. On the immediate run the component is not mounted, so shadowHost.value is null; ensureShadowRoot() returns null and mountShadowApp() returns at `if (!root || !shadowContainer.value) return`. On the async path (renderer registers later) canRenderShadow flips false->true, but the pre-flush watcher still runs before the div is patched in, so shadowHost.value is null again. The result is an empty .WidgetFrame-ShadowHost div with no widget in it and no error. Currently latent — no caller passes render-mode="shadow" (only the 'light' default is used by CoreBoxRender.vue:71 and PluginFeatureDetailCard.vue:751), so ~100 lines of shadow-DOM plumbing are dead and untested.
recommendation: Add `flush: 'post'` to the watcher (or move mountShadowApp into onMounted + a post-flush watcher), and either wire up a caller or delete the shadow path.

title: forTouchTip atomicKey is poisoned permanently if the dialog fails to render
summary: The atomic entry is only removed inside the dialog's close callback. If the promise executor throws — renderComponent throws when no app context has been captured — the rejected promise is still stored under atomicKey and every later call with that key returns the same rejected promise instead of showing a dialog.
failure_scenario: forTouchTip is called with an atomicKey from a non-Vue context (an IPC callback or a DOM listener) before captureAppContext() has run — renderComponent throws 'No app context available' at line 126. The executor's throw rejects `pending`, which is then stored in activeAtomicDialogs and never deleted because close() is never reached. The empty root <div> also stays appended to document.body. Every subsequent forTouchTip with that key hits `if (activeDialog) return activeDialog` and re-throws the same stale rejection, so that dialog can never be shown again for the life of the window.
recommendation: Attach a `.catch()` / `.finally()` to `pending` that removes the atomicKey entry and the root element, and register the entry before mounting so a synchronous close still cleans up.

title: agentTools.setEnabled() is fire-and-forget: the pill can show 'on' while the gateway never opened
summary: The computed setter writes the persisted flag and then calls the async main-process sync with `void`, discarding both the result and any rejection. There is no rollback and no error surface.
failure_scenario: User clicks the agent-tools pill. `appSetting.tools.agentTools` is set to true and persisted, but sdk.setEnabled rejects (gateway port in use, main handler not registered). The rejection is an unhandled promise rejection, the pill renders as active and `aria-pressed="true"`, and the setting survives a restart — so the UI permanently claims the assistant can run tools while the tool gateway is closed and every tool call the model attempts fails.
recommendation: Await the call in an async handler; on failure revert appSetting.tools.agentTools and show a toast.

title: Cancelled route transitions leak entries in AppShell's timing map
summary: routeTransitionStartedAt is filled in @before-enter and only drained in @after-enter. Vue fires @enter-cancelled (not @after-enter) when a transition is interrupted, and that hook is not bound, so interrupted navigations leave entries behind forever.
failure_scenario: The key is route.fullPath, and conversation routes are /home/c/<uuid> — an unbounded key space. A user clicking quickly through the conversation sidebar interrupts the 0.35s route transition each time, so @after-enter never fires and one entry per visited conversation id accumulates in the Map for the life of the window. AppShell is the root layout and never unmounts, so nothing ever clears it.
recommendation: Bind @enter-cancelled to the same cleanup, or cap/clear the map when it exceeds a small size.

title: SCStream is never stopped after a frame-extraction error, leaking a live screen capture
summary: `MacStreamSession::stop()` and `Drop` both use `callbacks.closed.swap(true)` as their guard, but the frame-output callback also latches `closed` on any extraction error. Once an extraction error fires, neither stop() nor Drop ever calls `stopCaptureWithCompletionHandler`, so the ScreenCaptureKit stream keeps capturing forever.
failure_scenario: A client opens a `frames` stream on a 1920x1080 display with maxFrameBytes = 1 MiB (any value >0 and <= max_stream_frame_bytes passes decode_frames validation). The first frame is 1920*1080*4 = 8.3 MB, so copy_complete_sample's `output_bytes > max_frame_bytes` check returns Err and latches `closed = true`. The consumer then tears the stream down: `stop()` sees closed==true, reports `completion(Ok(()))` and returns without calling stopCapture; Drop skips it for the same reason. ScreenCaptureKit keeps compositing and delivering frames at N fps for the rest of the process lifetime, burning GPU/CPU and leaving the macOS screen-recording indicator lit. A 6K display exceeding the 64 MiB max_stream_frame_bytes cap triggers the same path with default settings.
recommendation: Track stream-running state separately from the callback `closed` latch and always issue stopCaptureWithCompletionHandler exactly once from stop()/Drop.

title: MacFrameSource::stop() builds its Notified after the flag check and can hang forever
summary: `stop()` checks `stopped` and only then constructs `notified()`. tokio's Notified snapshots the notify_waiters counter at construction, so a `notify_waiters()` landing between the flag load and that construction is already accounted for and the future parks with no further wakeup coming.
failure_scenario: `ScreenshotCapability::invoke_stream` calls `source.request_stop()` then awaits `source.stop()`. The awaiting task loads `stopped` (false); the actor thread then runs `stopped.store(true)` + `notify_waiters()`; only afterwards does the task evaluate `control.stop_notify.notified()`, whose snapshot of num_notify_waiters_calls already includes that call, so poll_notified registers and parks. `stop()` never resolves: the frames operation never emits its terminal frame, its entry stays in NativeRuntime::streams, and finish_dispose() eventually fails with NATIVE_DISPOSE_TIMEOUT. The same crate gets this right elsewhere — native-core/src/stream.rs:53, native-core/src/runtime.rs:597 and backend/mod.rs:314 all build the Notified before checking state.
recommendation: Construct the `Notified` before reading `stopped` (or pin it and call `.enable()`), matching the pattern already used in stream.rs/runtime.rs.

title: CancellationToken::cancelled() builds its Notified too late and can miss a one-shot cancel
summary: The wait loop reads `reason()` first and only then constructs `notified()`. Because tokio's Notified snapshots the notify_waiters counter at construction and cancellation fires exactly once, a cancel landing in that window is lost permanently.
failure_scenario: An idle `frames` stream (static content, no new frames arriving) is torn down: begin_dispose() calls credit.cancel(Dispose) -> CancellationToken::cancel -> notify_waiters(). The stream task sits in `run_frame_stream` awaiting `LatestFrameSlot::next_frame`, whose `tokio::select!` arm is `cancellation.cancelled()`. That task had already read reason()==None and constructs its Notified after notify_waiters() ran, so the snapshot matches and it parks forever. Nothing publishes to the slot and nothing closes it, so the stream never terminates, `finish_dispose` returns NATIVE_DISPOSE_TIMEOUT, and the entry leaks in NativeRuntime::streams. Secondary hazard: `cancel()` stores `cancelled` before `reason`, so a concurrent `reason()` can observe cancelled==true with reason==REASON_NONE and wrongly report None.
recommendation: Build the Notified before checking reason (pin + `.enable()`), and store the reason before flipping the `cancelled` flag (or pack both into a single atomic).

title: startCapture blocks the Electron main thread on an unbounded channel recv
summary: `start_capture` is a synchronous `#[napi]` function that blocks on `ready_rx.recv()` with no timeout while a worker thread opens a cpal input stream. It is called directly from the Electron main process by voice-service.ts.
failure_scenario: apps/core-app/src/main/modules/voice/voice-service.ts:148 calls `nativeAudio.startCapture(...)` on the main process thread. If the user triggers dictation while a Bluetooth headset is (re)connecting, `default_input_device()` + `build_input_stream()` + `stream.play()` on CoreAudio can take seconds, and on first use macOS shows the microphone consent sheet before the AudioUnit starts. With no timeout on recv(), the whole Electron event loop is frozen for that duration — no IPC, no repaint, no CoreBox shortcut — and a wedged CoreAudio call hangs the app permanently.
recommendation: Use `recv_timeout` with a bounded budget and return a retryable error, or expose startCapture as an async napi function (AsyncTask/Promise).

title: Audio capture sessions are never garbage-collected, leaking threads and PCM buffers
summary: `start_capture` inserts a SessionHandle into a process-global map; entries are removed only by `stop_capture`/`cancel_capture`. There is no TTL or reaper, so any session the JS side abandons keeps its sample Vec and un-joined JoinHandle alive for the life of the process.
failure_scenario: The renderer that started dictation is closed or reloaded, or an exception in voice-service's async generator skips the stopCapture call. The capture thread self-stops at the 15 s max-duration cap and exits, but the SessionHandle stays in SESSIONS forever holding the interleaved f32 buffer (15 s x 48 kHz x 2 ch x 4 B ~= 5.8 MB) plus a never-joined thread handle. Repeated dictation attempts accumulate and there is no API to enumerate or purge orphaned sessions.
recommendation: Reap sessions whose `meta.stopped_reason` is Some once a TTL elapses, or have the capture thread drop its own entry when nothing has read it.

title: stopCapture/cancelCapture join the native capture thread from the JS thread
summary: Both synchronous napi entry points call `join_handle.join()` with no timeout. The capture thread only re-checks its stop flag every POLL_INTERVAL_MS (50 ms) and then drops the cpal stream, a blocking CoreAudio/WASAPI teardown.
failure_scenario: Every dictation stop from voice-service.ts:162/272/447 (and every abortCapture at :293) blocks the Electron main process for at least one 50 ms poll interval — `thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(POLL_INTERVAL_MS))` in capture_thread_main — plus the `drop(stream)` device teardown, after which the full downmix and WAV encode also run inline on the same thread. On a stalled audio device the teardown takes far longer and `join()` has no timeout, so the UI freezes.
recommendation: Wake the capture thread with a condvar/channel instead of a 50 ms poll, and move the join plus WAV encode off the JS thread.

title: snapshotCapture re-clones and re-encodes the whole recording on every 1.2 s poll
summary: `snapshot_capture` clones the entire accumulated interleaved buffer, downmixes all of it and re-encodes a full WAV on every call. voice-service polls it in a loop, so the work grows linearly per poll and quadratically over the session — all on the Electron main thread.
failure_scenario: apps/core-app/src/main/modules/voice/voice-service.ts:425 calls `snapshotCapture(sessionId)` every PARTIAL_INTERVAL_MS (1200 ms) until auto-stop, up to DEFAULT_MAX_DURATION_MS (15 s) — roughly 12 polls. The late polls each clone ~5.8 MB of f32 samples, allocate a ~2.9 MB mono Vec, and drive hound's per-sample `write_sample` over ~720k samples, synchronously on the main thread. Total work is O(n^2) in recording length and every poll stutters the UI during live dictation.
recommendation: Encode only the delta (as drain_capture already does) or cache the encoded prefix; at minimum move the encode off the JS thread.

title: playAudio decodes arbitrary audio synchronously on the JS thread
summary: `play_audio` is a synchronous napi function that runs the full symphonia decode loop plus a downmix on the calling (Electron main) thread before returning a playback id. Nothing caps the input size.
failure_scenario: TTS or a notification sound hands playAudio a multi-minute MP3. `decode_audio` walks every packet and accumulates all samples into a Vec<f32> (10 min stereo 44.1 kHz ~= 212 MB) on the main thread, freezing the UI for the whole decode. The inline comment justifies decoding on the calling thread so bad audio surfaces synchronously, but nothing bounds the input length.
recommendation: Cap input byte length / decoded sample count, and move the decode to the playback thread or an AsyncTask so errors surface via the returned promise.

title: compose_region decodes attachment PNGs with no working-set budget (memory blow-up)
summary: Source PNGs are decoded and retained in `decoded_sources` before any size check. Only the OUTPUT is checked against `max_static_output_pixels`; `max_static_working_set_bytes` (512 MiB) is never applied to decoded inputs, and image 0.25's per-decode default cap is 512 MiB each.
failure_scenario: A `screenshot.capture/compose` request supplies 8 attachments (MAX_ATTACHMENT_COUNT), each a ~50 KB PNG of an 11000x11000 solid-colour image. Each decode stays under image 0.25's Limits::default() max_alloc of 512 MiB so none is rejected, but all 8 RgbaImages are held simultaneously in `decoded_sources` (plus the transient copy from `into_rgba8()`), pushing the Electron main process past 4 GiB RSS and into an allocator abort — from a request payload of a few hundred kilobytes.
recommendation: Build the decoder with explicit `image::Limits` derived from limits.max_static_working_set_bytes() and accumulate decoded bytes against a running budget across sources.

title: compose rejects any request containing a non-intersecting source, making its skip branch dead
summary: The loop deliberately `continue`s past sources that do not intersect the requested rect, so their attachment ids are never inserted into `used_attachments` — but the post-loop check requires every supplied attachment to have been consumed and fails the whole request.
failure_scenario: On a 3-display setup the client freezes all three displays (one attachment each) and asks to compose a region covering only two of them. The third source hits the `continue`, so used_attachments.len() == 2 while attachments.len() == 3, and compose returns SCREENSHOT_INVALID_REGION for a perfectly valid request. The non-intersecting-source branch can therefore never succeed, and callers must pre-filter sources by intersection — a rule the wire contract never states.
recommendation: Either mark a skipped source's attachments as used, or drop the strict all-attachments-consumed check in favour of rejecting only genuinely unreferenced attachments.

title: Screenshot adapter is a OnceLock, so dispose() permanently kills the capability for the process
summary: The NapiRuntimeAdapter and its NativeRuntime live in a process-wide `OnceLock` with no reset path, while `dispose()` sets `NativeRuntime.disposed` permanently. A second carrier created after disposal handshakes successfully but every operation fails.
failure_scenario: The native-capabilities module is destroyed (module hot-reload in dev, or a module restart) and calls `nativeProtocolTransport.dispose()` -> nativeProtocolV1Dispose -> NativeRuntime::begin_dispose, which sets `disposed` forever. A newly constructed NapiCarrier from loadScreenshotCarrier() still receives a healthy server_hello (handshake never checks `disposed`) advertising screenshot.capture as available, but every invoke returns `Ok(error_response(..., transport_disposed()))`. Screenshots stay broken until the whole app restarts, and because the failure arrives as a well-formed ok=false response rather than a carrier error, no unavailable-backend fallback is triggered.
recommendation: Make the adapter re-creatable (e.g. RwLock<Option<Arc<..>>> rebuilt on the next handshake), or have `handshake` reject with TRANSPORT_DISPOSED so callers can detect the terminal state.

title: napi boundary flattens structured ProtocolError into a string, dropping category/retryable/details
summary: `to_napi_error` formats only `code: message` into a napi Error. The `category`, `retryable` and `details` fields the protocol defines and validates are discarded, so JS cannot distinguish a retryable timeout from a permanent validation failure without re-parsing the string.
failure_scenario: `NativeRuntime::open_stream` returns Err for NATIVE_BUSY (retryable: true), DUPLICATE_REQUEST_ID and CAPABILITY_NOT_FOUND (retryable: false). All three reach JS as `Error: <CODE>: <message>` with Status::GenericFailure, so protocol.js cannot tell 'busy, retry shortly' from 'capability missing, give up'. Any consumer wanting that distinction must string-split on ': ' and hardcode a retryable list, duplicating the flag ProtocolError already carries, and `details` — which validate_error explicitly permits — is unreachable from JS entirely.
recommendation: Serialize the ProtocolError to JSON and attach it to the napi Error (e.g. as `reason`) so JS reads code/category/retryable/details directly.

title: protocol.js discards every native error with bare catch blocks
summary: handshake/invoke/openStream/cancel/dispose all use `catch { throw carrierError(...) }` with no binding, so the original error object — the only place the native code and message survive — is dropped and never attached as `cause`.
failure_scenario: A stream open fails with NATIVE_BUSY because max_open_streams (16) is saturated. The napi Error carrying that code is swallowed by the bare `catch`, and the caller sees only `NativeCarrierError: CARRIER_OPEN_STREAM_FAILED / Native carrier could not open the stream` — no code, no message, no `cause` chain — so neither the retry-vs-abort decision nor any log-based diagnosis of native failures is possible. `acknowledge` (line 223) is the one method that binds the error and inspects `error.code`, proving the information is available at these sites.
recommendation: Bind the caught error and pass it through as `{ cause: error }` on NativeCarrierError, and include its `code`/`message` in safeLog.

title: request_stop silently orphans an SCStream when the macOS actor mailbox is full
summary: `MacFrameSource::request_stop` posts `Command::StopFrames` with `try_send`. On a full 16-slot mailbox it just marks the control as stopped and returns, so the ActorState entry and its live SCStream session are never torn down.
failure_scenario: The single actor thread is blocked inside `wait_for_image` (up to SYSTEM_CALLBACK_TIMEOUT = 5 s) while ACTOR_QUEUE_CAPACITY (16) refresh/capture commands queue behind it. A frames consumer disconnects and calls request_stop; try_send returns TrySendError::Full, the caller is told the stream stopped, but `ActorState::streams` still holds the MacStreamSession. ScreenCaptureKit keeps capturing that display or window at the configured fps until the entire actor shuts down.
recommendation: Retry the StopFrames command with a bounded blocking send, or keep a separate stop queue the actor drains, rather than reporting success on a dropped command.

title: Discarded ax_actor.reset() error permanently desyncs UI-element hit testing
summary: After a successful refresh the AX actor's generation is reset with `let _ = ...`, discarding BackendBusy/BackendFailed. If the reset never lands, the AX actor keeps the previous generation while the screen actor advances.
failure_scenario: The AX actor mailbox (AX_QUEUE_CAPACITY = 16) is saturated or its thread is mid-AX-call, so `submit` returns TrySendError::Full and reset() fails with SCREENSHOT_BACKEND_BUSY. The caller still sees refresh succeed with generation N while AxActorState.generation stays at N-1, so every later prepare_hit_test trips `self.generation.as_ref() != Some(&request.generation)` and returns AccessibilityFallback::UnverifiedWindow. UI-element hit testing silently degrades to window-only with no error surfaced, and the stale `elements` map (up to max_ax_elements = 512 retained AXUIElements) is never cleared.
recommendation: Propagate the reset failure (fail the refresh or mark the snapshot degraded), or let the AX actor adopt the generation carried on each request.

title: Windows with a degenerate frame are silently dropped from every content snapshot
summary: `refresh` converts SCK windows and CGWindow metadata with `filter_map(... .ok())`, discarding the reason a window failed validation. GlobalDipRect::new rejects any non-positive width/height, so such windows vanish with no diagnostic.
evidence:
let shareable_windows = system_windows
            .iter()
            .filter_map(|window| shareable_window(window, generation_number).ok())
            .collect::<Vec<_>>();
        let cg_windows = cg_windows
            .iter()
            .filter_map(|window| cg_window(window).ok())
            .collect::<Vec<_>>();
failure_scenario: A window is mid-creation or fully collapsed so ScreenCaptureKit reports a zero-height frame; `global_rect` -> `GlobalDipRect::new` fails with 'rectangle dimensions must be positive' and the whole window is dropped by `.ok()`. It never appears in the snapshot, `hit_test` cannot return it, and a later `capture` targeting it fails with SCREENSHOT_WINDOW_NOT_FOUND — with nothing in the logs explaining why, because the GeometryError was thrown away at the filter_map.
recommendation: Count and report dropped windows (a counter on the refresh response, or a debug log of the GeometryError) instead of discarding the Result silently.

title: Window selection ignores the configured ScreenshotLimits and hardcodes the defaults
summary: Every constructor in window_candidates.rs calls `ScreenshotLimits::default()` internally instead of accepting the limits the capability was built with, unlike the rest of the crate which threads `limits` through explicitly.
failure_scenario: `ScreenshotCapability::new(backend, limits)` and `platform_backend(limits)` both take a ScreenshotLimits, and decode_hit_test already clamps max_candidates against the configured limits — but WindowHitTestOptions::new then re-clamps against the hardcoded default of 16. The same applies to max_bundle_id_bytes / max_application_name_bytes / max_title_scalars in WindowOwner::new, ShareableWindow::new, SelfWindowPolicy::new and WindowSelectionPolicy::new. Any deployment or test constructing non-default limits gets them silently ignored for window selection while they are honoured everywhere else, so the two layers disagree about what is valid.
recommendation: Pass `ScreenshotLimits` into these constructors like the rest of the crate does instead of re-deriving the default.

title: audio.d.ts documents playAudio as throwing when the binding is unavailable; audio.js never does
summary: The declared contract says playAudio throws when the binding is unavailable, but the JS wrapper deliberately degrades to a no-op `{ playbackId: '' }` in exactly that case.
failure_scenario: A caller follows the .d.ts, wraps playAudio in try/catch to detect 'audio unavailable', gets no exception, and passes the returned `playbackId: ''` to stopPlayback. The empty id matches no entry in the playbacks map so stopPlayback is a silent no-op, and the caller believes playback started. The unavailable-binding branch is unobservable through the documented interface.
recommendation: Correct the JSDoc: it degrades to `{ playbackId: '' }` when disabled or unavailable and only throws on undecodable audio.

title: cancelCapture is typed as returning void but throws for an unknown session id
summary: `cancelCapture` is declared `: void` with no throw documented, while the Rust implementation returns Err for a missing session and audio.js forwards it unchanged. The adjacent `drainCapture` declaration documents exactly this throw, so the omission is an inconsistency inside one file.
failure_scenario: Calling cancelCapture for a session that already auto-stopped on trailing silence (so stop_capture removed it from SESSIONS) throws `session-not-found: <id>` instead of returning void. The only in-repo caller had to discover this the hard way and wrap it defensively — voice-service.ts:291-297 `abortCapture` catches with the comment 'best effort — session may already be gone'. Any new caller trusting the `: void` signature and the .d.ts's silence about throwing gets an unexpected exception on a routine abort-after-auto-stop.
recommendation: Document the throw in the .d.ts to match drainCapture, or make cancelCapture idempotent for unknown ids.

title: writeDarwinAppIcon calls a blocking *Sync native function on the JS thread
summary: The wrapper is `async` but only yields one macrotask before invoking `writeDarwinAppIconSync`, which performs the icon extraction and disk write inline on the Electron main thread.
evidence:
await new Promise(resolve => setImmediate(resolve))
  return nativeBinding.writeDarwinAppIconSync(options)
failure_scenario: apps/core-app/src/main/service/icon-service.ts imports writeDarwinAppIcon and calls it per application while indexing. The `setImmediate` hop drains one event-loop turn, but the native call itself is fully synchronous, so each icon read (NSWorkspace icon fetch + PNG encode + file write) blocks the main process. Batch-indexing dozens of apps produces a visibly stuttering UI behind an API whose signature promises asynchrony.
recommendation: Expose an async native binding (AsyncTask/Promise) or run the sync call on a worker thread rather than hiding a sync native call behind an async signature.

title: Plugin lifecycle hooks fire only once: signal listener deletes the whole hook array
summary: After a lifecycle signal is delivered, the listener deletes `sdk.__hooks[type]`, destroying every registered hook for that lifecycle type. All subsequent signals of the same type find no hooks and silently do nothing.
failure_scenario: A plugin calls `onPluginActive(() => refreshData())`. The first time CoreBox activates the plugin the callback runs and `__hooks['ac']` is deleted. On every later activation the transport listener still fires but `hooksMap['ac']` is undefined, so `refreshData()` is never called again -> the plugin shows stale data for the rest of the session with no error.
recommendation: Do not delete the hook array after dispatch; keep hooks registered for the lifetime of the plugin and only remove them on explicit unsubscribe.

title: onPluginActive/onPluginInactive documented boolean veto is never honoured
summary: JSDoc for `onPluginActive`/`onPluginInactive` promises `If return false, the plugin will not be activated`, but the hook's return value is discarded by `wrappedHook` and the default processor always calls `reply(true)`.
failure_scenario: A plugin implements `onPluginActive(() => { if (!licenseValid) return false })` to block activation while unlicensed. `hook(data)` result is thrown away and `processFunc` replies `true` unconditionally, so the plugin activates anyway - the documented gate silently does nothing.
recommendation: Collect hook return values in `wrappedHook` and pass `hooks.every(h => h(data) !== false)` into `reply`, or remove the veto claim from the JSDoc.

title: Lifecycle signal transport listener is never unsubscribed and re-registers per hook cycle
summary: `transport.on()` returns an unsubscribe function that is discarded. Combined with the `delete sdk.__hooks[type]` above, every re-registration after a delivered signal sees `hooks.length === 0` and attaches an additional listener for the same event.
evidence: transport.on(lifecycleSignalEvents[type], listener as (data: unknown) => void)
failure_scenario: A plugin re-registers `onPluginActive` on each of its own view mounts. After the first activate signal the hook array is deleted, so the next `injectHook` sees length 0 and adds a second transport listener while the first stays attached. After N mount cycles, N listeners fire per signal and none can ever be removed.
recommendation: Store and invoke the unsubscribe function, and guard registration with a per-type `registered` flag rather than `hooks.length === 0`.

title: Plugin channel replies serialize the raw IpcRendererEvent, which is not structured-cloneable
summary: `__parse_raw_data` stores the live `IpcRendererEvent` on `header.event`, and `__parse_sender` copies it straight into the reply object handed to `ipcRenderer.send`. `IpcRendererEvent` carries `sender`/`ports` and cannot survive structured clone.
failure_scenario: A plugin registers any synchronous channel handler. When the main process sends a request, `handInData.reply(DataCode.SUCCESS, res)` calls `ipcRenderer.send` with an object graph containing the original `IpcRendererEvent` -> Electron throws `An object could not be cloned`, the reply is never delivered, and the main-process caller hangs until its timeout.
recommendation: Strip `header.event` (and `_originData`) before constructing the reply payload; keep the event only in local scope.

title: Async plugin channel handlers never send a reply, hanging the main-process caller
summary: When a registered handler returns a Promise, `__handle_main` returns early and never awaits it, so `reply()` is never invoked for asynchronous handlers.
failure_scenario: A plugin registers `channel.regChannel('do-work', async (d) => await compute(d))`. The handler resolves normally but no reply is ever sent, so the main process's pending sync request for `do-work` sits in `pendingMap` until the 60s `CHANNEL_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT` fires and rejects.
recommendation: Await the promise and reply with its resolved value, replying with an error code when it rejects.

title: Unguarded JSON.parse in the plugin IPC listener throws on non-string payloads
summary: `__handle_main` assumes the IPC argument is always a JSON string, but `send()` in the same class posts a plain object on the same `@plugin-process-message` channel. Any non-string or malformed payload throws out of the IPC listener.
evidence:
__handle_main(e: IpcRendererEvent, _arg: any): any {
    const arg = JSON.parse(_arg);
failure_scenario: The main process (or a loopback of this class's own `send`, which posts an object at line 300) delivers an object rather than a JSON string. `JSON.parse` coerces it to `"[object Object]"` and throws `SyntaxError`, which escapes the ipcRenderer listener as an uncaught exception in the plugin renderer and drops every message on that channel.
recommendation: Wrap the parse in try/catch and accept objects directly: `const arg = typeof _arg === 'string' ? safeParse(_arg) : _arg`.

title: TuffRendererTransport.destroy() leaves every on() channel listener registered
summary: `on()` registers a listener with the underlying channel and returns its cleanup to the caller without storing it. `destroy()` only clears the `handlers` map, so all channel-level registrations survive and keep invoking handlers after the transport is destroyed.
evidence:
// Clear all handlers
    this.handlers.clear()
failure_scenario: A renderer view creates a transport, calls `transport.on(AppEvents.x, handler)`, then calls `transport.destroy()` on unmount without holding the per-handler cleanup. The channel registration remains, so `handler` keeps firing on every subsequent main-process broadcast, touching torn-down component state and leaking the closure for the lifetime of the window.
recommendation: Collect the `cleanup` returned by `this.channel.regChannel` per handler and invoke all of them in `destroy()`.

title: Response cache and batch dedupe collide on non-serializable payloads, returning another call's result
summary: `buildCacheKey` and `buildBatchKey` fall back to `Object.prototype.toString.call(payload)` when `JSON.stringify` throws. Every circular or non-serializable object collapses to the same key, so distinct requests share one cache entry / dedupe bucket.
failure_scenario: A consumer calls `transport.send(ev, payloadA, { cache: true })` and then `transport.send(ev, payloadB, { cache: true })` where both payloads contain a circular reference. Both build the key `"<event>:[object Object]"`, so the second call silently returns payloadA's response instead of issuing a request - wrong data with no error. The same collision merges unrelated requests under `mergeStrategy: 'dedupe'`.
recommendation: Throw or bypass caching/dedupe when the payload cannot be serialized, instead of falling back to a type-only key.

title: Batching sends requests strictly sequentially, making batch-enabled events slower than unbatched
summary: Despite the `BatchPayload`/`BatchResponse` protocol types, `flushEvent` never combines requests. For the default `queue` strategy it chains each entry through `reduce(...).then(...)`, serializing what would otherwise be concurrent IPC calls.
evidence:
await queue.queue.reduce<Promise<void>>(
      (promise, entry) => promise.then(() => this.flushEntry(eventName, entry)),
      Promise.resolve(),
    )
failure_scenario: An event declared with `batch: { enabled: true, windowMs: 50, maxSize: 50 }` receives 50 concurrent `send()` calls. Instead of one batched round-trip they are queued for 50ms and then issued one-at-a-time, so total latency becomes 50ms + 50x the per-request round-trip - strictly worse than not enabling batching.
recommendation: Either issue the queued entries with `Promise.all`, or implement the declared batch envelope so the queue becomes a single request.

title: Exported BatchPayload/BatchResponse/BatchResult types describe a protocol that is never implemented
summary: `BatchPayload`, `BatchResult` and `BatchResponse` are exported from the package's public transport surface, but a repo-wide search finds no producer or consumer - no code ever builds or parses the `{ event, requests: [{id, payload}] }` envelope.
failure_scenario: An external plugin developer writes a main-process handler typed against `BatchPayload` to receive batched storage reads. At runtime the renderer sends the bare per-request payload (see `flushEntry`), so `payload.requests` is undefined and the handler throws on every batch-enabled event.
recommendation: Either implement the batch envelope end-to-end or remove these types from the public export surface.

title: usePluginStorage().onDidChange passes the event envelope instead of the new file content
summary: The callback is typed and documented as `(newConfig: any) => void`, but the listener forwards the raw update payload `{ name, fileName }` (`PluginStorageUpdatePayload`), which carries no content at all.
failure_scenario: A plugin calls `storage.onDidChange('settings.json', cfg => applyTheme(cfg.theme))`. On every write it receives `{ name: 'my-plugin', fileName: 'settings.json' }`, so `cfg.theme` is `undefined` and the theme silently resets - the developer has no way to obtain the new value from the callback.
recommendation: Re-fetch via `getFile(fileName)` inside the listener before invoking the callback, or extend `PluginStorageUpdatePayload` to carry the content.

title: usePluginStorage().onDidChange fires for unrelated files when fileName is absent
summary: The subscription filter treats a missing `fileName` on the broadcast as a match for every subscribed file, so a whole-plugin storage event notifies all per-file subscribers.
evidence:
if (data.name === pluginName
          && (data.fileName === fileName || data.fileName === undefined)) {
failure_scenario: A plugin subscribes separately to `settings.json` and `cache.json`, then calls `clearAll()`, which broadcasts an update without `fileName`. Both subscribers fire as though their specific file changed, so each reloads and rewrites state that was just cleared.
recommendation: Treat a missing `fileName` as a distinct 'all files' signal the caller opts into, rather than matching every specific subscription.

title: setFile throws an opaque SyntaxError for undefined content
summary: `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(content))` is used to strip non-cloneables, but `JSON.stringify(undefined)` returns `undefined`, and `JSON.parse(undefined)` coerces to the string `"undefined"` and throws. Circular content throws a TypeError from the same expression.
evidence: return transport.send(PluginEvents.storage.setFile, { pluginName, fileName, content: JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(content)) })
failure_scenario: A plugin calls `storage.setFile('state.json', undefined)` to clear a value. Rather than the documented `{ success: false, error }` result it gets an unhandled `SyntaxError: "undefined" is not valid JSON` thrown synchronously from the SDK, which does not match the declared `Promise<{ success, error? }>` return contract.
recommendation: Guard the serialization and surface `{ success: false, error }` for non-serializable content instead of letting JSON throw.

title: PermissionIds constant omits the localization permissions, so PermissionId type cannot express them
summary: `PERMISSIONS` registers `i18n.read`, `lexicon.read` and `lexicon.register`, but the `PermissionIds` map - and therefore the exported `PermissionId` union used for type safety - has no entries for them.
failure_scenario: A plugin developer writes `const p: PermissionId = 'lexicon.register'` to declare a manifest permission. TypeScript rejects it as not assignable to the union even though `permissionRegistry.has('lexicon.register')` returns true at runtime, forcing a cast that defeats the constant's stated purpose ('Permission ID constants for type safety').
recommendation: Add `I18N_READ`, `LEXICON_READ`, `LEXICON_REGISTER` to `PermissionIds`, or derive the union from `PERMISSIONS` so the two cannot drift.

title: SupportOS.WATCHOS_9 and WATCHOS_10 have their values swapped
summary: The `WATCHOS_9` member is assigned the string `'watchOS 10'` and `WATCHOS_10` is assigned `'watchOS 9'`. `WINDOWS_11` is likewise assigned `'Windows 10 Pro'`.
evidence:
WATCHOS = 'watchOS',
  WATCHOS_9 = 'watchOS 10',
  WATCHOS_10 = 'watchOS 9',
failure_scenario: Any consumer that compares a detected OS string against `SupportOS.WATCHOS_10` matches devices running watchOS 9 and misses watchOS 10, inverting platform gating. `SupportOS.WINDOWS_11 === 'Windows 10 Pro'` similarly never matches a Windows 11 string.
recommendation: Swap the two watchOS values and correct `WINDOWS_11` to `'Windows 11'`.

title: TuffTransportError.fromJSON drops the original timestamp
summary: `toJSON` serializes `timestamp`, but `fromJSON` never restores it - the constructor unconditionally overwrites `this.timestamp` with `Date.now()` at reconstruction time.
failure_scenario: A renderer rehydrates an IPC-transported error to correlate it with a main-process log line. `err.timestamp` reads as the deserialization time rather than the moment the failure occurred, so the timestamps never line up and the round-trip is not lossless as `toJSON`/`fromJSON` imply.
recommendation: Assign `error.timestamp` from `obj.timestamp` when it is a finite number.

title: Plugin prelude channel always replies undefined, discarding every handler return value
summary: The injected prelude's `__dispatch` calls the listener and then unconditionally replies `undefined`, unlike the sibling `plugin/channel.ts` implementation which replies with the handler's result.
evidence:
func(handInData);
        handInData.reply(DataCode.SUCCESS, undefined);
failure_scenario: A Prelude script registers `$channel.regChannel('get-config', () => ({ theme: 'dark' }))`. The main process awaits the reply and receives `undefined` instead of the config object, so any main-side feature that round-trips a value through a prelude handler silently reads undefined.
recommendation: Capture `const res = func(handInData)` and reply with it (awaiting when it is a promise), matching `plugin/channel.ts`.

title: Plugin prelude accepts channel messages whose header has no uniqueKey
summary: The prelude validates `header.uniqueKey` against the injected key, but a message with no `uniqueKey` at all only logs a warning and is then processed normally. Only a mismatched key is rejected.
failure_scenario: Any code able to emit on the shared `@plugin-process-message` IPC channel omits `header.uniqueKey` and its payload is dispatched to this plugin's registered handlers. The key check that is the plugin channel's isolation boundary is bypassed by simply not supplying a key.
recommendation: Treat a missing `uniqueKey` the same as a mismatch: log and `return null`.

title: Plugin prelude earlyMessageQueue grows without bound when no listener registers
summary: Messages arriving for an event with no registered listener are pushed into `earlyMessageQueue` indefinitely. The queue is only drained by a matching `regChannel` call and has no size or age cap.
failure_scenario: A plugin never registers a handler for a broadcast event the main process emits on every search keystroke. Each keystroke appends an entry (holding the full `rawData` plus the IpcRendererEvent) to the queue, so a long session grows the plugin renderer's heap without limit and never releases it.
recommendation: Cap the queue per event name and drop the oldest entries, or expire queued messages after a short window.

title: TuffPluginTransport queues unclaimed port confirms forever, pinning live MessagePorts
summary: When a confirm arrives before its `openPort` waiter, the record is stored with no expiry. The sibling renderer transport attaches a `PORT_CONFIRM_TIMEOUT_MS` timer for exactly this case and documents that omitting it pins the port for the transport's lifetime.
failure_scenario: A plugin calls `openPort` and the upgrade round-trip rejects after the main process already transferred the port. The confirm lands with no pending waiter, so the live MessagePort sits in `queuedPortConfirms` until `destroy()` - each failed open permanently leaks one native MessagePort plus its entangled main-side channel.
recommendation: Mirror the renderer transport: attach a timeout that closes the port and sends `port.close` with reason `confirm_unclaimed`.

title: TuffPluginTransport.abandonedPorts is an unbounded Set with no eviction
summary: Every port-confirm timeout adds a portId to `abandonedPorts`, which is only cleared in `destroy()`. The renderer transport uses a Map with age and count bounds and explains why unbounded retention is wrong.
evidence: private abandonedPorts = new Set<string>()
failure_scenario: A plugin repeatedly opens a port on a channel the main process rejects. Each timeout adds a permanent string entry; since a confirm can never arrive once the main side has reaped the record, the set only ever grows across a long-running plugin session.
recommendation: Use the bounded Map-with-expiry approach already implemented in `renderer-transport.ts` (`ABANDONED_PORT_RETENTION_MS` / `ABANDONED_PORT_MAX_ENTRIES`).

title: TuffPluginTransport.destroy() leaves every on() channel registration attached
summary: `on()` creates `cleanupChannel` and returns it to the caller without storing it. `destroy()` clears only the `handlers` map, so the underlying `onMain`/`regChannel` registrations keep firing the original handlers after teardown.
evidence:
this.streamControllers.clear()
    this.handlers.clear()
failure_scenario: A plugin view registers `transport.on(PluginEvents.x, handler)` and tears down with `transport.destroy()` on unload without keeping the per-handler cleanup. The channel registration survives, so `handler` continues running against a destroyed transport on every subsequent main-process message - and re-creating the transport now double-dispatches.
recommendation: Track each `cleanupChannel` in a list and invoke them all during `destroy()`.

title: TuffPluginTransport response cache collides on non-serializable payloads
summary: `buildCacheKey` degrades to `Object.prototype.toString.call(payload)` whenever `JSON.stringify` throws, so all circular payloads for one event share a single cache entry.
failure_scenario: A plugin issues two cached sends on the same event with different circular request objects. Both hash to `"<event>:[object Object]"`, so the second call returns the first request's response without ever contacting the main process.
recommendation: Skip caching entirely when the payload cannot be serialized rather than falling back to a type-only key.

title: LoggerManager mutates the shared DEFAULT_CONFIG.modules object, so reset() never resets
summary: `{ ...DEFAULT_CONFIG }` is a shallow copy, so `config.modules` aliases the module-level `DEFAULT_CONFIG.modules`. `setModuleConfig` writes into that shared object, permanently polluting the defaults.
evidence: private config: LoggingConfig = { ...DEFAULT_CONFIG }
failure_scenario: A consumer calls `loggerManager.setModuleConfig('database', false, LogLevel.ERROR)` then `loggerManager.reset()` to restore defaults. `reset()` re-spreads `DEFAULT_CONFIG`, whose `modules` object still holds the `database` override, so the logger stays disabled and there is no way to get back to a clean state.
recommendation: Deep-clone the defaults: `{ ...DEFAULT_CONFIG, modules: {} }` in both the field initializer and `reset()`.

title: Per-module log level cannot be more verbose than the global level and is silently reverted
summary: `LogLevel` is ordered DEBUG=0 .. ERROR=3, so `Math.max(globalLevel, moduleLevel)` always selects the more restrictive level. `setModuleConfig` bypasses this and calls `logger.setLevel(level)` directly, but any later `applyConfig()` recomputes with `Math.max` and discards the override.
failure_scenario: With `globalLevel: 'warn'`, a developer calls `setModuleConfig('search-engine', true, LogLevel.DEBUG)` to debug one module. It works until the next `setConfig()` or `loadConfig()`, at which point `applyConfig` computes `Math.max(WARN, DEBUG) = WARN` and the module's debug output disappears with no warning.
recommendation: Let an explicit per-module level win outright instead of clamping it to the global level with `Math.max`.

title: TouchStorage logs an app-specific 'background.source' debug line on every hydrate and save
summary: Three unconditional `console.debug` calls in the generic, published `TouchStorage` class probe a hardcoded `(data as any)?.background?.source` field that belongs to one specific app store.
evidence: console.debug(`[TouchStorage] HYDRATE("${this.#qualifiedName}") remote version=${versionedResult.version}, background.source=`, (remoteData as any)?.background?.source)
failure_scenario: An external plugin creates a `TouchStorage('my-plugin-state', {...})` with autosave. Every keystroke-driven save prints `background.source= undefined` to the plugin's console, flooding devtools with debug output the consumer cannot disable and cannot interpret.
recommendation: Remove the debug lines or route them through the module logger at debug level.

title: Stream error delivered on the data channel never cleans up, leaking the stream registration
summary: The channel-path `data` handler reports an error and returns without calling `cleanup()`, unlike the dedicated error handler at line 215 and the MessagePort path at line 136 which both clean up.
