recommendation: Give the checked star `tabindex="0"` and the rest `tabindex="-1"`, and handle ArrowLeft/ArrowRight/Home/End on the group to move and commit the selection.

title: TxTabs tablist lacks roving tabindex, arrow keys and aria-controls/labelledby wiring
summary: TxTabs renders `role="tablist"`, `role="tab"` and `role="tabpanel"` with `aria-selected`, but there is no keydown handler in the whole `tabs/` directory, no tabindex management, and no id/`aria-controls`/`aria-labelledby` relationship between a tab and its panel.
evidence:
<button
  type="button"
  class="tx-tab-item fake-background"
  role="tab"
  :aria-selected="active"
  :class="{ 'is-active': active, 'is-disabled': disabled }"
  :disabled="disabled"
  @click="handleClick"
>
failure_scenario: A settings page uses TxTabs with eight tabs. Because each tab is a default-tabindex `<button>`, a keyboard user must press Tab eight times to walk past the tab strip to reach the panel, instead of the single tab stop the ARIA tabs pattern specifies. ArrowRight/ArrowLeft/Home/End do nothing (`grep -n 'keydown' tabs/src/*.vue` returns nothing). And because the `role="tabpanel"` div carries no `id` and the tabs carry no `aria-controls`, a screen reader announces the selected tab without being able to move to the region it controls.
recommendation: Add roving tabindex on the tab buttons, ArrowLeft/ArrowRight/Home/End handling on the tablist, and pair generated ids via `aria-controls` on each tab and `aria-labelledby` on the tabpanel.

title: Global install() calls app.use() on every export, including injection-key symbols and composables
summary: `install` iterates the whole `./components` namespace and passes each value to `app.use()`. That namespace is `export * from './<name>/index'` for all 129 components, so it also contains injection-key symbols and plain helper functions — neither of which is a Vue plugin.
failure_scenario: An app does `app.use(Tuffex)` (the documented global-registration path). Vue's `app.use` sees `SELECT_KEY`, `FLAT_SELECT_KEY`, `FLAT_RADIO_KEY` and `ORB_STATES` are neither functions nor objects with `install`, and logs 'A plugin must either be a function or an object with an "install" function.' for each. Worse, `isFunction(plugin)` is true for the exported helpers `useStickToBottom`, `createPositionCache`, `createBlockStream`, `shouldRenderSvgAsMask`, `formatSize` and `asTrustedDialogHtml`, so Vue invokes each of them as an install function with the App instance as their first argument — e.g. `createPositionCache(app)` builds a position cache seeded with an App object.
recommendation: Filter the loop to plugin-shaped values (`typeof v === 'function' || (v && typeof v.install === 'function')`), or maintain an explicit component list for install instead of reusing the type/value barrel.

title: TxCollapse in accordion mode emits an empty array where its model is a string
summary: In accordion mode the model is a single panel name (a string), but `setActiveNames` emits `[]` — an array — whenever the list is empty. Collapsing the open panel therefore changes the v-model's runtime type from string to array.
evidence:
function setActiveNames(names: string[]) {
  activeNames.value = names

  const first = names[0]
  const emitValue: string | string[] = props.accordion
    ? (first !== undefined ? first : [])
    : names

  emit('update:modelValue', emitValue)
  emit('change', emitValue)
}
failure_scenario: A settings page uses `<TxCollapse accordion v-model="openPanel" />` with `const openPanel = ref('general')`. The user opens 'advanced' (openPanel becomes the string 'advanced'), then clicks it again to collapse it. `handleItemClick` calls `setActiveNames([])`, `first` is undefined, and the component emits `[]` — so `openPanel.value` is now an empty array. Any parent code doing `openPanel.value === ''`, `openPanel.value.startsWith(...)` or persisting it to storage as a string now misbehaves, and the `change` listener receives a type it was never typed for at the call site.
recommendation: Emit `''` instead of `[]` in accordion mode so the model keeps a stable string type.

title: TxMarkdownView auto theme reads <body> but only observes documentElement
summary: `resolveAutoTheme()` checks `data-theme`, `.dark` and `.light` on both `documentElement` and `body`, but `setupThemeObserver()` observes only `documentElement` with no `subtree`. The sibling TxMarkdownEditor observes both and carries a comment stating the read surface and watched surface must match.
failure_scenario: An app that toggles dark mode with `document.body.classList.toggle('dark')` renders `<TxMarkdownView theme="auto" />`. The first paint is correct because `onMounted` calls `syncAutoTheme()` directly, but every later toggle is invisible to the observer, so the rendered markdown keeps the previous theme's colours against the newly switched page background. TxMarkdownEditor already fixes this with `if (document.body) themeObserver.observe(document.body, observerInit)`.
recommendation: Observe `document.body` alongside `documentElement`, mirroring TxMarkdownEditor's `setupThemeObserver`.

title: TxPopperDialog hardcodes DOM ids, breaking aria wiring when two dialogs coexist
summary: The title and content elements use literal ids `tx-popper-dialog-title` / `tx-popper-dialog-content` and `aria-labelledby`/`aria-describedby` point at those literals. Its two sibling dialogs (TxBlowDialog, TxTouchTip) both use `useId()` for the same job.
evidence:
:aria-labelledby="title ? 'tx-popper-dialog-title' : undefined" :aria-describedby="message || messageHtml ? 'tx-popper-dialog-content' : undefined" ...

...
failure_scenario: Two TxPopperDialogs are on screen at once (a confirm raised from inside an already-open dialog, or one closing with its exit transition still running while the next opens). Both teleport to `<body>`, producing two elements with id `tx-popper-dialog-title` and two with `tx-popper-dialog-content`. `getElementById` resolves to the first, so the second dialog's `aria-labelledby`/`aria-describedby` announce the first dialog's title and message to screen-reader users.
recommendation: Replace the literals with `useId()` values, matching TxBlowDialog (`const titleId = useId(); const contentId = useId()`).

title: z-index manager keeps module-level mutable state, leaking across SSR requests
summary: The allocator's counter lives in a module-scope object. In a Node SSR process that module is instantiated once and shared by every request, so one request's overlay allocation changes the z-index every later request renders — and the value the client computes on a cold load never matches.
evidence:
const state: ZIndexState = {
  seed: DEFAULT_Z_INDEX_SEED,
  current: DEFAULT_Z_INDEX_SEED,
  overrides: null,
  seedSource: null,
  seedSourceUnsubscribe: null,
  listeners: new Set(),
}
failure_scenario: apps/nexus runs with `ssr: ssrEnabled` (true in prod). Eleven components call `ref(getZIndex())` during setup — TxDrawer, TxModal, TxBaseAnchor, TxCommandPalette, TxFlipOverlay, TxPicker, TxLoadingOverlay and the four dialogs — and serialize the result into an inline `style`. TxDrawer's `watch(() => props.visible, ..., { immediate: true })` additionally runs `refreshZIndex(DRAWER_Z_INDEX_SEED)` then `nextZIndex()` during setup, so SSR-rendering a drawer with `visible: true` permanently moves the shared `state.current` to 10001 for every subsequent request handled by that process. The next request's TxModal then SSRs `style="z-index:10001"` while the freshly-loaded client module starts at 2000, producing a hydration mismatch on the style attribute.
recommendation: Scope the state per app instance (e.g. a Vue plugin providing the allocator, or an `app.runWithContext`-bound store) instead of a module singleton, or reset it per SSR request.

title: TxIcon SVG fetch has no request-token guard, so a stale icon can win the race
summary: `fetchSvg` awaits the injected fetcher and assigns the result unconditionally. Nothing records which request is current, so when the icon url changes while a fetch is in flight the later-resolving response overwrites the newer one. Sibling components TxCodeBlock and TxMermaidBlock both implement exactly this guard.
failure_scenario: A row in a list renders `<TxIcon :icon="{ type: 'url', value: row.iconUrl }" />` in theme-color mode (so `shouldInspectSvgColor` is true and the fetch path runs). The user scrolls or filters, the icon url changes from A to B, and the watcher fires `fetchSvg(B)` while `fetchSvg(A)` is still in flight. If A's fetcher resolves last, `svgContent` ends up holding icon A's markup while every other binding (`resolvedUrl`, the mask style) points at B — the mask is cut from the wrong glyph and stays wrong until the next url change.
recommendation: Add a `let requestToken = 0` / `const token = ++requestToken` guard and drop the assignment when `token !== requestToken`, matching TxCodeBlock's `runHighlight`.

title: TxMessageActions declares role="toolbar" with no accessible name and no arrow-key navigation
summary: The wrapper takes `role="toolbar"` but carries no `aria-label`/`aria-labelledby` and the component binds no keydown handler, so it satisfies neither half of the ARIA toolbar contract (named grouping plus single tab stop with arrow-key movement).
evidence:
<div class="tx-message-actions" :class="{ 'has-appear': appear }" role="toolbar">
  <button
    v-if="copyText !== undefined"
    type="button"
    class="tx-message-actions__btn"
    ...
failure_scenario: Every assistant message in a chat transcript renders a TxMessageActions row. A screen-reader user moving through the transcript hears an unlabelled 'toolbar' after each message with no way to tell one from another, and because the buttons keep their default tabindex the toolbar adds two or more tab stops per message — a 30-message conversation becomes 60+ extra tab stops instead of the 30 the toolbar role promises. Arrow keys, which assistive tech announces as the way to move within a toolbar, do nothing.
recommendation: Add an `aria-label` prop (defaulting to something like 'Message actions', consistent with the component's existing text-prop localization convention) and implement roving tabindex with ArrowLeft/ArrowRight handling, or drop `role="toolbar"` and let the buttons stand alone.
